research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for geospatial and geophysical prediction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Diana develops and evaluates machine learning approaches tailored to geospatial and geophysical datasets to produce robust maps and uncertainty-aware predictions. She applies supervised methods (random forests, artificial neural networks) and unsupervised techniques (DBSCAN, MCLUST) to fuse heterogeneous covariates and to identify patterns in peatland structure. A current focal point is Bayesian neural networks to quantify predictive uncertainty and support decision‑sensitive mapping of peat thickness, carbon stocks and greenhouse gas implications. Diana investigates ensemble and non‑linear models versus linear baselines, optimal covariate selection, cross‑validation and spatially aware validation procedures, and sampling‑size effects. Her work emphasizes reproducible workflows and interpretable ML outputs so that modelled products are actionable for monitoring, field planning and downstream policy reporting.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Sensor fusion and on‑the‑go geophysical workflows
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Diana researches practical sensor hierarchies and fusion strategies that combine proximal and airborne datasets (gamma‑ray spectrometry, electromagnetic induction, ground‑penetrating radar, transient EM and LiDAR) to map and monitor peatland properties. She evaluates which sensors perform best under differing peatland conditions—e.g., GR for rapid extent delineation and drone‑borne surveys, EMI for minerotrophic fens and as a predictor of GPR suitability, and GPR for thick, resistive bogs—and develops decision rules for integrated survey design. Her methodological contributions include workflows for continuous, on‑the‑go surveys, protocols for co‑registered multi‑sensor data, and strategies to translate geophysical signals into geologically meaningful predictors for statistical models and maps used in restoration planning.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Peatland carbon, subsidence monitoring and policy translation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Diana focuses on quantifying long‑term peatland subsidence, carbon losses and greenhouse‑gas consequences to inform restoration and national inventory efforts. She combines historical analyses, field campaigns and modelled spatial products to estimate carbon stocks, emission trajectories and the impacts of land‑use and management. Her research develops robust sampling and validation procedures and demonstrates how to translate geophysical and statistical outputs into policy‑relevant metrics and reporting formats. Diana emphasizes practical tools for land managers—such as soil‑functional maps, monitoring designs, and emission reporting workflows—that support restoration prioritization, climate mitigation strategies and evidence‑based policy decisions at local and national scales.

Contributions.Title: [Remote] Delineation of peatland areas based on drone-borne radiometric surveys and unsupervised machine learning

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning Foundations for Experimental Biophysics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Noah seeks a comprehensive grounding in machine learning concepts tailored to experimental biophysics. As a relative novice, he wants practical exposure to supervised and unsupervised methods, model selection, cross-validation, and best practices for avoiding overfitting in small experimental datasets. Noah is particularly interested in understanding how statistical learning and probabilistic modeling can be integrated with physical intuition from biophysics experiments, how to interpret model outputs in the context of measurement uncertainty, and how to ensure reproducibility and rigorous evaluation. He aims to leave with hands-on skills to build, train, and validate models that directly support experimental decision-making and hypothesis testing in single-molecule biosensing workflows.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Image Analysis & Computer Vision for Single-Molecule Biosensing
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Noah focuses on image analysis pipelines that extract quantitative information from microscopy data of single-molecule and nanowire biosensing experiments. He is interested in methods for denoising, segmentation, single-particle localization, tracking, and feature extraction that are robust to low signal-to-noise ratios and varying experimental conditions. Noah wants to learn how to prepare and augment training datasets, apply convolutional neural networks and transfer learning, and implement evaluation metrics relevant to localization accuracy and detection sensitivity. He also values interpretable approaches that link image-derived features back to physical events at the sensor surface and practical workflows for deploying these analyses in routine experimental pipelines.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Signal Processing and Time-Series ML for Nanowire Sensors
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Noah is interested in advanced signal processing and time-series machine learning techniques for electrical readouts from nanowire-based single-molecule sensors. His priorities include noise reduction, baseline drift correction, event detection, classification of transient signatures, and extraction of kinetic parameters from noisy traces. Noah wants to explore classical DSP approaches alongside deep-learning architectures (e.g., CNNs for waveform patterns, RNNs/transformers for temporal dependencies) and techniques for real-time inference and low-latency deployment. He is keen to understand how to generate labeled training data, quantify detection limits, and combine physics-informed models with data-driven methods to improve robustness and interpretability of sensor-level analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph- and Transformer-based Materials Modeling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Dmitry is interested in developing and applying graph- and transformer-based machine learning models to relate perovskite composition, surface chemistry and superlattice structure to optoelectronic properties. Working with structured and numerical data derived from multilayer diffraction, X-ray scattering, DFT outputs and microscopy, he uses graph neural networks to represent atomistic and ligand–nanocrystal connectivity and transformers to capture long-range correlations in composition and stacking. He applies these models to predict stability, halide segregation, doping limits and emergent collective phenomena such as superradiance, and to fuse experimental and simulated datasets for improved interpretability. He also explores generative models conditioned on structural constraints to propose novel compositions, ligand motifs and superlattice architectures, with uncertainty quantification to prioritize experiments for synthesis and structural refinement.

research_interests.research_interest_title: ML for Ultrafast Spectroscopy & Exciton Dynamics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Dmitry seeks to integrate machine learning with ultrafast and time-resolved spectroscopy to extract mechanistic insight into exciton dynamics, energy transfer, and nonradiative processes in lead-halide and related perovskite nanocrystals. Using transformer architectures and sequence models tailored to 2D, pump–probe and temperature-resolved datasets, he aims to deconvolve overlapping spectral features, recover hidden state kinetics, and identify signatures of superradiance, exciton–phonon coupling and inter-nanocrystal transfer. He leverages ML-driven dimensionality reduction and latent-space modeling to compare dynamics across material compositions, ligand treatments and assembly states, and to flag anomalous aging behavior. These tools help translate complex transient datasets into physically meaningful parameters that guide synthesis, surface passivation strategies and device-relevant stability improvements.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Active Learning & Generative Design for Synthesis and Stability
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Dmitry is focused on applying active learning, closed-loop experimentation and generative design to accelerate synthesis, ligand engineering and encapsulation strategies for robust perovskite nanocrystals. He leverages quantitative assays of aqueous stability, automated polymer capsule encapsulation results and high-throughput structural readouts to train models that propose next experiments, optimize ligand formulations and predict long-term photostability. Generative models are used to suggest candidate organic ligands and composite encapsulants constrained by synthetic feasibility and surface chemistry rules; acquisition functions and uncertainty estimates prioritize experiments in the lab. By integrating experimental metadata, multilayer diffraction refinements and microscopy-derived structural descriptors, these ML workflows aim to shorten discovery cycles, improve reproducibility and produce materials with targeted optical performance for imaging and device applications.

Contributions.Title: AI/ML Impact Areas in Physics and Materials Discovery of Halide Perovskite Nanomaterials

research_interests.research_interest_title: Magnetized plasma microphysics & instabilities
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Thomas studies how kinetic plasma processes and microinstabilities shape macroscopic behaviour in astrophysical plasmas. He focuses on weakly collisional media such as the intracluster and circumgalactic media, exploring instabilities including firehose, mirror, whistler, Kelvin–Helmholtz, magnetothermal (MTI) and heat-flux-driven buoyancy (HBI). Using analytic theory and targeted simulations, Thomas examines anisotropic transport (Braginskii viscosity, suppressed thermal conduction), microscale instability closures, and how microscale regulation of heat flux can produce critical transitions that alter turbulence and magnetic-field amplification. His work aims to connect microphysical closure models to large-scale dynamics, quantify when microscale suppression quenches or enables instabilities, and provide subgrid prescriptions that capture kinetic effects in MHD models while remaining computationally tractable for galaxy- and cluster-scale studies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: High-performance simulation methods & reproducible code
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Thomas develops and applies high-resolution numerical tools to probe nonlinear plasma and fluid dynamics, emphasizing reproducibility and open science. He contributes modules and testbeds (Psecas, Paicos, Arepo modules) and validates algorithms through analytic wave solutions and convergence studies. His interests cover Vlasov-fluid hybrids, Braginskii MHD implementations, and strategies for resolving multiscale interactions between microscale instabilities and macroscale flows. Thomas also focuses on computational best practices: public code release, rigorous validation, and synthetic diagnostics that connect simulations to observations. By combining scalable HPC techniques with carefully designed numerical experiments, he seeks to enable robust, community-useable tools that let other researchers reproduce results and integrate kinetic-aware subgrid physics into large-scale astrophysical simulations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for simulations, diagnostics & discovery
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Thomas is keen to learn how machine learning is being applied across astrophysics and computational plasma physics and to explore practical ways ML can augment his workflow. Although he currently has no ML project, he is interested in surrogate models and emulators for expensive kinetic simulations, ML-based closure models for unresolved microscale physics, automated feature extraction from large simulation outputs, and learned synthetic-diagnostic pipelines that map simulation states to observational signatures. He is also curious about uncertainty-aware ML methods and active-learning strategies to guide expensive simulation campaigns. Through the workshop he aims to identify ML methods and collaborations that can be realistically integrated into his reproducible-code ethos and HPC workflows to accelerate discovery without compromising physical interpretability.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Polymer Topology and Knot Sampling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jonas focuses on the statistical physics of polymers where topology — knots, braids and links — crucially shapes material and dynamical properties. He develops computational and theoretical tools to generate and characterise knotted configurations, combining braid-theoretic invariants (e.g. Jones polynomials) with physically informed measures of entanglement and aggregation transitions. A central challenge is efficient sampling of rare, highly knotted states in high-dimensional polymer configuration spaces; Jonas is interested in algorithmic advances that respect topological constraints and produce unbiased ensembles. Although he does not currently work in machine learning, he is actively seeking collaborations with ML researchers (notably those experienced with generative flow methods such as GFlowNets) to design proposal distributions, topology-aware moves, and validation benchmarks that accelerate exploration of knot space while preserving thermodynamic fidelity.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Non-equilibrium Statistical Physics and Active Matter
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jonas studies non-equilibrium phenomena in soft and active systems, with emphasis on minimal scalar models, interacting run-and-tumble particles, and mechanisms that yield collective condensation and anomalous transport. His work has revealed Bose–Einstein–like and reentrant condensation transitions, strong deviations from Gaussian tagged-particle dynamics, and novel steady states driven by diffusivity edges and activity. He combines analytic iteration methods with numerical simulations to probe how microscopic activity, interactions and constraints produce macroscopic phases and dynamical heterogeneity. Jonas is interested in bridging theory and experiment, developing reduced models for emergent behaviour, and exploring how topology and interactions modify standard non-equilibrium universality classes in active matter and soft condensed systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Analytic & Computational Methods for Nonlinear Dynamics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jonas develops and extends analytic-computational frameworks for nonlinear ODEs and PDEs, notably the BLUES (Beyond Linear Use of Equation Superposition) function method, convergence-acceleration strategies, and matrix formulations that handle second-order time derivatives and hybrid models. He applies these tools to wavefronts, telegrapher and interface-growth (Burgers–KPZ hybrid) problems, epidemics, heat transfer, dune formation and option-pricing (Black–Scholes), and benchmarks them against ADM, VIM and perturbation theory. Beyond closed-form iteration schemes, Jonas explores numerical validation, multi-function optimisation and principled approximations that improve convergence and stability. He also investigates stochastic thermodynamics applications — universal Fano-factor bounds, Pareto-optimal trade-offs and information–dissipation relations — and seeks collaborators to translate analytical advances into robust, scalable algorithms.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative Machine Learning for Event Generation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christian explores the use of generative neural networks as novel engines for particle-level event generation and for augmenting traditional Monte Carlo simulations. He investigates normalizing flows, autoregressive models and bespoke architectures such as HOMER to learn hadronization patterns and produce ML-driven particle showers that can be interfaced with or reweighted against established generators. His work emphasizes rigorous validation, uncertainty-aware reweighting and curated MLHAD datasets so that learned models can be compared to physics-driven alternatives. Christian is particularly interested in hybrid workflows where generative models either replace expensive subcomponents, accelerate sampling, or provide differentiable surrogates that preserve interpretability and control over systematic variations relevant for collider analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Microscopic String Models and Hadronization
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christian develops and applies microscopic, string-based descriptions of hadronization and collective effects to explain baryon and strangeness enhancement as well as flow-like signals in small and large collision systems. He implements mechanisms such as rope hadronization, string shoving, colour reconnection and junction formation within event generators, and has led core PYTHIA 8 development including the Angantyr heavy-ion extrapolation. His modelling philosophy stresses physically transparent, non-thermalised explanations that can be tested against experimental observables, offering alternatives to a thermalised QGP. Christian couples these approaches to hadronic cascades to quantify rescattering and to provide robust hybrid baselines for spectra, elliptic flow and jet quenching studies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Open Monte Carlo Tools, Validation and Uncertainty Quantification
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christian champions reproducible Monte Carlo methodology, modular publicly released code and community validation frameworks. He contributes extensive tooling — from PYTHIA extensions and PISTA for heavy-ion event construction to Rivet analyses and automated fragmentation variations — that enable systematic tuning, validation and propagation of uncertainties. He couples event generators to hadronic transport (UrQMD) and develops uncertainty-aware reweighting schemes and automated variations to produce defensible theory baselines. Christian prioritises datasets, software and workflows that allow other researchers to reproduce, validate and extend results, preparing the community for precision studies in electron–ion and future collider environments while facilitating outreach and broader adoption of robust simulation practices.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Image Segmentation with U‑Nets
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jack focuses on developing and adapting U‑Net architectures for high-quality image segmentation problems. He investigates encoder–decoder backbones, skip‑connection strategies and multi‑scale feature aggregation to improve boundary delineation and small‑object detection. Jack experiments with loss formulations tailored to imbalanced segmentation tasks (Dice, focal, boundary losses), explores regularization and fine‑tuning strategies for limited labeled data, and evaluates performance using IoU, Dice score and calibration metrics. He also considers practical deployment aspects such as inference speed, model compression and uncertainty estimation for segmentation outputs. Jack’s approach bridges architectural design, training protocol and post‑processing to produce reliable segmentation maps for scientific and engineering imaging pipelines.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Data Augmentation and Robust Training
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jack studies data augmentation strategies to improve model generalization and robustness, particularly for scarce or noisy datasets. He evaluates classical geometric and photometric transforms alongside advanced methods such as synthetic data generation, domain randomization and generative adversarial approaches. Jack is interested in automated augmentation policies (e.g., AutoAugment), mixing techniques (MixUp, CutMix) and task‑aware augmentations for dense prediction problems like segmentation. He also examines the effect of augmentations on model calibration, out‑of‑distribution behavior and uncertainty estimates, and develops augmentation pipelines that balance invariance with preservation of task‑relevant structure. Jack’s work emphasizes reproducible augmentation workflows and empirical protocols to quantify how different strategies impact downstream performance and reliability.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Experimental Plasma Physics and Fusion Diagnostics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jack aims to translate his data science skills into experimental plasma physics applications, building on prior experience collecting and analyzing data from an IEC fusion reactor. He explores ML techniques for processing diagnostic data streams, including image‑based plasma diagnostics, time‑series analysis of sensor signals and sensor fusion across heterogeneous instruments. Jack is interested in anomaly detection, real‑time inference for experiment control, predictive maintenance for hardware, and physics‑aware models that incorporate constraints or surrogate models to respect domain knowledge. He also investigates domain adaptation and transfer learning to move models trained on simulated data into real experimental settings. Ultimately, Jack seeks to bridge computer science methods and laboratory practice to deliver tools that accelerate experimental insight and support careers at the intersection of data science and plasma physics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Physics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Raphael focuses on developing interpretable and trustworthy machine learning methods tailored for physics applications. He is interested in model-agnostic explanation techniques, feature-attribution and saliency methods, surrogate models, and causal approaches that reveal how predictions relate to physical inputs and uncertainties. Raphael emphasizes the need for uncertainty-aware explanations, robustness to dataset shifts, and methods that integrate domain knowledge so that outputs remain physically meaningful. Practical goals include building transparent pipelines for detector diagnostics, bias identification, and model validation that enable physicists to inspect, debug, and trust ML-driven results. Raphael also explores visualization and human-centered tools that make complex model behaviour accessible to experimental collaborators, facilitating adoption of ML in high-stakes analyses where interpretability and accountability are essential.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neutrino and Astrophysical Transient Searches
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Raphael is interested in applying machine learning to neutrino physics and searches for astrophysical transients such as supernovae. His work targets real-time detection pipelines that can isolate low-significance, time-correlated signals from high-rate backgrounds in noisy detector data. Raphael explores time-series classification, anomaly detection, denoising, and domain-adaptive algorithms to improve sensitivity to burst-like events, while maintaining control of false alarms for prompt multi-messenger alerts. He also investigates simulation-to-real transfer, generative models for rare signal augmentation, and interpretable selection criteria to ensure discoveries are physically credible. A major aim is to bridge instrumentation, theory, and ML tools so that neutrino detectors and multi-messenger networks can rapidly and reliably identify and characterize astrophysical transients.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning Across High-Energy Physics (LHC & Beyond)
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Raphael seeks to explore and compare machine learning applications across collider and astroparticle experiments, with particular interest in LHC physics. He studies ML-driven approaches for event reconstruction, particle identification, anomaly detection, and fast simulation that scale to the large datasets and high-throughput environments of modern experiments. Raphael is keen on cross-pollinating methods between collider and neutrino/astrophysical communities—transferring domain adaptation, unsupervised discovery, and calibration techniques to shared challenges. He prioritizes reproducible benchmarks and interpretable workflows that allow experimentalists to evaluate performance, systematic uncertainties, and robustness. Ultimately, Raphael aims to identify versatile ML components that accelerate discovery across HEP subfields while ensuring results remain physically transparent and experimentally deployable.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Model-based reinforcement learning and regret minimization
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hippolyte studies model-based reinforcement learning with a focus on rigorous regret minimization under the average-reward criterion. His work tightens exploration by integrating modern time-uniform and variance-aware concentration inequalities into UCRL-style algorithms, redesigning extended value iteration to ignore low-probability transitions and introducing UCRL3. He formally characterizes problem-dependent quantities such as local diameter and local effective support, and proves stronger high-probability and non-asymptotic regret bounds while demonstrating substantial empirical speedups. Hippolyte balances theory and practice: he derives matching lower bounds, evaluates algorithms on standard benchmarks, and emphasizes designs that are computationally efficient and robust to sparse transitions. This interest centers on principled, model-based techniques that yield provable performance guarantees in unknown decision processes, especially where average reward and long-run behavior matter.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Structure discovery and equivalence-aware learning
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hippolyte explores how structural priors and state-action equivalences can be discovered and exploited to accelerate learning in sequential decision problems. He formalizes state-action similarity notions to build equivalence-aware confidence sets and proposes algorithms such as ApproxEquivalence and C-UCRL to automatically identify latent classes. When C equivalence classes exist, his methods provably reduce regret by roughly a factor of sqrt(SA/C), and they remain effective when class membership must be estimated online. His research blends algorithm design, statistical concentration (variance-aware) and support estimation to adaptively ignore irrelevant transitions and aggregate information across similar contexts. Hippolyte is particularly interested in approaches that combine theoretical guarantees with scalable procedures for model selection and structure learning in practical RL settings.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning applications for experimental condensed matter
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hippolyte is keen to connect his ML and RL expertise with experimental condensed matter physics. As he begins a postdoc collaborating with experimental groups, he wants to learn which ML approaches—bandit strategies, reinforcement learning controllers, clustering, and supervised models—are already impactful in lab workflows and where theory informs practice. He is interested in adaptive experimentation (online bandits and RL for automated measurement or control), data-driven analysis pipelines (clustering and supervised learning for feature discovery), and how structural priors or reward-machine abstractions can encode high-level experimental tasks. Hippolyte seeks transferable methodologies that respect experimental constraints (noise, cost, sparse data) and that leverage provable guarantees to make automated experimental design and control reliably practical.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics‑Informed & Data‑Driven Neural Networks
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jan-Matthias develops and applies data-driven and physics-informed artificial neural networks to bridge empirical observations and mechanistic models. He focuses on architectures that embed conservation laws, symmetries, and known differential operators into learning pipelines to improve generalization from limited or noisy experimental data. His work spans custom LSTM nodes, autoencoder graphs and hybrid models that combine domain priors with flexible function approximators, emphasizing interpretability and computational efficiency for deployment on low-power hardware. Jan-Matthias also investigates robust training strategies, uncertainty quantification, and explainable components to ensure that learned representations remain physically plausible and actionable for downstream tasks such as prediction, state estimation, and control in complex physical systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Plasma Physics Modeling & ML‑Enhanced Diagnostics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jan-Matthias pursues research at the intersection of plasma physics and machine learning, aiming to accelerate modeling and improve diagnostic interpretation. He studies kinetic and fluid descriptions of plasmas and uses ML tools to extract patterns from experimental and simulated datasets, enabling faster surrogate models, parameter inference, and anomaly detection. His approach emphasizes physically consistent surrogates that respect conserved quantities and known instabilities, while remaining efficient enough for real‑time analysis and control. He also explores hardware‑aware implementations—mapping ML-enabled diagnostics and decoders to FPGA and embedded platforms—to support deployable sensors and feedback systems in laboratory and industrial plasma applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Chaos, Nonlinear Dynamics & Predictive Control
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jan-Matthias investigates chaotic and nonlinear dynamical systems with the dual goals of understanding fundamental behavior and enabling reliable prediction and control. He develops methods to reconstruct attractors, quantify sensitivity to initial conditions, and design reduced-order models that retain essential nonlinear features. Combining ideas from dynamical systems theory with modern machine learning, he creates predictors and controllers that are robust to noise and model uncertainty, and that can operate on limited observational data. A strong emphasis on translational impact leads him to craft embedded, energy-efficient implementations for real‑time monitoring, adaptive control, and decision support in systems exhibiting complex spatiotemporal dynamics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative and diffusion models for biomedical imaging
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Nuno explores advances in generative and foundation models—with special focus on diffusion models—to synthesize, denoise and enhance biomedical images. Nuno develops probabilistic sampling schemes and architecturally specialized U‑Net backbones that leverage recent progress in score‑based and latent diffusion to produce high‑fidelity, uncertainty‑aware reconstructions. He studies adversarial training and likelihood‑based objectives to balance realism and calibration, and evaluates how foundation‑model pretraining and fine‑tuning improve transfer across heterogeneous ophthalmic datasets. Nuno also investigates methods to quantify and visualize epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty from generative pipelines, and to integrate conditioning signals (optical parameters, acquisition metadata) to control synthesis. The goal is reliable generative tools that assist clinicians, improve downstream analysis, and provide interpretable uncertainty for safe deployment.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics‑informed models of corneal optics and light scattering
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Nuno works at the interface of machine learning, optics and biophysics to create physics‑informed models of corneal transparency and light scattering. Nuno combines forward physical models of beam propagation and scattering with data‑driven neural surrogates and physics‑informed neural networks (PINNs) to build hybrid models that respect conservation laws and known optical constraints. By embedding scattering theory, refractive index heterogeneity and optical priors into architectures and loss functions, Nuno enhances interpretability, robustness and extrapolative behavior beyond available training images. These hybrid models enable mechanistic parameter estimation, hypothesis testing about tissue microstructure, and diagnostic indices directly linked to physical optical properties. Nuno aims to translate such models into clinically actionable metrics while maintaining rigorous uncertainty quantification and validation against experimental measurements.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Segmentation, denoising and super‑resolution for ophthalmic imaging
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Nuno develops and refines image segmentation, denoising and super‑resolution methods tailored to ophthalmic imaging, with particular emphasis on corneal layer segmentation using U‑Net architectures. Nuno integrates diffusion‑based denoisers and GAN‑driven super‑resolution pipelines to recover microstructural detail while preserving clinically relevant contrasts. He emphasizes interpretability and robustness by designing loss functions, uncertainty estimation and explainable failure modes that yield calibrated segmentation maps and reliable outputs across devices. Nuno also pursues domain adaptation and annotation‑efficient training to reduce labeling burden and improve generalization to diverse clinical settings. His work is evaluated with rigorous cross‑validation, clinically oriented metrics and ablation studies to ensure reproducibility, translational readiness and practical utility for early detection of transparency impairments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for lattice quantum field theory
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Pietro develops machine-learning tools tailored to nonperturbative quantum field theory on the lattice, combining dynamical Monte Carlo simulations with representation learning. He employs autoencoders and normalizing flows to discover compact, interpretable latent coordinates that capture collective modes and long-range correlations, and to build learned generative models that accelerate sampling and reduce critical slowing down. His work connects rigorous scale-setting and continuum extrapolation techniques from lattice studies with ML-driven variance reduction, reweighting, and surrogate-modeling strategies, aiming to extract effective degrees of freedom that respect symmetries and topological structure. Pietro is particularly interested in methods that maintain control over systematic errors so that ML-augmented calculations can provide trustworthy, physics-aware predictions for strongly interacting gauge theories.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Latent-space dynamics and forecasting with neural ODEs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Pietro focuses on learning and forecasting latent dynamics from high-dimensional simulation and observational data using RNNs, neural ODEs and stochastic neural ODEs. He seeks compact latent descriptions where slow, emergent variables evolve according to low-dimensional differential laws, enabling long-time prediction of transport, relaxation, and phase-evolution phenomena. By combining autoencoder encodings with deterministic or stochastic continuous-time latent integrators, Pietro studies how to capture multi-scale interactions, propagate uncertainty, and incorporate conservation laws or symmetries into the learned dynamics. He also explores renormalization-group-inspired coarse-graining in latent space to separate fast transients from relevant slow modes, producing interpretable, physically constrained forecasting models for non-equilibrium systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics-informed ML for contagion and market dynamics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Pietro applies physics-informed machine learning to problems in epidemiology and financial markets, using ideas from percolation theory, renormalization-group dynamics and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics. He models contagion as percolation-like spreading on heterogeneous networks and uses latent-space ML to infer effective transmission kernels and coarse-grained thresholds from incomplete data. In market settings he studies emergent, out-of-equilibrium phenomena—volatility clustering, liquidity crises, and cascade events—by combining stochastic latent dynamics with agent- and field-like descriptions. A major goal is to develop predictive, uncertainty-aware tools that bridge mechanistic models and data, with particular interest in health-science applications where interpretable, physics-grounded ML can inform policy or clinical decision-making. Pietro seeks collaborators applying these techniques to real-world health and socio-economic datasets.

Contributions.Title: Machine Learning and Quantum Field Theory: a two-way dialogue

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for insurance risk modeling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: William focuses on applying machine learning techniques to quantify and predict insurance risk exposure. He is interested in how supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms—such as gradient-boosted trees, deep neural networks, and clustering methods—can complement traditional actuarial models to improve pricing, reserving, and scenario analysis. William explores feature engineering tailored to policy and exposure data, model interpretability for regulatory and business transparency, and robust validation strategies specific to low-frequency, high-severity events. His work emphasizes the integration of domain knowledge from actuarial mathematics with data-driven approaches to produce calibrated risk measures that support decision-making in underwriting and capital allocation. William aims to identify thesis topics that bridge method development with practical deployment in insurance operations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Claims analytics and operational risk
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: William investigates machine learning approaches to claims analytics, with a focus on improving claims triage, cost estimation, and fraud detection. He is drawn to projects that leverage structured insurance records, text from loss descriptions, and temporal claim histories to predict claim severity, accelerate settlement, and prioritize investigations. William studies anomaly detection and sequence models to capture evolving claim trajectories, and emphasizes methods that balance predictive power with explainability for claims handlers and regulators. He is also interested in the challenges of data quality, censoring, and class imbalance common in claims datasets, and in developing workflows for model monitoring and maintenance to ensure reliable operational performance over time.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Actuarial mathematics and probabilistic foundations for ML
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: William is motivated by the intersection of classical actuarial mathematics and modern machine learning, studying how probabilistic modeling, survival analysis, and stochastic processes can inform and be informed by data-driven techniques. He explores Bayesian and frequentist frameworks for uncertainty quantification, credibility theory extensions with hierarchical models, and how loss reserving and ruin theory can be augmented by flexible function approximators while preserving theoretical guarantees. William values approaches that maintain actuarial interpretability—such as parametric-tail modeling and exposure-adjusted risk measures—while exploiting ML for pattern discovery and nonlinearity. His interest includes methodological work that can serve as a rigorous foundation for a master thesis linking actuarial theory to practical ML tools used in risk management.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Supersymmetry and Dark Matter Phenomenology
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Sascha studies supersymmetric interpretations of particle-physics observations with a strong emphasis on neutralino dark matter and global pMSSM fits. He has led profile-likelihood analyses that connect astrophysical hints — for example, the Fermi Galactic Center GeV excess — to concrete neutralino parameter regions and has explored naturalness and fine-tuning across SUSY constructions. His work spans concrete proposals for LHC search strategies and direct-detection experiments, and includes predictions for non-standard neutrino and gamma-ray spectra from annihilating dark matter. Throughout these projects Sascha emphasizes robust uncertainty quantification and model-recasting so that theoretical hypotheses can be compared to experimental constraints in a reproducible, practical way.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Collider Phenomenology and Precision QCD Modelling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Sascha focuses on reducing and quantifying theoretical uncertainties relevant for collider phenomenology, with particular attention to QCD fragmentation, parton-shower modelling and NLO effects. He has systematically studied fragmentation and shower uncertainties that impact dark-matter gamma-ray spectra and collider observables, and developed methods to make precision calculations practical for large scans and recasting. His work includes fast, frequency-correct event-generation tools and ultra-fast NLO cross-section approximations that bridge high-precision theory with the computational demands of LHC-scale analyses. Sascha aims to make theory–data comparisons at colliders more reliable by combining careful uncertainty treatment with computationally efficient implementations suitable for experimental workflows.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning Tools for Simulation, Search and Analysis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Sascha develops and benchmarks machine-learning toolchains tailored to particle and astro-particle physics problems, from deep generative models (VAEs/GANs) with density-information buffers for fast, frequency-correct event generation to transformer and graph architectures for tracking and event classification. He builds anomaly-detection frameworks — ensemble One-Class DSVD with flows, mixture-of-theories training and other approaches — and runs large public benchmarks such as the Dark Machines challenge, spanning billions of events. His ML work also covers active learning for high-dimensional parameter scans, neuromorphic energy/latency benchmarking, uncertainty-aware inference and open-source visualization and astronomy pipelines. Reproducibility, uncertainty quantification and model-independence are central to Sascha’s tool-driven approach.

research_interests.research_interest_title: X‑ray timing and spectroscopy of compact objects
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jerome leads observational studies that use X‑ray timing and spectroscopy to probe accretion onto neutron stars and black holes. He focuses on thermonuclear (Type‑I) X‑ray bursts, QPOs, energy‑dependent phase lags, and cyclotron line characterization, combining high‑time‑resolution and broadband spectral data from missions such as INTEGRAL, NuSTAR, NICER and RXTE. Jerome uses reflection modeling, burst–disk interaction analysis, and inner‑disk truncation measurements to constrain the physics of disks, boundary layers and magnetospheres, and to infer compact object properties. His work frequently couples targeted case studies with population‑scale catalogs to derive robust constraints on accretion regimes and transient behavior, emphasizing careful instrument calibration, spectral modeling, and physically motivated interpretation of timing–spectral phenomena.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transient discovery, monitoring and survey catalogs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jerome develops and exploits large survey programs and catalogs to find and monitor high‑energy transients across the Galactic Bulge and beyond. He leads efforts in long‑term monitoring (INTEGRAL Galactic Bulge program), catalog construction (MINBAR and intermediate/long burst catalogues), and coordinated multi‑mission follow‑up to characterize transient populations and evolution. Jerome blends mosaicking, pipeline development, and performance assessment of instruments to maximize sensitivity to faint or short‑lived events, and contributes to efforts to identify electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational‑wave events. He emphasizes reproducible data products and cross‑mission synthesis so that demographic inferences and rapid discovery alerts feed both targeted physical studies and broader population analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning and data mining for FITS images, time series and graphs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jerome is interested in applying ML/AI methods to astrophysical FITS data, including images, numerical tables and time series, and graph‑structured representations derived from multi‑wavelength observations. He seeks to learn and implement techniques for automated transient detection, anomaly and outlier identification, feature extraction from burst lightcurves and spectra, and graph‑based association of multi‑instrument detections. Jerome values interpretable models and robust pipelines that account for instrument systematics, heterogenous formats, and the need for reproducible catalogs. His goal is to marry domain expertise in X‑ray instrumentation and timing with modern data‑mining approaches to accelerate discovery and enable scalable analysis of large archival and survey datasets.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Super-resolution with U‑Net–style architectures for climate fields
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Clément develops and tests super-resolution methods tailored to gridded climate fields, exploiting U‑Net–like encoder–decoder architectures to reconstruct fine-scale structure from coarse model output. He is interested in architectures that preserve spatial coherence and physical balances, incorporating skip connections, multi-scale loss terms and physics‑aware regularization to prevent spurious artifacts. Clément explores training strategies that combine reanalysis, satellite retrievals and high-resolution model campaigns, and assesses temporal consistency when upscaling sequences rather than isolated snapshots. He also studies uncertainty quantification for super-resolved fields, evaluating ensemble and Bayesian variants to capture epistemic and aleatoric error. Practical challenges he targets include domain shifts between observational and modeled data, computational scalability across polar domains, and metrics that reflect scientific usefulness rather than only pixel-wise error.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative climate data and synthetic field generation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Clément investigates generative ML approaches — including GANs, variational autoencoders and normalizing flows — to create realistic synthetic climate datasets for downscaling, ensemble augmentation and process studies. He focuses on conditional generation techniques that can produce physically consistent fields given large‑scale drivers (e.g., synoptic state, boundary conditions), enabling the synthesis of plausible small‑scale variability not resolved in coarse models. A strong emphasis in his work is on injecting physical constraints (conservation, monotonicity, seasonal cycles) and on quantifying generative uncertainty so synthetic ensembles are useful for impact assessments. Clément also explores how synthetic data can be used to train emulators for expensive processes, to fill observational gaps in polar regions, and to test sensitivity of ice‑sheet surface mass balance estimates to subgrid variability.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Polar regional climate models and surface mass balance of ice sheets
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Clément works at the intersection of polar regional climate modelling and glaciological surface mass balance (SMB) studies. He investigates the processes that determine accumulation and melt over Greenland and Antarctica — including orographic precipitation, wind‑driven redistribution, radiative fluxes and melt–refreeze cycles — and how regional climate models represent them at high latitudes. He is interested in coupling detailed SMB process understanding with model evaluation against sparse in situ and remote observations, and in developing ML‑based surrogates to accelerate SMB estimation for long ensembles and sensitivity experiments. Clément is also concerned with the propagation of climate model biases into sea‑level projections, developing strategies for bias correction, downscaling and robust uncertainty characterization specifically targeted to polar climates.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph Neural Networks for Structured Experimental Data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel explores Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) as a natural framework for his large, somewhat structured experimental datasets. He is interested in representing instruments, sample environments, and measurement chains as graphs where nodes encode components or measurement sites and edges encode physical relationships or signal flow. Daniel aims to use GNNs not merely to classify or cluster observations but to learn relational patterns that reveal how measurements arise from underlying instrument configurations and sample conditions. His interests include transfer learning across beamlines, interpretable node- and edge-level attributions, and uncertainty-aware GNNs that can flag anomalous configurations or suggest targeted additional measurements. He also considers hybrid approaches that combine physics-based simulation priors with learned graph representations to improve generalization across experimental setups.

research_interests.research_interest_title: High-fidelity Neutron Instrument and Sample Environment Simulation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel focuses on simulation of neutron scattering instruments with particular emphasis on sample environment simulations and cost-sensitive instrument design. Building on experience with McStas and with work demonstrating that piecewise linear approximations of elliptical guides can preserve transport performance for beamlines such as BIFROST, he is keen to investigate how machine learning can accelerate, compress, and differentiate these simulations. His goals include training fast surrogate models that reproduce Monte Carlo outputs, developing differentiable emulators for gradient-based design optimization, and quantifying surrogate uncertainty so that simulation-informed decisions remain robust. He is also interested in coupling detailed sample-environment models with ML surrogates to enable rapid exploration of experimental parameter spaces and to inform practical tradeoffs between performance and manufacture cost.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Inverse Modeling and Causal Discovery of Data-Generating Processes
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel wants to use neural network methods to infer the processes that generated his datasets rather than only describing observed patterns. He is particularly interested in inverse modeling, causal discovery, and generative approaches (invertible networks, normalizing flows, and Bayesian deep learning) that can reconstruct instrument settings, environmental histories, or sample states from measured data. Key priorities are physically informed priors from simulation, explicit uncertainty quantification for calibrated inference, and model interpretability so that inferred causes can guide experimental design and troubleshooting. Daniel sees value in methods that can recommend minimal new measurements to disambiguate hypotheses about data provenance and that can be integrated into iterative simulation–experiment loops for efficient instrument commissioning and problem diagnosis.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics‑informed Machine Learning for Condensed Matter
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hans develops and applies physics‑informed machine learning approaches to bridge theoretical models and data in condensed matter systems. He focuses on architectures and loss functions that embed conservation laws, symmetries, and known effective Hamiltonians to improve generalization from simulated data to experimentally relevant regimes. Hans is particularly interested in using generative models and surrogate ML emulators to accelerate parameter sweeps and inverse problems, enabling fast exploration of phase diagrams and response functions. By combining domain knowledge with probabilistic ML, he seeks interpretable, uncertainty‑aware predictions that guide experiments and suggest new model refinements, while ensuring that learned representations respect physical constraints and scale with system size.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Simulation and Modeling of Strongly Correlated Materials
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hans studies strongly correlated electron systems using a mix of numerical simulation, model reduction, and data‑driven analysis. He develops and benchmarks simulation pipelines that generate high‑fidelity synthetic datasets (quantum Monte Carlo, DMFT, tensor networks) to train and validate ML methods for identifying collective behavior. His interests include learning effective low‑energy descriptions, accelerating many‑body solvers with learned preconditioners or surrogates, and extracting order parameters and emergent excitations from noisy or limited observables. By linking simulated ensembles to statistical inference frameworks, Hans aims to quantify model selection, causal links between microscopic couplings and macroscopic phases, and to propose experimentally testable signatures of strong correlation phenomena.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum Transport, Topology and New Phase Discovery
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Hans investigates quantum transport and topological phenomena with the goal of discovering novel phases of matter. He leverages simulated transport datasets and ML classifiers/regressors to map conductance signatures, localization transitions, and topological invariants across disorder, interaction, and driving parameters. Hans explores unsupervised and manifold‑learning techniques to reveal hidden order and to cluster transport regimes, and he employs active learning to prioritize simulations or measurements that maximize discovery potential. Through a combination of compact transport models, realistic device simulations, and interpretable ML tools, Hans aims to propose robust experimental probes for emergent phases and to understand how topology and correlations coevolve in nanoscale systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Free‑Electron Laser (FEL) Physics and Seeding Techniques
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Francesca investigates the physics of free‑electron lasers with an emphasis on seeding strategies and coherence enhancement. She combines experimental demonstrations, theoretical analysis and particle‑tracking simulations to characterize seeded versus SASE FELs, quantify coherence and spectral properties, and optimize temporal and energy extraction performance. Notable work includes first direct high‑harmonic‑generation (HHG) seeding at 38.2 nm (with GW‑level output and coherent second harmonic at 19.1 nm) and seeded VUV pulse generation on storage rings. Francesca develops model‑based undulator taper optimization, explores phase‑jump techniques, and evaluates sensitivity and mitigation for echo‑enabled harmonic generation (EEHG) under CSR and chirped beams. Her focus is on improving pulse coherence, temporal resolution and FEL efficiency to enable next‑generation light‑source experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Accelerator and Beamline Design, Bunch Dynamics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Francesca works on accelerator and beamline design with hands‑on involvement in injector and photocathode gun development, bunch compression schemes, and longitudinal and transverse diagnostics. She contributes to linac and soft X‑ray laser projects, proposing linac extensions and implementing double‑achromat bunch compressors, transverse RF deflectors and advanced beam‑delivery systems. Her research addresses collective effects such as wakefields and coherent synchrotron radiation (CSR), longitudinal phase‑space tailoring and start‑to‑end simulation to preserve beam brightness and stability. Francesca employs analytic Vlasov/kinetic approaches alongside numerical tracking to inform practical mitigation strategies, aiming to maximize stability, temporal fidelity and energy‑extraction efficiency for high‑performance photon sources.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Accelerator Diagnostics and Imaging
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Francesca applies machine learning to accelerator diagnostics, exploiting image data and simpler signals from accelerator components to extract actionable information in real time. She integrates ML methods with traditional instrumentation — including MCP/intensity monitors, Ce:YAG BPMs, spectrometers and timing/overlap diagnostics — to perform feature extraction, anomaly detection, and predictive maintenance. Her interests include image‑based beam monitoring, data‑driven calibration of diagnostics, surrogate modelling to accelerate start‑to‑end simulations, and ML‑assisted optimization of undulator tapering and timing overlap. Francesca seeks collaborations with ML experts to develop robust, uncertainty‑aware models and deployable workflows that bridge experimental measurements and control for improved stability and automated operation.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Deep neural networks for protostellar observations
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel seeks a practical grounding in deep neural networks (DNNs) to analyze multi-epoch and multi-instrument observations of protostars. He aims to learn architecture design, training strategies, and evaluation techniques tailored to astronomical imaging and spectral time series, with attention to preprocessing heterogeneous datasets and augmenting limited labeled samples. Daniel plans to focus on methods to mitigate overfitting, quantify predictive uncertainties, and apply interpretability tools so that learned features can be related to physical processes. He is interested in end-to-end pipelines that map raw or minimally processed observations to physically meaningful parameters, enabling consistent inference across datasets and supporting robust scientific conclusions during his PhD work at the Niels Bohr Institute.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Representation learning with autoencoders and hybrid DNNs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel is interested in autoencoders as a route to compact, physically informative representations of protostellar and disk data, and in how to combine those representations with supervised deep networks. He plans to explore variational, denoising, and convolutional autoencoders to compress noisy, heterogeneous observations into latent spaces useful for denoising, anomaly detection, domain adaptation, and data augmentation. Daniel will investigate strategies to fuse learned latents with downstream regressors or classifiers for parameter estimation, and to preserve interpretability by relating latent modes to astrophysical variables. This line of work aims to bridge sparse labels and diverse instruments while producing robust features that improve inference and guide further physical modelling.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Dust evolution and disk substructures using similarity learning
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel focuses on dust physics in protoplanetary disks and on understanding the formation pathways of observed substructures, using machine learning tools such as Siamese networks and metric learning. He intends to apply pairwise and similarity-based methods to multi-wavelength and time-resolved observations to match features across epochs and instruments, detect subtle morphological changes, and prioritize candidates for physical follow-up. Daniel is particularly motivated to connect ML-identified patterns to grain growth, migration, dust–gas interactions, and planet–disk interactions by training on simulations and observational forward models. He seeks robust similarity metrics that are resilient to instrumental differences and that help reveal the evolutionary processes shaping disks and early planet formation.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for astrophysical data analysis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Liam applies and investigates machine learning techniques tailored to astrophysical data analysis, with a practical emphasis on boosted decision trees (BDTs), neural networks (NNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). He focuses on problems such as transient identification in time-domain surveys, source classification in crowded fields, denoising of imaging and spectroscopic data, and automated extraction of morphological features from large multi-wavelength catalogues. Liam places strong value on model interpretability, uncertainty quantification and rigorous cross-validation across survey conditions to ensure scientific reliability. He also works on scalable inference strategies to make ML workflows deployable for next-generation sky surveys, aiming to increase sensitivity to faint or rare signals while controlling false positive rates for downstream scientific analysis.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Deep learning for imaging, simulation and emulation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Liam explores deep learning architectures—particularly CNNs and feed-forward NNs—as tools for both analysis of astronomical imagery and as fast emulators of complex physical simulations. He investigates convolutional networks for tasks like morphological classification, deblending, and image restoration, while using neural-network-based surrogate models to accelerate parameter inference from costly forward models. Liam is interested in domain adaptation and data augmentation strategies to bridge differences between simulated and observational data, and in physics-informed network designs that embed known symmetries and conservation laws. He also examines training efficiency, calibration of predictive uncertainties, and hybrid workflows that combine traditional simulation pipelines with learned fast approximators for large-scale parameter studies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Cross-disciplinary ML methods and methodology transfer
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Liam is keen to discover and evaluate applications of machine learning beyond astrophysics, with the goal of importing useful methods and best practices back into his own research. He studies the use of BDTs, ensemble methods and neural approaches in other scientific domains to identify ideas for model validation, interpretability, and robust uncertainty estimation. Liam is interested in transferable pipelines, reproducible training workflows, and tooling that facilitates collaboration between domain experts and ML practitioners. At the workshop he aims to learn about evaluation metrics, data curation strategies, and deployment patterns from other fields, and to assess how methodological advances elsewhere can improve sensitivity, reliability and computational efficiency in astrophysical analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative Models for Recommendation (GANs & Matrix Factorization)
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Ervin investigates the application of generative modeling, particularly Generative Adversarial Networks, to collaborative filtering and matrix factorization for recommender systems. He is interested in how adversarial training can be adapted to learn user-item interaction distributions from structured numerical data, improving recommendation diversity and robustness while remaining computationally efficient. Building on his work on GAN-based matrix factorization, Ervin explores model architectures, training strategies and loss formulations that align generative outputs with ranking objectives and practical constraints of large-scale recommender problems. He also studies techniques to integrate content signals and side information, and to mitigate mode collapse or instability in training so that generated latent representations reliably support downstream ranking and personalization tasks.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Disentanglement and Interpretability in Recommender Models
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Ervin studies the relationship between representation disentanglement and interpretability in recommendation models, focusing on empirical reproducibility and quantitative evaluation. He examines whether disentangled latent factors lead to more interpretable feature attributions and whether that interpretability aligns with or trades off against recommendation effectiveness. Through reproduction studies across several models and datasets, Ervin evaluates metrics for disentanglement, inspects learned dimensions for semantic coherence, and probes how disentanglement techniques influence downstream ranking performance. He is particularly interested in rigorous experimental protocols, open code and datasets, and practical diagnostic tools that help practitioners decide when disentanglement is beneficial for transparency, debugging, or user-facing explanations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Applying ML to Astronomy and Structured Scientific Data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Ervin is keen to bridge machine learning methods for structured and numerical data with domain knowledge in astronomy. He aims to learn physics-domain concepts that improve model design, feature engineering and interpretation when working with large astronomical surveys, time series of observations, and simulation outputs. His interest spans generative approaches for synthetic data augmentation and anomaly detection, probabilistic models for measurement uncertainty, and scalable pipelines that respect domain constraints. By combining generative models with structured-data techniques, Ervin seeks to enable better scientific discovery workflows — for example improving detection of rare events, reconstructing incomplete observations, and producing physically plausible simulations for downstream analysis.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Image-based ML for electron microscopy and tomography
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Image-based characterization and analysis using convolutional neural networks for electron microscopy and tomography. Giuseppe develops CNN workflows to extract quantitative 2D and 3D information from TEM/STEM, EDS maps and tomograms—leveraging ferritin’s iron‑oxide core contrast to resolve protein spatial distributions inside MOFs, segment nanocrystalline UiO‑66 gels, and quantify particle-size and phase heterogeneity. His approach combines transfer learning and physics-aware data augmentation to overcome limited labeled data, uncertainty estimation for robust measurement of nucleation and growth, and interpretable saliency mapping to link model outputs to experimentally meaningful features. Giuseppe aims to integrate ML-derived morphological descriptors with diffraction and spectroscopic observables (PXRD, NMR) to build multimodal datasets that accelerate mechanistic understanding and enable automated, high-throughput characterization pipelines for enzyme@MOF assemblies, filtration membranes, and supramolecular devices.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph neural networks for structure–property relationships
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Graph neural networks for structure–property modeling of MOFs, supramolecular assemblies and molecular electronics. Giuseppe employs GNNs to represent crystallographic nets, linker connectivity and interfacial contact maps as graphs that capture multiscale topology—from atomic coordination to mesoscale gel networks. He trains models to predict adsorption affinities (PFOA/PFAS removal), catalytic activity of enzyme@MOF composites, electronic conductance and anisotropic magnetoresistance in metalloporphyrin wires, and to infer synthesis–structure relationships that govern particle size and phase selection. His workflow couples physics-informed node and edge features (coordination numbers, bond orders, interfacial energies) with experimental constraints from PXRD, TEM and spectroscopy, enabling interpretable attributions and design heuristics. Giuseppe prioritizes models that generalize across chemistries, facilitate inverse design, and integrate with active-learning experiments to accelerate discovery and optimization of functional materials.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative models for materials and molecular design
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Generative models for materials and molecular design, including VAEs, diffusion models and conditional GANs tailored to MOFs, protein@MOF biocomposites and supramolecular wires. Giuseppe explores generative strategies to propose linker chemistries, cyclodextrin functionalizations, protein mutations compatible with confinement, and synthesis-parameter recipes that target properties such as high PFAS uptake, preserved enzymatic activity, or tuned magnetoresistance. He emphasizes conditional generation constrained by experimental observables (PXRD patterns, TEM signatures, adsorption isotherms) and uncertainty-aware scoring to prioritize experimentally tractable candidates. By closing the loop with active learning and rapid characterization, Giuseppe aims to reduce the design cycle time from ideation to validated prototypes, enabling discovery of novel nanomaterials, protective delivery vehicles, and electronic supramolecular motifs while retaining mechanistic interpretability and synthetic feasibility.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine-learning Interatomic Potentials & Graph Neural Networks
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Atefe develops and refines machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) that combine neural-network architectures and graph neural networks to capture complex many-body interactions in condensed-phase systems. She focuses on building transferable, data-efficient potentials trained on density functional theory and ab initio molecular dynamics data, emphasizing robust representations of local environments, symmetry preservation, and uncertainty-aware predictions. Her work includes employing variational autoencoders and latent-space models to compress high-dimensional atomic configurations and accelerate sampling, as well as active-learning strategies to minimize expensive quantum calculations. By integrating graph-based message passing with physically informed descriptors, Atefe aims to produce MLIPs that balance accuracy and scalability for simulations of materials with strong structural heterogeneity, defects, and phase transitions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Long-range Electrostatics and Polarization in Dense Systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Atefe is actively extending ML potentials and simulation toolchains to include long-range electrostatic interactions and explicit polarization, motivated by their central role in ferroelectrics, ionic conductors, and dense condensed phases. Her interests span methods for embedding Ewald/PME-like treatments into ML-driven force models, learning environment-dependent partial charges or multipoles, and coupling ML short-range potentials with efficient long-range solvers. She seeks collaborative approaches to represent dielectric response, charge transfer, and screening in systems where classical short-range ML models break down, and explores hybrid schemes that combine learned energy terms with physics-based electrostatics to maintain extensivity and stability. Atefe prioritizes scalable implementations suitable for large-scale molecular dynamics and active learning datasets that probe polarization under varied boundary conditions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Atomistic Design of Functional Materials for Solar-driven Water Treatment
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Atefe bridges experiment and theory to design and optimize materials for solar-driven desalination, antimicrobial surfaces, and energy-relevant interfaces. Experimentally she engineers sustainable wood-based photothermal absorbers incorporating reduced graphene oxide, silver nanoparticles, and doped VO2 coatings to achieve salt-resistant, broadband light absorption and rapid vapor generation with intrinsic antibacterial functionality. Theoretically she applies DFT and ab initio molecular dynamics to design alkali-metal-decorated 2D materials (e.g., phosphorene) for gas adsorption and hydrogen storage, elucidating donor–acceptor and dispersion interactions that enable high adsorption capacities. Her research agenda combines surface decoration, doping strategies, and scalable templates to translate atomistic interaction mechanisms into robust devices, using data-driven screening and multiscale simulations to accelerate materials discovery and lifetime optimization for environmental and clean-energy applications.
