research_interests.research_interest_title: Photonics and Experimental Optics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Katrine works primarily in photonics, focusing on experimental optical setups, characterization of light–matter interactions, and precision measurement. She is interested in how machine learning can be applied to interpret experimental signals from photonic systems, improve calibration of optical components, and accelerate parameter searches in complex optical experiments. Katrine values concrete examples where ML methods provide measurable improvements on real-world photonics data, especially in the presence of detector noise, drift, or limited sampling. She is also curious about approaches that preserve physical interpretability and enable insight into underlying optical phenomena rather than acting as black-box predictors. Practical demonstrations showing how ML integrates with existing optical instrumentation and yields clearer, faster experimental outcomes would be particularly useful to inform her lab practice.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Experimental Hardware & Workflow Efficiency
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Katrine’s daily work centers on hardware, instrumentation control, and hands-on maintenance of experimental setups. She seeks methods to make laboratory workflows more efficient by reducing manual tuning, automating routine calibration tasks, and streamlining data acquisition pipelines. Katrine is interested in concrete toolchains that connect sensors, controllers, and analysis software with ML components for closed-loop experiment control or real-time feedback. Practical concerns such as robustness to flaky hardware, low-latency decision making, and ease of deployment in existing setups are important. Demonstrations of how modest AI/ML additions can cut experiment turnaround time, reduce human intervention, and improve reproducibility would directly inform her efforts to modernize lab workflows while keeping systems reliable and maintainable.

research_interests.research_interest_title: ML for Limited and Noisy Experimental Data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Katrine is particularly interested in strategies for applying ML when experimental data are scarce, expensive to collect, or contaminated by noise. She wants to learn about sample-efficient approaches such as transfer learning, physics-informed models, active learning for targeted data collection, and generative augmentation tailored to photonics experiments. Robust uncertainty quantification, model interpretability, and techniques that exploit known physical constraints are key priorities so that predictions remain trustworthy under real-world conditions. Katrine is also curious about case studies that demonstrate measurable benefits on small experimental datasets and practical guidance on validation, model selection, and avoiding overfitting in the lab context.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine-learning quasi-inverses for quantum channels
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Muhammad develops neural-network-based quasi-inverses to approximate the inverse action of noisy qubit channels. He trains architectures that map noisy outputs back toward intended quantum states, using ensembles of physically motivated noise models and realistic device calibrations. His work emphasizes robust generalization across channel families rather than simple interpolation: networks are regularized with physics-inspired constraints, tested on out-of-distribution noise, and evaluated by fidelity and resource overhead on small-circuit benchmarks. Muhammad aims to transform these learned quasi-inverses into deployable error-mitigation primitives that can be integrated into near-term quantum workflows, enabling higher effective circuit depths and improved observable estimation without full fault tolerance. He combines simulation, optimization, and experimental validation to quantify trade-offs between accuracy, complexity, and implementability.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Error mitigation and noise-resilient quantum algorithms
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Muhammad studies how realistic noise affects core quantum algorithms — notably quantum phase estimation and Grover-type search — and develops mitigation strategies that blend analytic insight with data-driven tools. He analyzes error propagation, identifies dominant failure modes, and constructs corrective schemes that reduce bias and variance in algorithmic outputs. His approach couples closed-form channel inversion where possible with learned quasi-inverse maps when analytic inversion is intractable. Muhammad evaluates mitigation protocols on simulated hardware noise profiles and small experimental platforms, prioritizing methods that minimize additional circuit depth and measurement overhead. The goal is to make near-term quantum algorithms more reliable by delivering practical, benchmarked techniques that integrate seamlessly with existing compilation and control stacks.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics-informed model discovery for quantum and photonic systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Muhammad pursues model-discovery methods that go beyond black-box functional fitting, bringing physics structure into machine-learning for both quantum information and photonics. He integrates priors from electromagnetic theory, modal dispersion, and fractional-calculus-inspired operators into learning pipelines, aiming for interpretable surrogate models that reproduce salient physics while remaining compact and generalizable. Applications include identifying effective descriptions of noise channels, reduced-order photonic device models, and interpretable mappings between structured metamaterial geometries and optical responses. Methodologically, Muhammad combines numerically rigorous tools (RCWA, FEM, Green-function formalisms) with sparsity-promoting discovery, symbolic regression, and constrained neural architectures to extract latent model components. The resulting models are intended to accelerate design, provide physical insight, and enable trustworthy extrapolation across parameter regimes.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Anomaly detection in quantum-dot noise time-series
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Reyhaneh focuses on applying anomaly-detection techniques to time-series recordings of charge and current fluctuations in quantum-dot experiments. She uses algorithms that flag rare or transient deviations—such as telegraph switching, bursty charge events, sudden drifts, or instrumentation glitches—that can obscure or mimic quantum signatures. By combining sequential detectors, change-point methods, and reconstruction-based models (e.g., autoencoders, isolation forests, and recurrent architectures), Reyhaneh aims to detect anomalies both in real time and in post-processing. These tools help her separate experimental artifacts from physics-relevant events, enable robust post-selection of measurement windows, and trigger adaptive experimental responses. Ultimately she seeks methods that are interpretable for experimentalists, tolerant of limited labeled examples, and capable of operating on high-throughput, noisy time-series from cryogenic transport measurements.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Probabilistic ML and uncertainty quantification for noisy measurements
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Reyhaneh is interested in probabilistic machine-learning approaches that explicitly quantify uncertainty in highly noisy quantum-dot transport data. She explores Bayesian neural networks, Gaussian processes, and probabilistic graphical models to obtain calibrated posterior distributions and predictive intervals for extracted parameters and inferred latent states. Quantifying both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty allows Reyhaneh to distinguish instrument-limited noise from intrinsic quantum fluctuations, to assess confidence in detected phenomena, and to prioritize follow-up experiments. Probabilistic models also enable principled model comparison and propagation of uncertainty into downstream decision-making (e.g., gate tuning, parameter estimation, or active learning). She seeks techniques that scale to long time-series, incorporate domain priors from solid-state physics, and can be connected with theoretical collaborators to interpret statistical outputs in terms of physical mechanisms.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Unsupervised learning to discover hidden transport regimes and patterns
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Reyhaneh uses unsupervised learning to reveal latent structure in multidimensional measurements of quantum-dot transport and noise without requiring extensive labeling. Techniques such as clustering, dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP, t-SNE), mixture models, and latent-variable frameworks can expose recurring regimes—e.g., Coulomb blockade, cotunneling, charge traps, or correlated switching—and identify subtle transitions between them. By mapping high-dimensional time-series and device-control parameter sweeps into low-dimensional representations, Reyhaneh aims to accelerate hypothesis generation about underlying mechanisms and to detect regime-dependent features in noise statistics. She is particularly interested in methods that produce physically interpretable components, can incorporate temporal correlations, and help guide targeted experiments and collaborations with theorists to validate and model newly discovered transport behaviors.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Privacy- and Robustness-aware Distributed Learning
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Vinay develops algorithms and analysis for federated, decentralized and multitask learning that explicitly balance privacy, robustness, and communication constraints. His work spans differential-privacy mechanisms integrated with partial-sharing and asynchronous update protocols, defenses against Byzantine and model-poisoning attacks, and RL-driven control of inter-cluster cooperation to optimize performance under resource limits. Vinay combines theoretical convergence and stability analysis with practical schemes for online and streaming settings, emphasizing mean and mean-square guarantees, bounded degradation under adversarial conditions, and efficient partial-parameter exchange. He is interested in applying these methods to large models (including LLMs) and graph-structured tasks, exploring how privacy and fairness constraints interact with uncertainty quantification in real-world, bandwidth- and latency-constrained deployments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum Machine Learning and Hybrid Quantum–Classical Models
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Vinay investigates quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms and hybrid quantum–classical pipelines that can leverage near-term quantum hardware for practical signal-processing and learning tasks. He explores quantum kernels, variational quantum circuits for feature extraction, and QML-aware adaptations of classical constructs such as graph filters and kernel methods. His focus includes theoretical characterization of uncertainty and generalization in quantum-enhanced learners, robustness to noise in quantum devices, and interfaces between quantum models and classical architectures (e.g., GNNs or ViT-inspired encoders). Vinay pursues methods that are resource-aware—designing algorithms tolerant to limited qubit counts and coherence times—and seeks collaborative opportunities to translate QML primitives into end-to-end solutions for sensing, communication, and distributed inference.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Resource‑aware Signal Processing and Algorithm–Architecture Co‑design
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Vinay focuses on designing low-complexity, hardware-friendly signal-processing and learning algorithms with provable performance and real-time implementability. His contributions include fractional-order correntropy filters for impulsive noise, proportionate and hard-thresholding sparse identification, affine-projection diffusion strategies, RFF-based scalable kernel regression, and nonlinear adaptive graph filters. He couples algorithmic advances with VLSI and fixed-point architecture reformulations—pipelined implementations, quantization-aware optimization, and compressed-sensing codecs—to achieve energy- and compute-efficient deployments. Vinay emphasizes measurable trade-offs among convergence speed, stability bounds, communication overhead, and silicon cost, and applies these techniques to hyperspectral anomaly detection, RIS channel estimation, SHM, and scalable video coding, often leveraging CNN/ViT backbones or GNN frontends when appropriate.

Contributions.Title: Efficient Quantum Vision Transformers

research_interests.research_interest_title: Robust, Resource-Aware Adaptive Signal Processing
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Vinay researches robust, resource-aware adaptive signal processing methods for non-Gaussian and impulsive environments, emphasizing algorithms that are stable, efficient, and implementable in real time. His work includes fractional-order correntropy filters for α‑stable processes, correntropy- and logarithmic-cost-based adaptive rules, proportionate and hard-thresholding schemes for sparse identification, and affine-projection-based multitask/diffusion strategies (including partial-diffusion and controlled inter-cluster cooperation). Vinay evaluates convergence (mean and mean-square) and derives stability bounds while optimizing communication and computation for pipelined, fixed-point VLSI implementations. He also explores how these techniques integrate with modern ML models — CNNs, ViTs, GNNs and LLMs — for resource-constrained inference and on-device learning in sensor, imaging, and communications applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Privacy-Preserving and Robust Federated/Decentralized Learning
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Vinay focuses on federated and decentralized learning frameworks that account for practical constraints such as limited bandwidth, asynchronous updates, partial sharing, and adversarial participants. He develops graph-federated multitask and personalized learning strategies with differential privacy guarantees, mechanisms for robustness to Byzantine and model-poisoning attacks, and RL-driven controllers for adaptive inter-cluster cooperation. His contributions include partial-sharing FL paradigms, machine unlearning protocols, and scalable online/asynchronous algorithms that trade off privacy, robustness, and efficiency. Vinay emphasizes rigorous theoretical analysis alongside empirical evaluation, designing methods that maintain provable convergence while minimizing communication and computation overhead for real-world deployments across healthcare, hyperspectral sensing, and distributed sensing networks.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum Machine Learning and Algorithm–Architecture Co-design
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Vinay explores quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms and hybrid classical–quantum approaches with an emphasis on uncertainty, privacy, and hardware-aware design. He is interested in developing QML methods that are robust to noise and model uncertainty, efficient in terms of quantum and classical resources, and compatible with differential privacy and fairness constraints. Vinay pursues algorithm–architecture co-design, mapping scalable kernels, graph-based methods, and randomized-feature approximations to near-term quantum processors and hybrid architectures while preserving convergence guarantees and implementability. He actively seeks collaborations that bridge QML algorithm development, distributed learning paradigms, and practical deployment on quantum-classical systems for applications in signal processing, communication channel estimation, and scientific data analysis.

Contributions.Title: Machine Unlearning

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum education and workforce development
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Simon focuses on designing and evaluating education and workforce pathways for Quantum Science and Technologies (QST). He develops competence frameworks (e.g., European CFQT v1–2.5), a proficiency triangle, and nine qualification profiles to standardize skills and enable certification across formal and informal learning. Simon proposes programmatic models such as the Quantum Curriculum Transformation Framework and the Open Master model to support transnational, flexible degrees and lifelong learning. His empirical work draws on surveys, interviews, and program mapping to align secondary and tertiary curricula with industry needs and outreach priorities. Emphasizing community-building, activity-theoretic analysis, and responsible research and innovation, Simon aims to produce a diverse, quantum-ready workforce while offering policy-relevant recommendations for credentialing, teacher development, and cross-sector collaboration.

research_interests.research_interest_title: ML-driven ecosystem mapping and NLP for emerging technologies
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Simon applies machine learning—especially NLP, topic modelling, and GPT-based classification—to map and analyse the ecosystem surrounding emerging technologies. He uses topic models and clustering to surface thematic patterns in community profiles, curricula, policy discourse, and industry needs, and deploys GPT-classification for rapid coding of interviews and outreach materials. This work supports global mapping of programs, identification of skills gaps, and comparison of stakeholder priorities by automating synthesis of large textual datasets (e.g., program descriptions, survey responses, and industry interviews). Simon is particularly interested in combining quantitative topic signals with qualitative validation to ensure interpretable, action-ready outputs that inform curriculum design, certification criteria, and responsible stakeholder engagement.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Software-enhanced teaching, visualization and pedagogical tools for QST
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Simon develops and evaluates software-enhanced pedagogies and visualisation tools to make quantum concepts accessible and technology-relevant. His work includes educator–developer dialogues to co-design interactive tools such as Quantum Composer Bloch-sphere models and assisted tunnelling simulations, which scaffold conceptual understanding and link physics ideas to applied technologies. He explores culturo-scientific storytelling and discipline-culture analysis to reframe which quantum concepts matter for technology versus physics education, and he tests classroom and outreach interventions across diverse contexts. By integrating tool development, pilot evaluation, and competency-aligned learning activities, Simon seeks scalable teaching resources that support certification, teacher training, and inclusive public engagement with quantum technologies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Very‑High‑Energy Gamma‑Ray Astrophysics & Transients
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jarred investigates the physics of extreme particle accelerators through very‑high‑energy (VHE) gamma‑ray observations, emphasizing rapid transient follow‑up and coordinated multi‑instrument campaigns. He studies blazar variability, polarization and spectral‑energy‑distribution modeling for sources such as Mrk 421/501 and TXS 0506+056, analyzes gamma‑ray bursts detected at GeV–TeV energies, and probes Galactic PeVatron candidates and supernova remnants. Jarred combines time‑dependent leptonic, hadronic and lepto‑hadronic modeling with rigorous statistical inference to interpret spectral and timing signatures, derive physical constraints, and place limits on phenomena like the intergalactic magnetic field, Lorentz invariance violation, and dark‑matter/ALP parameter space. His work prioritizes rapid reaction to transients, multiwavelength context, and translating observational data into robust physical conclusions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescope Instrumentation & Calibration
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jarred focuses on instrumentation development and advanced calibration techniques for Imaging Atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes (IACTs). His activities include SiPM camera research and development, involvement with MAGIC, the CTA LST‑1 prototype and the ASTRI mini‑array, and innovations in star‑tracking pointing and cross‑calibration. He develops precision calibration pipelines, timing and synchronization strategies, and hardware–software integration to improve sensitivity and systematic control. Jarred also explores stellar intensity interferometry on IACTs and advocates open data formats and robust software practices to enable reproducible analyses and inter‑experiment comparisons. This instrumentation work aims to reduce systematic uncertainties, enhance transient responsiveness, and extend the science reach of ground‑based gamma‑ray observatories.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning, Graph Methods & Generative Models for Gamma‑Ray Data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jarred is actively exploring machine learning approaches tailored to gamma‑ray telescope data, with experience spanning tabular data, images and graph representations. He applies deep‑learning reconstruction tools (e.g., CTLearn) and is keen to extend methods to graph neural networks and generative models that respect instrument geometry and event topology. His interests include uncertainty quantification, domain adaptation, simulation‑based inference, and generative techniques for fast surrogate modeling or data augmentation. Jarred seeks collaborations with ML experts to address the specific challenges of IACT data — irregular sampling, heterogeneous sensors, low signal‑to‑noise, and strict calibration needs — aiming to develop interpretable, robust models that integrate with physical priors and rigorous statistical pipelines.

Contributions.Title: When MAGIC met IceCube: Doing Gamma-Ray Astronomy with Neutrino Event Reconstruction

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics-informed data assimilation with deep autoencoders
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johann is developing physics-informed data assimilation workflows that couple experimental observations with computational models to enable automatic parameter tuning. He focuses on integrating convolutional autoencoder architectures to compress high-dimensional image measurements into low-dimensional latent representations that interact with forward physics solvers. The aim is to use the encoder to capture measurement errors and experimental variability, and to use assimilation techniques (e.g., variational methods, ensemble Kalman filters) to update model parameters in a principled way. During the workshop Johann wants to validate this approach, explore loss formulations that respect physical constraints, and assess stability and uncertainty quantification in the tuned parameters. Practical concerns include handling noisy diffraction and optical data, designing computationally efficient surrogate models, and establishing metrics to compare tuned models with independent experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Image-based experimental analysis with convolutional models
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johann works on image-based experimental methods and has strong expertise with convolutional neural networks for microscopy, diffraction pattern analysis, and optics imaging. He is interested in improving end-to-end pipelines that go from raw detector frames to robust feature extraction, denoising, segmentation and parameter estimation. Johann aims to examine architectures and training strategies that incorporate physical priors, realistic data augmentations, and uncertainty-aware losses so models generalize across experimental conditions. At the workshop he plans to discuss practical preprocessing, annotation strategies, transfer learning from simulation to experiment, and diagnostics for failure modes. He also seeks guidance on evaluation metrics that reflect experimental priorities such as resolution limits, sensitivity to strain or plasticity signatures, and interpretability for controllers used in online tuning.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph neural networks for microstructure and materials modeling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johann is curious about applying graph neural networks to problems in materials science where microstructure, grain networks, and interfacial connections are naturally expressed as graphs. Coming from an image-centric background, he wants to understand how to convert image-derived microstructure representations into graph nodes and edges, which GNN architectures (message passing, spectral convolution, equivariant networks) are suitable, and how to couple GNN-based surrogates with continuum plasticity models and diffraction-informed observations. At the workshop Johann hopes to learn best practices for featurization, training with limited labeled data, multi-scale coupling strategies, and how to incorporate symmetry and conservation laws. He also wants to assess whether GNNs can improve parameter inference and predictive generalization compared to CNN-based latent representations in experimental workflows.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Atmospheric and climate physics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Lærke focuses on fundamental and applied problems in meteorology and climate physics, exploring energy balances, boundary-layer processes, cloud microphysics, and large-scale circulation patterns that shape regional climate behavior. She aims to connect observational evidence, theoretical frameworks, and model diagnostics to identify mechanisms behind variability and change in the atmosphere. Her work often integrates field measurements, reanalysis products and process-based simulations to interrogate coupling between surface processes and atmospheric dynamics. In preparation for a thesis, Lærke seeks inspiration for tractable, impactful questions that balance analytical clarity and observational constraints. She is particularly interested in bridging scales — from turbulent mixing and cloud formation to synoptic systems — and in translating physical understanding into metrics that improve model evaluation and climate projections.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Climate data and netCDF analysis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Lærke specializes in working with large gridded climate datasets stored in netCDF format, developing reproducible workflows for data ingestion, quality control, subsetting and aggregation. She emphasizes robust metadata handling, coordinate conventions and provenance tracking to ensure analyses are transparent and reproducible. Lærke is adept at using command-line tools, Python and specialized libraries to automate extraction of variables, compute diagnostics and produce time-aggregated products suitable for thesis-scale studies. Her interest includes efficient strategies for handling multi-decadal reanalyses and multi-model ensembles, addressing issues such as temporal sampling, interpolation, and bias characterization. By combining careful data management with clear documentation, Lærke aims to produce datasets tailored to test hypotheses in meteorology and to enable reproducible comparisons between observations and models.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for meteorology
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Lærke is interested in applying machine learning techniques to extract patterns, accelerate diagnostics, and support predictive tasks in meteorology and climate science. She explores supervised and unsupervised methods to detect regimes, classify cloud types, emulate parametrizations, and correct systematic model errors. A pragmatic priority is to combine physics-aware features and physically informed constraints with data-driven models to maintain interpretability and generalization across variable climates. For a thesis, Lærke seeks inspiration for projects that balance methodological novelty with clear scientific payoff, such as hybrid ML-physics emulators, transfer learning across climate datasets, or interpretable feature attribution for extreme weather drivers. She values reproducible pipelines, careful cross-validation across temporal and spatial domains, and clear evaluation metrics that reflect meteorological significance rather than purely statistical performance.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Computer Vision for Detector and Jet Imaging
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Joachim applies advanced computer vision techniques to particle and heavy-ion physics, focusing on turning detector readouts and jet constituents into structured image-like representations. He leverages convolutional networks, vision transformers and attention mechanisms to improve jet tagging, substructure analysis and noise-robust reconstruction in high-occupancy environments. His work emphasizes domain adaptation from simulation to real data, interpretable feature maps, and calibrated uncertainty estimates so that ML outputs can be integrated into physics analyses. Joachim is particularly interested in cross-pollinating state-of-the-art CV methods from other fields into collider and heavy-ion contexts, exploring how spatial inductive biases and learned representations can reveal signatures of quark-gluon plasma dynamics and rare processes while keeping computational and systematic costs tractable for experimental workflows.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph Neural Networks for Interacting Systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Joachim develops and applies graph neural network (GNN) architectures to problems where relational structure matters, drawing on his experience in traffic modelling and recent physics applications. He represents jets, particle showers and collision events as graphs of constituents or detector hits and designs message-passing schemes that respect permutation symmetry and conservation laws. Joachim investigates dynamic and hierarchical graph constructions to capture multi-scale correlations in heavy-ion collisions and jet fragmentation, while addressing scalability, training stability and interpretability. He is interested in hybrid approaches that inject physics priors into GNNs, benchmarking graph-based surrogates against traditional simulation, and using learned relational models for tasks such as event classification, anomaly detection and fast emulation of interaction networks.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative Models for Fast Simulation and Discovery
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Joachim explores generative modelling techniques — including GANs, VAEs, normalizing flows and diffusion models — to accelerate simulation and enable new analysis strategies in particle and heavy-ion physics. His interests span fast, high-fidelity emulation of detector responses and jet substructure, conditional generation of events for rare processes, and using generative reconstructions for unsupervised anomaly searches. He also studies how generative models can capture the complex, non-Gaussian fluctuations of the quark-gluon plasma and heavy-ion backgrounds, while providing calibrated uncertainties and controllable systematic variations. Joachim combines methodological rigor in likelihood-based training and evaluation with domain-specific constraints to produce generative tools that are computationally efficient, physically interpretable and ready for integration into experimental pipelines.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformers for Quantum Chemical Systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Alexandra focuses on adapting transformer architectures to problems in computational quantum chemistry, with the goal of modeling electronic structure and molecular properties directly from chemical representations. She is interested in how attention mechanisms can capture long-range electron correlation, how to incorporate 3D geometric information and physical symmetries into tokenization and positional encodings, and how to hybridize learned representations with established quantum-chemical priors. Alexandra plans to explore architectures that handle graphs, grids, and continuous coordinates, investigate equivariant attention layers, and probe interpretability of learned attention patterns in relation to chemical intuition. Her aim is to learn practical modeling and training strategies that scale to realistic datasets while remaining faithful to underlying physics for her thesis work.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative Diffusion and Flow Matching Models for Molecules
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Alexandra is interested in score-based diffusion models and flow-matching approaches as tools for generating molecular structures, sampling conformational ensembles, and learning complex Boltzmann-like distributions for small molecules and materials. She wants to understand how forward–reverse stochastic processes and deterministic flow matching can be adapted to respect chemical constraints (valence, stereochemistry) and 3D geometry, and how to increase sampling efficiency for high-dimensional molecular spaces. Alexandra is also keen to study conditional generation—producing structures with target energies or spectral properties—and to combine fast learned samplers with quantum-chemical validation to produce chemically valid, physically meaningful candidates for downstream simulation or design.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Foundation Models and Transfer Learning in Computational Chemistry
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Alexandra sees foundation models and large pretraining paradigms as a route to leverage vast chemical and simulation data for many downstream quantum-chemistry tasks. She is exploring self-supervised pretraining on multi-modal chemical corpora—SMILES, graphs, 3D coordinates, spectra—and strategies for fine-tuning and few-shot adaptation to electronic property prediction, potential-energy surfaces, and reaction modeling. Alexandra wants to investigate scaling behaviors, data curation and representation choices that enable zero-shot or few-shot transfer, and methods to inject domain knowledge so that pretrained models remain consistent with conservation laws and symmetries. Her aim is to build robust, generalizable models that accelerate thesis experiments while remaining interpretable to chemists.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Kinetic plasma physics and collisionless shocks
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Troels develops and applies large-scale, high-resolution particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations to study kinetic plasma processes in collisionless shocks. He demonstrates how Weibel-instability–driven magnetic fields form and evolve, characterizes non‑Fermi electron energization channels, and synthesizes the resulting jitter and synchrotron-like radiation spectra to connect simulation physics with observable signatures. Troels emphasizes three-dimensional models and spectral post-processing so that synthetic observables can be compared directly to high-energy transient and afterglow data. His work combines algorithm and code development with careful convergence and parameter studies to quantify uncertainty, and he publishes simulation tools and datasets to enable reproducibility and community reuse.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Star and planet formation, turbulence, and accretion
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Troels studies the multi-scale physics of star and planet formation by coupling adaptive-mesh hydrodynamics with synthetic observational pipelines. He shows that supernova-driven turbulence naturally reproduces molecular-cloud statistics, formulates an empirical star-formation law in which the efficiency per free-fall time (ε_ff) scales with t_ff/t_dyn, and introduces the inertial-inflow model for the assembly of massive stars. Using RAMSES simulations and radiative-transfer post-processing (ALMA / RADMC-3D), Troels quantifies episodic and infall-driven accretion, disk formation, and observational diagnostics of cores and clumps. He interrogates the CMF–IMF connection with extensive synthetic surveys, testing the fidelity of core and clump measurements and providing observability-driven constraints on fragmentation and early stellar growth.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Observational cosmology, inhomogeneous models, and open computational tools
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Troels rigorously tests observational cosmology scenarios by confronting inhomogeneous Lemaître–Tolman–Bondi (LTB) void models and local-structure hypotheses with supernova, CMB, BAO, and kSZ data, quantifying how peculiar-velocity fields and local Hubble-bubble effects bias cosmological inferences. He develops and integrates numerical methods for non-linear neutrino treatments and radiative transfer, producing tools such as νCOnCEPT, Lampray, Paicos and photon-plasma, and releases datasets and analysis pipelines to ensure reproducibility. Troels focuses on creating interoperable, well-documented code and synthetic-observation frameworks so that theoretical predictions can be robustly compared to surveys and used by the community to assess systematic uncertainties in precision cosmology.

Name: Philip Hofmann

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning–driven autonomous experiments
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Philip focuses on integrating machine learning into experimental condensed-matter workflows to enable autonomous, adaptive measurements at synchrotron and free-electron-laser facilities. He works on clustering-based analysis pipelines for high-dimensional spectroscopic datasets, and has implemented Gaussian process regression to steer experiments and optimize measurement parameters in real time. Philip is also experienced with autoencoder networks for dimensionality reduction and anomaly detection in photoemission and nanoscale imaging data. His immediate goal is to establish collaborations with computer scientists to develop robust, uncertainty-aware ML tools that can control instrumentation, prioritize acquisition of informative data, and extend the reach of conventional experiments—making new phases, transient states, or weak signals accessible within limited beamtime and under complex sample conditions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Ultrafast and nanoscale photoemission spectroscopy
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Philip advances spectroscopic imaging methods—particularly ARPES, TR-ARPES, nanoARPES and time-of-flight momentum microscopy—to reveal electronic structure and carrier dynamics on femtosecond and nanometer scales. He develops measurement protocols and instrumentation to extract hot-carrier temperatures, map momentum-resolved dynamics, and perform in-operando nanoscale studies of 2D materials and interfaces. Philip applies these tools to graphene, single-layer MoS2, transition-metal dichalcogenides, and topological insulators to study ultrafast thermalization, carrier extraction, valley/spin polarization, and symmetry-driven band modifications. His approach combines precise sample preparation with optimized time-resolved detection strategies to push temporal and spatial resolution boundaries, enabling direct observation of transient electronic states and their coupling to lattice and spin degrees of freedom.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Electronic structure and many-body modeling of surfaces and 2D systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Philip studies the electronic structure of low-dimensional solids and surface-confined systems by combining advanced spectroscopies with first-principles many-body modelling (DFT and GW). He investigates spin–orbit and Rashba effects, electron–phonon coupling, quantum confinement, and engineered band gaps through intercalation or patterned adsorption. Philip’s work explores 2DEGs, band engineering of graphene via oxygen or bismuth intercalation, and spin/valley phenomena in transition-metal dichalcogenides. By integrating ab-initio calculations with high-resolution ARPES and scanning-probe measurements, Philip aims to quantify many-body renormalizations, predict tunable electronic responses, and design heterostructures that realize targeted transport and spin functionalities in atomically thin materials.

Contributions.Title: Understanding angle-resolved photoemission data in space and time

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph neural networks for particle and neutrino event reconstruction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Moust develops and applies graph neural network (GNN) architectures to reconstruct particle interactions in sparse, irregular detector geometries. Drawing on GraphNeT experience with IceCube, KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD, he frames detector readouts as graphs where nodes encode sensor responses and edges model geometric or causal relationships. His work focuses on message-passing schemes that respect detector symmetries, incorporate physics priors (timing, topology, energy conservation), and produce calibrated uncertainties for direction and energy estimates. He also investigates scalability to large arrays, semi-supervised training to exploit scarce labeled events, and robustness to noise and inhomogeneous sensor performance. The goal is practical, deployable reconstruction pipelines that improve angular and energy resolution while delivering uncertainty-aware outputs suitable for downstream astrophysical inference and real-time triggers.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformers and sequence models for detector time series and environmental signals
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Moust explores transformer-style sequence models to capture long-range dependencies in detector time series, atmospheric electric-field records, and astrophysical transient signals. He adapts attention mechanisms to irregularly sampled measurements and multiresolution streams—tokenizing pulses, waveforms, or event clusters and conditioning attention on physics-informed features such as propagation delays and dispersion. Applications include noise-robust denoising, anomaly and transient detection, domain adaptation between laboratory and in-situ data, and model-based calibration of timing and gain. He also investigates hybrid architectures that combine convolutional front-ends or graph encoders with transformer decoders to leverage both local structure and global context. Emphasis is placed on interpretability of attention weights for physical insight and on efficient inference for online experiment pipelines.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative and probabilistic modeling for dielectric breakdown, emissivity and synthetic data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Moust applies generative models and probabilistic methods to characterize material failure, emissivity measurements, and to create realistic synthetic datasets for machine learning. He uses VAEs, diffusion models and Bayesian hierarchical models to capture unit-to-unit variability in dielectrics, model the heavy-tailed statistics of breakdown voltages, and produce calibrated synthetic samples that preserve correlations across electrode area and inhomogeneity. This work ties directly to safety-factor guidance and sample-size planning by propagating uncertainty through measurement and prediction pipelines. In parallel, generative approaches help infer in-situ emissivities from infrared probe data under varying deposit conditions, enabling forward models of thermal loss and optical response. The overall emphasis is on principled uncertainty quantification, model-based augmentation for scarce experimental labels, and tools that translate statistical insight into engineering-relevant decisions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformer-based regression and classification for IceCube
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johann develops and evaluates transformer-based architectures tailored to the event reconstruction tasks of the IceCube experiment. Focusing on regression of continuous quantities (energy, direction) and classification of event types, Johann adapts attention mechanisms to handle sparse, irregular detector geometries and the temporal sequences of photon hits. Work addresses positional encoding strategies for 3D sensor layouts, efficient sparse attention to scale to full-detector rates, and hybrid losses that combine likelihood-inspired terms with supervised objectives. Johann also investigates inference speed and robustness, enabling near-real-time analysis chains for alerting and follow-up while explicitly testing generalization from simulation to real data and strategies for mitigating systematic mismatch during training.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Self-supervised learning on unlabeled detector data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johann explores self-supervised learning (SSL) to leverage the vast unlabeled streams produced by IceCube and reduce reliance on costly simulation labels. By designing pretext tasks—masked hit modeling, contrastive objectives across detector augmentations, and predictive temporal tasks—Johann seeks robust, transferable representations that improve downstream performance for classification and regression with limited labeled examples. Emphasis is placed on contrastive and reconstruction-based SSL variants that are resilient to noise, detector artifacts, and domain gaps between simulation and data. Johann also examines fine-tuning protocols, representation interpretability, and calibration of uncertainty after SSL pretraining, with the goal of deploying pretrained models that accelerate discovery and lower systematic biases in physics analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neutrino physics applications and IceCube analyses
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johann applies machine learning solutions to core neutrino-physics questions probed by IceCube: separating atmospheric and astrophysical neutrino fluxes, reconstructing neutrino energy and arrival direction, and identifying rare topologies such as tau neutrinos or neutrino-induced cascades. Johann integrates ML-driven outputs into physics analyses, quantifying impacts on sensitivities for point-source searches, diffuse flux measurements, and oscillation studies. Priority is given to methods that provide uncertainty estimates and are interpretable to enable robust systematic studies. Johann collaborates closely with experimental teams to ensure that ML improvements translate into stronger physics constraints while maintaining consistency with traditional reconstruction and calibration pipelines.

Name: Marc Jacquart
Affiliation: Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph Neural Networks for Sparse Detector Arrays
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Marc investigates graph neural networks (GNNs) as a principled approach to analyse data from sparse, irregularly spaced sensor arrays such as those in neutrino telescopes and distributed optical imagers. He is interested in representing detector elements and their optical/electrical coupling as graph nodes and edges to perform event classification, hit-level denoising, and direction/energy regression in a way that respects detector geometry and variable multiplicity. Marc aims to apply GNNs for robust background rejection and uncertainty-aware reconstruction, enabling improved sensitivity in low-signal regimes and greater resilience to missing or malfunctioning channels. He is also exploring how GNN architectures can be efficiently deployed for near-real-time inference on edge hardware used in fielded instruments, combining physics-driven priors with learned features for interpretable, portable processing pipelines.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neutrino Event Reconstruction & IceCube Applications
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Marc pursues methods to improve neutrino event reconstruction, calibration, and multi-messenger triggering with a focus on IceCube-like detectors. He studies how advanced ML — including deep learning and hybrid physics-ML approaches — can enhance vertex/time reconstruction, energy estimation, and particle identification in the presence of scattering, absorption, and sparse photoelectron statistics. Marc emphasizes rigorous validation against simulated and calibration datasets, quantification of systematic uncertainties, and transferability between lab-calibrated components and in-ice performance. He is particularly interested in algorithms that enable low-latency alerts for follow-up observations and that scale to large detector volumes while retaining interpretability necessary for cross-collaboration deployment and publication-quality analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: High‑Resolution Imaging, Spectroscopy & Onboard ML for Remote Sensing
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Marc focuses on the design and validation of high-resolution imaging spectrometers and active imagers across airborne, orbital, and laboratory platforms, and on integrating machine learning for on-board and real-time processing. He develops dual-band MWIR/LWIR systems and flash-lidar imagers where ML can enable superresolution, automated target tracking, anomaly detection, and compressed sensing for bandwidth-limited CubeSat links. Marc is also exploring ML approaches to extract subtle spectral signatures from long‑coherence 2D‑IR detectors and to accelerate end-to-end atmospheric and instrument modelling for quantitative retrievals. A key objective is creating deployable, validated ML pipelines that bridge laboratory spectroscopy, field testing, and student-built satellites to improve situational awareness, environmental monitoring, and science-driven operational sensors.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Energy Systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Kasper explores the application of machine learning to operational and planning problems in the energy sector, with a focus on tools that can scale from research prototypes to real-world utility deployments. He is interested in forecasting demand and production, optimizing storage and dispatch, and designing data-driven controls for distributed resources. Kasper prioritizes methods that respect physical constraints and provide interpretable, robust predictions suitable for regulatory and industrial contexts. His current work for a thesis combines large-scale time series analysis, feature engineering for heterogeneous sensor networks, and frameworks for validating models against domain benchmarks. He aims to bridge academic ML advances with practical energy-system needs to improve resilience, cost-efficiency, and integration of variable renewables.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generative Models & Applied ML in Startups
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Kasper investigates generative modelling techniques and their pragmatic use in entrepreneurial environments. He studies how variational autoencoders, diffusion models, and conditional generators can produce realistic synthetic datasets, accelerate anomaly detection, or support scenario generation for energy and climate applications. In the startup context he cares about rapid prototyping, model interpretability, sample efficiency, and deployment constraints such as latency and limited labels. Kasper is also interested in evaluation metrics and practices that ensure generative outputs are physically plausible and useful to stakeholders. By combining research-grade generative methods with product-focused MLOps, he seeks to enable small teams to deliver value quickly while maintaining scientific rigor and reproducibility.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Climate Physics and Data-driven Climate Analysis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Kasper brings a physics-informed perspective to climate change research, integrating computational methods from computer science with core physical understanding of atmospheric and energy systems. His interests include leveraging large climate datasets and Earth system model outputs to study regional impacts, downscaling, and attribution of extreme events. He works on uncertainty quantification, interpretable surrogate models, and hybrid approaches that combine process-based models with machine learning to respect conservation laws and thermodynamics. Kasper values collaborations that connect domain scientists, data engineers, and policymakers to translate analytical results into actionable insights for mitigation and adaptation, and he aims to make his thesis work applicable to both academic and decision-making communities.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformer-driven neutrino event reconstruction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Cyan explores advanced transformer architectures to improve reconstruction and classification of neutrino events in sparse, high-latency detector data. Cyan focuses on applying positional encoding strategies tailored to the geometry and timing of optical sensor arrays, enabling sequence- and graph-aware models to capture the spatiotemporal structure of Cherenkov light patterns. Work emphasizes robustness to noise, calibration shifts, and incomplete coverage, using techniques such as domain adaptation, uncertainty quantification, and interpretability methods to make model outputs physically meaningful. Cyan aims to bridge modern ML advances with detector-specific constraints, producing scalable pipelines that can run on both offline analysis and near-real-time alert systems for multimessenger follow-up.

research_interests.research_interest_title: IceCube instrumentation and neutrino astrophysics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Cyan investigates the physics of neutrino detection and the astrophysical interpretation of IceCube observations, combining expertise in particle interactions, sensor characterization, and large-scale data analysis. Cyan works on optimizing event selection, background rejection (including atmospheric muons and neutrinos), and energy/angular reconstruction to increase sensitivity to transient and steady astrophysical sources. Research includes studying calibration strategies, in-situ environmental effects, and the integration of IceCube data with electromagnetic and gravitational-wave observatories for multimessenger science. Cyan is particularly interested in developing methods that translate detector-level improvements into enhanced discovery potential for cosmic accelerators and tests of fundamental particle properties.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Climate and atmospheric dynamics relevant to observatories
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Cyan studies climate science and meteorology with an emphasis on processes that affect ground- and ice-based observatories, including atmospheric transport, temperature profiles, and seasonal variability. This interest spans modeling of atmospheric backgrounds that modulate detector noise, assessing how changing climate conditions impact site performance and long-term operations, and using meteorological datasets to refine event background models. Cyan combines physical understanding of atmospheric dynamics with data-driven techniques to quantify environmental impacts on measurements and to design mitigation strategies. The goal is to ensure reliable interpretation of observational data while contributing to interdisciplinary work at the intersection of Earth system science and experimental astrophysics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Mathematical foundations of machine learning and kernel methods
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Robert focuses on the rigorous mathematical and learning-theoretic underpinnings of machine learning, with particular emphasis on kernel methods and sampling theory. He investigates generalisation bounds, kernel design, and sampling strategies that are tailored to problems in atomic physics and materials science, seeking provable guarantees that link data structure to algorithmic performance. Robert is interested in bridging abstract learning theory with practical model-building by developing kernels that respect physical symmetries, quantifying sample complexity in high-dimensional quantum settings, and characterising the limits of reconstruction and interpolation from physically constrained measurements. His work aims to deliver tools that are both mathematically sound and practically deployable for scientists who want transparent, reliable ML components in computational experiments and data-driven discovery.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Relativistic quantum information and entanglement harvesting
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Robert studies how information and entanglement propagate in quantum fields across flat and curved spacetimes, combining conceptual questions with rigorous proofs and operational protocols. He develops and analyses models—often via Unruh–DeWitt detector frameworks—that probe when entanglement can be extracted from the vacuum, how to distinguish genuine entanglement harvesting from communication-assisted effects, and the circumstances that permit communication without net energy transfer. His research addresses entanglement behaviour near acceleration and black-hole horizons, including lensing-amplified vacuum correlations, and formulates no-go theorems and bounds on entanglement extraction from bilocal sources. Robert’s approach emphasizes clear operational definitions and mathematically controlled approximations to illuminate foundational aspects of quantum field theory and open quantum systems in relativistic settings.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Nonperturbative many-body and quantum-optical methods
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Robert develops and applies nonperturbative techniques to treat ultra-strong coupling regimes, giant atoms, and observables beyond common approximations in quantum optics and many-body physics. He leverages chain-mapping and Lanczos transformations together with matrix-product-state simulations to obtain numerically exact descriptions of light–matter interactions, energy-transport mechanisms, and signalling across horizons. His interests include deriving rigorous limits on broadcasting and qubit-transfer motivated by no-cloning, quantifying minimal energy costs for entanglement extraction, and building constrained random models to capture mode correlations in curved-spacetime scenarios. Robert also explores fermionic entropies and structures in causal fermion systems, aiming to connect abstract mathematical frameworks with computational methods that can handle realistic, strongly coupled quantum systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Deep learning for time-series prediction in quantum sensing
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jia applies deep-learning time-series methods to problems in quantum sensing and interferometric metrology. She focuses on using recurrent and attention-based architectures (LSTM, GRU, Transformer) to predict and denoise continuous sensor streams—phase readouts from SU(1,1) and nested SU(2)-in-SU(1,1) interferometers, atomic spin oscillator outputs, and broadband squeezed-light measurements. Jia combines physics-informed priors and model-based constraints with data-driven learning to improve generalization from limited experimental data, enable real-time forecasting of drift and noise, and produce uncertainty-aware estimates suitable for feedback and control. Her approach emphasizes robustness to loss, nonstationary noise, and limited labeling, while integrating waveform-processing techniques (wavelets) and online adaptation for deployed instruments. The objective is to translate sequence-model gains into measurable improvements in phase sensitivity, SNR, and calibration speed for laboratory and field metrology applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Recurrent and attention-based sequence models (LSTM, Transformer)
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jia studies recurrent and attention-based sequence models—LSTM, GRU and Transformer architectures—with the aim of mastering their capabilities and limitations for experimental time-series. She investigates architecture selection, memory horizons, positional-encoding strategies, and sparsity/regularization techniques tailored to limited and noisy laboratory datasets. Jia explores supervised and self-supervised objectives, data augmentation, curriculum learning, and transfer learning from simulated to experimental signals to reduce overfitting and improve sample efficiency. She evaluates training regimes, loss functions, and calibration of predicted uncertainties to ensure reliability for metrological decision-making. Practical targets include low-latency implementations for real-time control, quantifying how model choices affect ability to forecast transient disturbances, and building interpretable modules that expose physically meaningful modes (e.g., spin oscillation frequencies, interferometer fringe evolution).

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum convolutional neural networks and hybrid modeling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jia pursues quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) and hybrid quantum–classical models to analyze and classify quantum optical measurement data and to probe potential quantum advantages in sensing pipelines. She investigates circuit ansätze that emulate convolutional filters acting on multimode photonic or spin-variable encodings, and studies how noise, loss, and finite squeezing affect QCNN performance compared to classical CNNs. Jia develops hybrid training strategies that combine classical pretraining on simulated data, fine-tuning with experimental measurements (twin-beam squeezing, four-wave mixing outputs), and variational quantum circuits for feature extraction. Applications include discriminating subtle phase shifts, identifying correlated noise patterns across detectors, and designing compact quantum-enhanced classifiers embedded in control loops. Emphasis is placed on realistic resource accounting, implementability on near-term quantum processors or photonic hardware, and interoperability with classical signal-processing pipelines used in instrumentation.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Convolutional Neural Networks for Earth Observations
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Josephine develops and applies convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures to extract physical signals from Earth observation data. She focuses on adapting CNNs to handle multi-resolution satellite imagery, radar returns and seismic sections, addressing challenges such as limited labelled data, spatial heterogeneity and the need for model interpretability. Her work explores transfer learning, data augmentation, and physics-aware network designs to embed geophysical constraints directly into architectures. Josephine is particularly interested in uncertainty quantification for CNN predictions and in creating models that can generalize across regions and instruments. She aims to combine classical signal-processing insights with modern deep learning to produce robust, explainable tools for geoscientific analysis and to discover methodological advances through collaboration and cross-disciplinary exchange.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Glaciology and Ice Dynamics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Josephine studies glacier and ice-sheet processes by integrating observations, numerical models and machine learning techniques. Her interests include mapping surface and subglacial features from remote sensing, diagnosing ice-flow anomalies, and inferring basal conditions that control fast flow and instabilities. She seeks to merge physical ice-dynamics constraints with data-driven methods to improve short- and long-term predictions of glacier response to climate forcing. Field measurements, radar imaging and time-series satellite data are central to her approach, and she is keen to develop tools that translate observational patterns into mechanistic insight. Networking with glaciologists and method developers inspires Josephine to explore new measurement types and analytical approaches that better capture the coupled behavior of ice, hydrology and climate.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Multimodal Geophysical Data Integration & Inversion
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Josephine works on integrating diverse geophysical datasets—seismic, gravity, electromagnetic, and remote-sensing products—into coherent subsurface models. She is interested in joint inversion strategies, data assimilation and hybrid frameworks that combine physics-based forward models with machine-learned surrogates to accelerate inference. Her research emphasizes robust uncertainty quantification, scalability to large regional problems, and methods to reconcile inconsistent or sparse observations. Josephine explores using CNNs and other ML tools to learn efficient representations for complex forward operators and to guide adaptive survey design. By bridging geophysical theory and modern computational methods, she aims to enable more accurate imaging of the Earth’s interior and to discover novel algorithms through collaboration across disciplines.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Dissipative quantum dynamics and engineered Lindbladians
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Michael studies the mathematical foundations and practical design of open quantum systems with a focus on engineered dissipation. Michael develops and analyzes Lindbladian models for dissipative state preparation, timed dissipative gadgets, and cavity-mediated entanglement protocols, combining rigorous estimates (mixing times, cutoff phenomena, χ^2-divergence) with constructive dissipative engineering prescriptions. Michael connects functional-analytic tools—non-commutative log-Sobolev and Nash inequalities, Hilbert’s projective metric, and hypercontractivity—to dynamics relevant for quantum thermodynamics and thermalization, and uses those connections to prove bounds on rapid mixing and to design efficient dissipative maps for target states. Michael’s work bridges abstract operator-algebraic techniques with implementable primitives for near-term experiments, emphasizing how controlled dissipation can be a resource for robust state preparation and for bounding the complexity of quantum simulation tasks.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum information, error correction and topological memories
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Michael investigates quantum information protection in many-body and condensed-matter settings, with particular emphasis on error correction, topological memories, and dynamical decoders. Michael analyzes limits on quantum storage, cellular-automaton and dissipative decoders, and emergent symmetry-breaking in driven-dissipative lattices to understand stability of encoded information under realistic noise models. Michael studies locality–gap relations for projected entangled pair states (PEPS) and derives criteria linking spectral gaps, clustering of correlations, and rapid mixing to efficient thermal-state preparation and memory lifetimes. Michael’s research unites rigorous bounds with candidate architectures, exploring how local interactions and engineered dissipation can enable scalable, robust quantum memories and how renormalization-like techniques inform decoder design and fault-tolerance thresholds.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Tensor networks, variational algorithms and machine-learning for many-body systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Michael develops algorithms and theory for variational and learning-based simulation of many-body quantum systems, emphasizing tensor-network methods and neural-network quantum states. Michael analyzes expressivity and learning geometry of restricted Boltzmann machines, studies natural-gradient and linear-method optimizers for VQE, and constructs tensor-network simulations for boson sampling and financial applications. Michael is particularly interested in bridging tensor-network techniques with moderate uses of physics-informed neural nets (PINNs) and neural operators to accelerate continuum limits and learn effective low-dimensional dynamics. Michael also proves complexity and simulation results (dissipative Church–Turing theorem, Gibbs sampling bounds) and designs efficient samplers and Metropolis-like constructions to make variational and learning approaches practical for near-term quantum devices and classical emulators.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Exotic BSM searches in ATLAS
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Simon develops and applies machine-learning techniques to search for exotic beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) signatures in the ATLAS experiment. He is particularly interested in using graph-based representations of detector information to capture non-standard topologies—displaced vertices, long-lived particles, and unusual energy deposit patterns—that can evade conventional reconstruction chains. Simon works on designing end-to-end pipelines that combine low-level calorimeter and tracking hits with GNN-driven feature extraction and classification, optimizing sensitivity while controlling backgrounds. He also explores trigger-level implementations to enable real-time selection of rare events, evaluating resource and latency constraints of deployment on experimental hardware. Through simulation studies and collaborations with experimental groups, Simon aims to translate novel architectures into robust searches that improve discovery potential for unconventional new physics scenarios at the LHC.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph Neural Networks for detector data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Simon focuses on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) as a natural framework to model the irregular, relational data produced by particle detectors. He investigates message-passing architectures, attention mechanisms, and permutation-invariant pooling schemes to reconstruct complex objects such as jets, track segments, and particle flow candidates. Simon evaluates different graph construction strategies—edge definitions, dynamic graphs, and sparsification—to balance performance with computational cost, and benchmarks architectures on standard and bespoke HEP datasets. He is also interested in training strategies that leverage weak supervision, contrastive learning, and multi-task objectives to improve generalization across simulation and real data. Through profiling and optimization, Simon aims to make GNNs scalable for large event topologies and suitable for integration into common ATLAS analysis workflows.

research_interests.research_interest_title: ML methods, uncertainty & deployment for HEP
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Simon is interested in machine-learning methodologies that address the practical challenges of high-energy physics: limited simulation fidelity, systematic uncertainties, interpretability, and deployment. He studies domain adaptation and simulation-to-real techniques to reduce biases when transferring models trained on Monte Carlo to ATLAS collision data, and explores uncertainty quantification methods—calibrated probabilistic outputs, Bayesian approximations, and ensemble approaches—to provide robust significance estimates. Simon also prioritizes model interpretability, developing tools to visualize learned graph features, attribute importance, and failure modes so that results are trustworthy to physicists. Finally, he evaluates latency and resource-efficient inference strategies, such as model compression and hardware-aware design, to enable adoption within trigger and reconstruction chains.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Few‑body quantum scattering and resonances
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Balazs develops and applies advanced theoretical and numerical methods to describe bound, resonant and scattering states of charged few‑body quantum systems. His work implements formulations such as the Faddeev–Merkuriev integral equations and Coulomb‑Sturmian separable expansions together with continued‑fraction representations of Green’s operators, stochastic variational Gaussian bases, complex scaling and Gamow‑state techniques. These methods are used to compute electron–electron–positron resonances (including S‑state structure up to n=5), H− and three‑alpha resonances, and to demonstrate Efimov‑type accumulation near two‑body thresholds. Balazs also studies alpha‑like structures in 12C and relativistic single‑particle continuum phenomena relevant across nuclear, atomic and molecular contexts, producing precise benchmarks and physically transparent descriptions of few‑body continuum dynamics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning and foundation models for physics imagery and video
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Balazs is interested in applying foundation models and modern machine learning to image and video modalities arising in physics: detector readouts, simulated event visualizations, microscopy and time‑dependent simulation outputs. He explores how large pretrained architectures and multimodal models can accelerate detection, classification and anomaly discovery while respecting physics priors and uncertainty quantification. Key emphases include domain adaptation from simulation to experiment, physics‑informed architectures, interpretable latent representations, active learning for scarce labelled data, and automated pipelines that couple numerical solvers to learned surrogates. By combining his expertise in rigorous numerical methods with foundation model techniques, Balazs aims to help create robust, reproducible tools for automated scientific research on complex image and video data.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Distributed e‑infrastructure, middleware and sustainable HPC
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Balazs works on middleware, information models and architectures that enable large‑scale scientific computing across Grids, hybrid clouds and HPC environments. He has contributed to GLUE schema versions 1.3 and 2.0, participated in the European Middleware Initiative and MEDIA collaborations, and continued development of the ARC Compute Element. He leads practical deployments — from ATLAS data challenges on NorduGrid to lightweight distributed computing for LDMX and services such as the DNS‑embedded registry ARCHERY. Recurring themes in his work are interoperability, minimal‑intrusion deployment, sustainability, reproducible release processes and rigorous quality assurance. Balazs focuses on scalable orchestration of compute and data, metadata and registry services, and pragmatic architectures that support long‑lived scientific collaborations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Detector–AI integration and physics-aware architectures
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Michał focuses on tight integration between radiation detectors and machine learning pipelines to produce robust, interpretable, and deployable systems for experimental physics. He works to bridge hardware realities (timing resolution, charge collection, readout constraints) with algorithm design, ensuring that models respect detector response, calibration drifts, and latency requirements. His interest includes developing modular workflows where neural networks are co-designed with detector electronics, validation with realistic testbeds, and strategies for uncertainty propagation from sensor output through inference. Michał seeks collaborations that combine expertise in instrumentation, real-time inference, and model interpretability to produce AI components that are physically grounded, traceable, and suitable for production in physics experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics‑Informed Neural Networks for photon–matter and particle simulations
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Michał is exploring Physics‑Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) as a pathway to embed conservation laws, boundary conditions, and known transport physics directly into learning models for photon interactions, charge transport, and particle scattering. He aims to use PINNs to accelerate or complement Monte Carlo and PDE-based simulators, produce differentiable surrogate models for inverse problems, and enforce physically meaningful constraints that improve generalisation from limited data. His work targets hybridization of domain knowledge and data-driven components, calibration of PINNs against experimental benchmarks, and quantification of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties. Michał is particularly interested in using PINNs to make simulation workflows faster, more interpretable, and better coupled to experimental detector behaviour.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Nanosecond-scale time-series ML for photon event reconstruction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Michał develops machine learning methods tailored to nanosecond-resolved photon interaction time-series, applying MLPs, CNNs and temporal architectures to denoise, classify and reconstruct event-level quantities from raw readout traces. He investigates feature extraction strategies, temporal convolutions, and architecture inductive biases that respect causality and detector physics, with an emphasis on high-throughput, low-latency inference for real-time processing. His interests include synthetic data generation for rare event regimes, domain adaptation between simulated and laboratory data, and hardware-aware model compression for field deployment. Collaborations that couple signal-processing expertise, detector characterization, and requirements from downstream physics analyses are a priority to translate time-series ML into reliable scientific measurements.
