research_interests.research_interest_title: High‑dimensional Quantum Photonics and Free‑Space Quantum Links
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mario develops and implements high‑dimensional photonic science that expands practical quantum information carriers beyond qubits. Mario's experimental program spans orbital angular momentum (OAM) and structured modes (Laguerre‑ and Ince‑Gauss), demonstrating very‑high OAM entanglement, (100×100)-dimensional bipartite states, multi‑photon high‑dimensional GHZ/qutrits, and high‑dimensional teleportation. Mario also builds single‑photon Pauli‑X gates, radial‑mode sorters, and long‑range free‑space transmission systems that operate across urban and intersite links (up to 143 km), including turbulence forecasting for secure quantum channels. Mario couples theoretical design with practical laboratory implementations, optimizing mode generation, detection, and error mitigation for scalable quantum communications and sensing. The work emphasizes harnessing large Hilbert spaces to increase information capacity, robustness to noise, and real‑world deployability of advanced photonic quantum protocols.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph‑Theoretic Foundations of Photonic Interference and Entanglement
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mario formulates conceptual and computational frameworks that reveal deep connections between photonic experiments and graph/hypergraph theory, enabling new perspectives on quantum interference and entanglement. Mario introduced the concept of “entanglement by path identity” and mapped multi‑photon interference patterns to perfect matchings in graphs, exposing links to #P complexity and computational hardness. Mario develops tools to translate optical layouts into combinatorial objects, using hypergraphs to classify multi‑photon correlations and to predict novel interference phenomena based on path indistinguishability. This line of work clarifies which experiments can generate complex entangled states, identifies resource requirements, and guides automated design by framing experimental possibilities as graph‑theoretic search problems. Mario's approach unites abstract computational complexity with physically realizable optical circuits, providing conceptual insight and practical heuristics for experimenters.

research_interests.research_interest_title: AI‑Driven Discovery and Robust Molecular/Materials Design
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mario designs and applies AI, algorithmic, and human‑machine tools to accelerate discovery in photonics, chemistry, and materials. Mario created and benchmarked automated experiment‑design systems (Melvin, PyTheus, Theseus, Klaus, TAROQQO, XLuminA) that search vast design spaces for implementable optical circuits and novel quantum experiments. In chemistry and materials Mario co‑founded SELFIES and developed STONED, PASITHEA and hybrid strategies (GA+DNN, curiosity‑driven RL) for robust generative and exploratory molecular search. Mario emphasizes interpretability — applying deep‑dreaming, LSTM analyses, language‑model meta‑design, logic‑SAT encodings, and VR tools — so that machine suggestions can be understood and transferred to the lab. Mario integrates benchmarking, human‑in‑the‑loop refinement, and experimental constraints to produce reproducible, deployable designs, bridging digital ideation and laboratory realization for faster, trustworthy scientific discovery.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Multiscale Particle-based Plasma Simulation & GPU PIC
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christoph develops and applies particle-based, multiscale simulation methods to capture kinetic plasma phenomena across laboratory, atmospheric and astrophysical settings. He focuses on particle-in-cell (PIC) and Monte Carlo approaches implemented for modern high-performance hardware, including 3D GPU-parallel engines (ASTRAP) and adaptive-fluid couplings (AMReX). Christoph works on algorithmic innovations that bridge microphysics and macroscale observables: efficient hybrid schemes for runaway-electron dynamics, scalable collision and cross-section treatments, and coupling strategies that combine kinetic and fluid representations. His interest includes optimizing parallel performance, ensuring numerical fidelity for stochastic processes, and producing synthetic diagnostics that let simulations be directly compared with measurements. Christoph seeks techniques that make large, multiscale kinetic calculations tractable while preserving the underlying particle physics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Atmospheric Electricity, Streamer Dynamics & High‑Energy Emissions
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christoph investigates the physics of gas discharges in planetary atmospheres, with emphasis on streamer coronas, lightning leader formation and associated high-energy signatures such as terrestrial gamma‑ray flashes (TGFs), X‑rays, positrons and neutrons. He studies detailed collisional and radiative microphysics, including novel cross sections (electron–electron bremsstrahlung and refined Bethe–Heitler treatments), and simulates streamer collisions, pre‑ionization effects, air‑density perturbations and space‑leader evolution using coupled PIC/Monte Carlo tools. Christoph places simulations into observational context through direct comparisons with instruments like ASIM, LIS and radio arrays, and explores transient optical phenomena (blue corona discharges, elves, sprites). His aim is to connect kinetic-scale discharge processes to measurable electromagnetic and particle emissions, improving interpretation of high-energy atmospheric observations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Particle Monte Carlo Methods for Nucleation, Planetary Discharges & Astrophysical Plasmas
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Christoph applies particle Monte Carlo techniques beyond traditional plasmas to problems such as nanoscale nucleation, cluster growth and astrophysical instability-driven radiation. He models H2SO4–H2O and TiO2 cluster formation to reveal stochastic, ion‑mediated growth pathways and nanocluster mobility effects, and couples particle Monte Carlo with continuum finite‑element methods (FEM+random‑walk) for nanoscale electrodeposition. In astrophysical contexts he uses PIC and Monte Carlo tools to examine relativistic jet microphysics (Weibel, kKHI, MI instabilities) and synthetic jitter‑like spectra. Christoph is interested in transferable stochastic modeling strategies and hybrid algorithms that can treat charged-particle kinetics, nucleation kinetics and transport consistently across disparate physical regimes and scales.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Ice‑sheet dynamics and palaeoclimate reconstruction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mikkel investigates Greenland Ice Sheet dynamics through physics‑based modelling and model–data integration to reconstruct past evolution and quantify sea‑level contributions. His work uses the Parallel Ice Sheet Model (PISM), large ensembles (hundreds of members), and Bayesian/MCMC calibration of mass‑balance schemes to constrain Holocene and glacial–interglacial changes, including documented events such as an ice‑bridge collapse ~4.9 ± 0.5 ka. He combines ice‑core elevation histories, GPS, and remote sensing to interrogate interior stability and ongoing transient responses, and explores sensitivity to interannual temperature variability. Mikkel emphasises robust uncertainty quantification, diagnostic metrics, and paleoproxy constraints to produce reproducible reconstructions that link process understanding to regional and global sea‑level implications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neural networks and machine‑learning methods for geoscience
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mikkel is focused on applying and critically evaluating neural networks as tools for geoscientific inference and model acceleration. He is particularly interested in surrogate modelling, physics‑informed architectures, and integrating NNs with mechanistic ice‑sheet and geophysical models to speed ensemble experiments and enable richer Bayesian calibration. His work examines how learned models handle nonstationarity, interannual variability, and extrapolation beyond training regimes, while retaining interpretable diagnostics for physical plausibility. Mikkel also seeks cross‑disciplinary lessons on how different fields use NNs for noisy, sparse, or heterogeneous data, and how uncertainty estimates from ML can be reconciled with traditional ensemble and MCMC approaches to produce robust, decision‑relevant predictions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Instrumentation, inversion and rigorous uncertainty quantification
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mikkel develops and applies novel measurement and inversion methods across domains — from airborne distributed fiber‑optic seismology and Backus–Gilbert inversions that resolve multiple wave modes and high‑resolution S‑wave profiles, to robust spectrometric techniques for biochemical assays. He combines methodological innovation with statistical rigor: designing diagnostics, deterministic inversions, random‑matrix theory contributions, and MCMC calibration workflows that characterise systematic and aleatoric uncertainty. This interest encompasses improving surface‑energy models (dEBM), reconstructing glacier variability from sediment records, and creating reproducible pipelines that link instrument design, forward modelling, and probabilistic inference so that observational advances directly inform mechanistic understanding.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Cold ISM, Dust and Multi-line Diagnostics in Early Galaxies
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Minju studies the cold interstellar medium and dust properties of galaxies from the local universe to cosmic dawn by exploiting multi-wavelength facilities (ALMA, JWST, VLA, NOEMA, HST and large spectrographs). Minju focuses on far‑IR/submm fine‑structure lines ([CII], [OIII], [NII], [OI]), multiple CO and [CI] transitions, and dust continuum to derive gas, metal and dust masses, excitation conditions, and obscured star‑formation across z~0–8. A recurring goal is to constrain dust production and the physical state of ISM in very early systems (including z>8 candidates and hot dust constraints) through combined line+continuum diagnostics and statistical stacking. Minju bridges detailed case studies and survey-level analyses to quantify how dust, metals and cold gas evolve across cosmic time and to provide observational constraints that inform models of galaxy assembly and chemical enrichment.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Internal Dynamics, Accretion and Feedback in Galaxies
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Minju investigates internal physics and kinematics of galaxies with an emphasis on compact and clumpy starbursts, radial inflows, non‑corotating accretion, baryon‑dominated disks, and reduced inner dark matter signatures. Minju combines high-resolution imaging and spectroscopy to recover rotation, dispersion, inflow/outflow signatures and to isolate signatures of molecular tori, shocks and AGN‑driven feedback. Work spans targeted case studies (including lensing-reconstructed systems) and statistical kinematic analyses from deep ALMA and optical/IR surveys, aiming to connect small‑scale dynamical processes to global galaxy growth and quenching. Minju places particular weight on disentangling overlapping kinematic components, quantifying mass distributions, and assessing how environment and AGN interplay shape the baryon cycle.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Interferometry, Survey Analysis and Instrument Science
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Minju is interested in bringing modern ML tools—particularly convolutional neural networks and graph neural networks—to problems in interferometric imaging, survey analysis and instrument development. Minju seeks to apply CNNs for denoising, deconvolution, source detection and morphological classification in multi-band continuum and spectral‑line cubes, while using GNNs to represent interferometer sampling patterns, telescope networks and complex relational structure in lensed or clustered fields. Emphasis is on uv‑domain stacking, high‑resolution lensing reconstructions, explainable ML for physical parameter inference, and training strategies that combine realistic simulations with limited labels. Minju aims to use hands‑on AI workflows to accelerate science from ALMA, JWST and future facilities and to integrate ML pipelines into large survey and instrument design efforts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Temporal and multi-scale network methodology
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Sune develops principled, scalable methods to characterize and model complex networks that evolve across time and organizational scales. His work spans link- and hierarchical-link community detection, node-level layer coupling, extensions to Infomap, and embedding approaches such as HBDM, with an emphasis on generative and statistical models that capture realistic temporal structure. Sune also designs algorithms for surrogate temporal-network generation and model validation, enabling robust hypothesis testing on high-resolution empirical data. The methodological contributions prioritize scalability, interpretability, and integration with causal or experimental designs, making them directly applicable to problems in science-of-science, urban systems, and digital contagion. He routinely demonstrates how these tools reveal latent mesoscale structures and dynamic processes that simpler static analyses miss.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Human mobility, sensing and behavioral rhythms
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Sune studies human movement and daily behavior using large-scale, high-resolution sensor datasets (notably the Copenhagen Networks Study) collected from mobile phones, wearables, WiFi and Bluetooth. He characterizes conserved location sets, mobility predictability, trip-frequency laws, and proximity inference from WiFi signals, combining empirical analysis with compact models. Sune also probes temporal patterns such as chronotypes and sleep using NMF and Bayesian sleep models, and links individual mobility and social-network features to outcomes like academic or team performance. Across this work he emphasizes reproducible, privacy-aware processing of sensitive sensor streams and the extraction of actionable, interpretable insights for urban science, workplace design, and personalized interventions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Epidemic dynamics, contact tracing and privacy-preserving interventions
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Sune evaluates epidemic processes on empirical contact networks and designs evidence-based interventions that respect privacy and scalability. He combines detailed proximity data with epidemic models to assess manual and digital contact tracing, exploring decentralized architectures and their trade-offs for effectiveness and user privacy. His research connects behavioral signals, mobility, and pathogen genomics to understand transmission pathways and intervention impacts, and he uses experiments and causal inference where possible to validate tools in real-world settings. Sune prioritizes interpretable models and policy-relevant recommendations, providing quantitative guidance on tracing strategies, testing regimes, and mitigation measures for public-health decision-makers.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Photometric and Image-based Classification of Transients
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Giorgos focuses on developing robust classification pipelines that identify the physical nature of explosive transients from photometry and host-galaxy images when spectroscopy is unavailable. He is interested in applying and comparing classical methods (random forests) and modern deep-learning approaches (convolutional neural networks and transformer-based models) to noisy, irregularly sampled light curves and to heterogeneous image data. His work emphasizes probabilistic outputs, domain adaptation between surveys (e.g., Rubin-era vs. legacy datasets), active learning to prioritize scarce spectroscopic labels, and interpretability to connect learned features with astrophysical diagnostics. The goal is to enable reliable population studies and efficient follow-up strategies for surveys producing millions of transient alerts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Time-series Modelling and Early Classification of Light Curves
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Giorgos explores advanced time-series methodologies to model transient brightness evolution across multiple wavelengths and to enable early, accurate classification. He investigates Gaussian-process frameworks for uncertainty-aware interpolation, sequential neural networks and transformer architectures for capturing long-term dependencies, and hybrid models that combine physical light-curve templates with machine-learned residuals. Emphasis is placed on forecasting observables, quantifying selection biases, producing calibrated probabilistic class assignments early in an event's evolution, and integrating multi-messenger triggers. This research aims to extract maximal physical information (e.g., rise times, peak luminosities) from partial light curves to inform rapid spectroscopic or multi-band follow-up while maintaining rigorous error propagation for cosmology and population inference.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Real-time Alert Filtering, Anomaly Detection and Follow-up Prioritization
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Giorgos is interested in real-time ML systems that sift high-volume alert streams to detect unusual transients and prioritize targets for limited follow-up resources. He studies streaming anomaly-detection algorithms, ranking models that combine scientific value and observational feasibility, and reinforcement-learning or utility-based frameworks to optimize follow-up scheduling across multi-facility networks. Practical concerns include latency, robustness to non-astrophysical artifacts, explainable scoring for human vetting, and interoperability with broker and telescope APIs. The aim is to enable rapid discovery of rare phenomena (e.g., kilonovae, unusual SLSNe, relativistic explosions) and to coordinate timely spectroscopy or polarimetry to maximize scientific return in the Rubin and multi-messenger era.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Relativistic Two‑Body Dynamics & PM Hamiltonians
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhengwen develops and applies an effective-field-theory and scattering-based toolkit to the relativistic two-body problem in general relativity, with emphasis on Post-Minkowskian (PM) expansions for conservative and dissipative dynamics of compact binaries. Zhengwen computes scattering angles, reconstructs radial actions and Hamiltonians via the boundary-to-bound map, and systematically includes spin, tidal and finite-size effects to produce local Hamiltonians suitable for waveform and dynamics modeling. Methodological advances include the explicit treatment and removal of nonlocal-in-time tail terms, Schwinger–Keldysh in-in worldline EFT for radiation reaction, and cross-checks against scattering-amplitude and post-Newtonian results. Zhengwen's work bridges analytic results and phenomenology, providing high-precision inputs for gravitational-wave templates and fostering connections between collider multiloop techniques and gravitational two-body physics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Integrals, Sampling and Foundation Models
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhengwen explores machine-learning methods to accelerate multiloop Feynman integral evaluation and Monte Carlo sampling workflows relevant to both collider and gravitational-wave physics. Zhengwen applies boosted decision trees, neural networks and foundation models to learn integrand structures, propose importance sampling strategies, and to bootstrap master integrals across velocity orders. Zhengwen's approach couples physics-informed architectures with amplitude-inspired analytic constraints — differential equations, expansion by regions, and analytic continuation — enabling more efficient numerical integration and symbolic reconstruction. Zhengwen is also interested in how large pretrained models and generative techniques can encode perturbative patterns, assist in hypothesis generation, and integrate with traditional EFT and scattering frameworks to expand the reach of multiscale computations and reduce human overhead in high-precision predictions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Scattering Amplitudes, Multiloop Techniques and QCD Currents
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhengwen's research leverages scattering-amplitude technology to compute high-order analytic contributions in both gravity and gauge theories. Zhengwen develops differential-equation strategies for multiloop integrals, bootstraps master integrals to all orders in velocity, and uses expansion by regions and elliptic/iterated-elliptic integrals to capture subtle analytic structures. Complementary work addresses scattering-equation and twistor-string formulations, soft theorems, multi-soft QCD currents, and numerical algebraic methods for CHY solutions. By synthesizing amplitude methods with EFT and boundary-to-bound mappings, Zhengwen provides cross-checked results across PM and PN literature and supplies precision building blocks that inform both theoretical understanding of fundamental interactions and practical inputs for waveform modeling.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Space-based Particle Instrumentation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johan develops and flies space-based and ground-based high-energy particle instruments, with a long record on the PAMELA cosmic-ray mission. He leads payload design, calibration at CERN, and in-orbit performance studies of key subsystems such as the permanent-magnet silicon spectrometer, silicon–tungsten imaging calorimeter, time-of-flight, neutron detector, anticoincidence systems, and flight-level triggers and data handling. His work emphasizes electron–hadron separation, light-nuclei charge identification, antiproton/positron measurements, antinuclei searches and solar/heliospheric observations, combining detector physics with system-level engineering. Johan's approach balances sensitivity and reliability for harsh radiation and space environments, including vibration and irradiation qualification campaigns. He also translates instrument performance into astrophysical measurements, ensuring calibration, systematic-error control and robust operational techniques used on current experiments worldwide.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Radiation‑Hardened Electronics & Optical Links
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johan specializes in radiation-tolerant electronics and high-speed optical links for particle and collider detectors, developing and testing VCSEL devices, packaged components and readout architectures under irradiation. He conducts single-event upset analyses, total-ionizing-dose and displacement-damage experiments, and devises mitigation strategies including dual-link architectures and redundancy to maintain data integrity in harsh environments. His expertise spans high-speed serializer/deserializer design, optical transceivers, power-system behavior and harmonic distortion in converters, with a practical emphasis on manufacturability and space qualification. Johan integrates laboratory irradiation campaigns with system-level testing (vibration, thermal vacuum) and provides guidance for component selection, error detection/correction schemes and fault-tolerant readout design to ensure reliable long-term operation in both space missions and collider experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Image Regression & Diagnostics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Johan applies machine learning and neural-network methods to accelerator diagnostics, image regression and detector signal processing. He uses combinations of standard feedforward networks and convolutional neural networks in supervised training for regression tasks on images—calibration maps, calorimeter shower reconstruction, and charge identification—emphasizing robust data handling, preprocessing, and uncertainty quantification. Johan is interested in practical workflows: generating realistic training datasets from test-beam and flight data, simulation-to-real domain adaptation, augmentation strategies for radiation-induced artifacts, normalization and loss-function choices for regression, and evaluation metrics that reflect physics performance. He also explores ML for storage-ring tuning and RF optimization, combining frequency mapping features with learned models to accelerate commissioning and fault detection. Johan seeks advice on best practices for image data pipelines, training regimes, and deployment in constrained real-time environments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Halogen Cycling and Sea‑Ice Proxy Development
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Niccolo focuses on reconstructing past sea‑ice and halogen cycling by integrating high‑resolution ice‑core chemistry with statistical calibration and mechanistic interpretation. He developed and validated bromine enrichment (Brenr) as a first‑year sea‑ice proxy through satellite calibration and ARMA reconstructions, produced 120 kyr bromine‑based sea‑ice records, and generated the longest Northern Hemisphere iodine time series from RECAP, NEEM and EGRIP cores. His work couples proxy development with process understanding—linking halogen photochemistry, sea‑ice dynamics and ocean bioproductivity—to interpret palaeoclimate signals across sub‑decadal to 125 kyr timescales. Niccolo emphasizes rigorous proxy validation, uncertainty quantification, and the translation of multi‑archives (ice, marine sediment, atmosphere) into coherent reconstructions that inform past Arctic–Nordic variability and provide boundary conditions for future polar climate projections.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Hybrid Machine‑Learning & Physics‑Informed Models for Polar Processes
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Niccolo develops and applies hybrid machine‑learning approaches that combine data‑driven models with physical constraints to solve polar geoscience problems. He designs frameworks that leverage BDTs, neural networks, PINNs and GNNs to automate particle detection in continuous‑flow analysis (ICELEARNING), to generate synthetic glacier geometries (IceBoost and SKYNET-style generative/GNN architectures), and to fuse sparse ice‑core observations with process models for improved reconstructions. His research emphasizes interpretability and mechanistic consistency: embedding conservation laws, photochemical pathways and spatial graph structure into ML architectures to enhance extrapolation and physical plausibility. By bridging statistical learning and domain knowledge, Niccolo aims to produce robust, transferable tools for sea‑ice reconstruction, thickness and volume estimation, and the detection of abrupt climate events from multi‑sensor polar datasets.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Polar Atmospheric Chemistry, Aerosols and Climate–Health Impacts
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Niccolo investigates halogen‑driven atmospheric chemistry in polar regions and its consequences for aerosol formation, ozone and deposition with implications for climate and human health. He combines state‑of‑the‑art analytical methods (non‑target HRMS, ICP‑MS halogen analysis, low‑background neutron activation, high‑resolution CFA) with observational ice‑core and atmospheric records to quantify historical iodine and bromine variability and recent anthropogenic trends, including the post‑1950 tripling of atmospheric iodine. His research links halogen photochemistry and ocean bioproductivity to new‑particle formation, aerosol composition, tropospheric ozone modulation, and deposition pathways, assessing feedbacks on radiative balance and pollutant exposure. Niccolo emphasizes mechanistic attribution and the translation of palaeo‑chemical evidence into actionable understanding of present and future polar atmospheric impacts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Experimental Quantum Optomechanics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Peyman focuses on experimental quantum optomechanics, combining precision optics and mechanical resonators to probe quantum behavior at mesoscopic scales. As a PhD student he works hands-on with cavity optomechanical setups, alignment, cryogenic integration, and noise mitigation strategies. He is interested in advancing measurement sensitivity, ground-state cooling protocols, and coherent light–mechanical coupling for quantum control and information applications. Peyman seeks practical skills in designing robust experiments, characterizing mechanical and optical modes, and implementing feedback and feedforward control. He values approaches that bridge theory and experiment, using simulations and data to refine device geometry and readout strategies. Through collaborations he aims to translate optomechanical proof-of-principle demonstrations into reproducible techniques for sensing, transduction, and hybrid quantum systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Physical Modeling and Optimization
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Peyman is eager to learn and apply machine learning methods to physical model creation and experimental optimization. With no prior ML experience he aims to build foundational competence in supervised and unsupervised learning, parameter estimation, and model selection specifically tailored to physical systems. He is interested in using ML to accelerate inverse design of devices, optimize control sequences for cooling and state preparation, and extract weak signals embedded in noisy measurements. Peyman plans to learn practical workflows: preprocessing experimental data, building interpretable models, cross-validation, and integrating ML-based surrogates with numerical simulations. He values techniques that respect physical constraints, such as physics-informed neural networks and hybrid model-based/data-driven approaches, and seeks mentorship on best practices to avoid overfitting and ensure reproducibility in experimental quantum optics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Nanophotonics & Plasmonic Waveguides: Simulation and Fabrication
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Peyman’s background in photonics and plasmonic waveguides informs his interest in nanoscale light–matter interactions and device fabrication. During his master’s he worked on simulation and fabrication of plasmonic waveguides, developing skills in electromagnetic modeling, nanofabrication processes, and characterization techniques. He wants to continue exploring how subwavelength confinement, field enhancement, and dispersion engineering can be harnessed in integrated photonic and hybrid quantum systems. Peyman is particularly interested in optimizing fabrication tolerances, improving coupling between plasmonic and dielectric elements, and employing simulation-driven design to accelerate iteration cycles. By combining these skills with optomechanics and emerging ML tools, he aims to develop compact, high-performance photonic components for sensing, transduction, and on-chip quantum experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neuromorphic photonic computing and luminescent memory
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Oleksandr explores neuromorphic photonic computing by developing all-photonic luminescent memories and devices that leverage history-dependent photoluminescence and mixed ionic–electronic conduction. He introduced the memlumor, a device that unites volatile and nonvolatile dynamics across timescales from nanoseconds to minutes, using photodoping, photochemistry, and trap-state dynamics to encode and process information optically. His interest covers design principles for energy-efficient, fast photonic inference hardware, strategies for in-memory optical computing, and architectures that exploit intrinsic material hysteresis for state retention and spiking behavior. Oleksandr aims to translate materials-level phenomena into scalable neuromorphic functions, assessing device endurance, energy consumption, and integration pathways with conventional electronics and photonic interconnects.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Nanoscale time-resolved luminescence spectroscopy
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Oleksandr focuses on nanoscale optical spectroscopy and time-resolved luminescence to quantify charge trapping, hidden excitations, and dynamics of light emission in novel materials. He applies multipulse time-resolved photoluminescence and spatially resolved fluorescence mapping to disentangle fast photophysical processes from slower ionic and trap-mediated dynamics, enabling separation of electronic, excitonic, and chemical photodoping effects. His work emphasizes methods to extract carrier lifetimes, trap densities, and recombination pathways in perovskites, MOF crystals, and carbon-nanotube hybrid systems under realistic conditions. By combining temporal resolution across nanoseconds to minutes with nanoscale spatial probes, Oleksandr aims to link microscopic defect physics to macroscopic device behavior and to develop robust spectroscopic protocols for characterizing materials for optoelectronic and neuromorphic applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Multifunctional optoelectronic materials and device engineering
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Oleksandr works on materials and device engineering for multifunctional optoelectronic systems, including perovskite–SWCNT hybrids, metal–organic-framework single crystals, and aligned carbon-nanotube electrodes. He designs flexible, ambient-stable photodetectors and electroluminescent photodetectors that simultaneously emit and detect light using ion-modulated Schottky barriers, and develops fabrication techniques for free-standing, aligned films and composition-tunable microstructures. His interests include understanding device endurance under mechanical stress, ambient stability, and mixed ionic–electronic transport to enable multifunctionality such as combined sensing, emission, and memory. Oleksandr seeks to bridge materials synthesis, interface engineering, and scalable device architectures to create compact, energy-efficient optoelectronic components suitable for integrated photonics and neuromorphic hardware.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantitative Neurotrophin Signaling Modeling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Chao is focused on turning rich numerical measurements of receptor signaling into predictive, mechanistic models. He uses time‑series phosphorylation data, dose–response curves, and transport kinetics to infer how Trk and p75 cooperation, transactivation by GPCRs, and specific tyrosine phosphorylation events bias cells toward survival or apoptosis. Chao is interested in applying modern machine‑learning techniques for parameter estimation, model selection, and uncertainty quantification so that complex pathway hypotheses can be discriminated quantitatively. By combining mechanistic ordinary differential equation models with data‑driven components (surrogate models, emulators), he aims to accelerate hypothesis testing, identify minimal molecular switches that explain phenotypic outcomes, and produce interpretable predictors from numerical datasets gathered in biochemical and trafficking assays.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Proteomics and Trafficking Data Integration for Mechanistic Discovery
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Chao seeks to mine large proteomic and trafficking datasets (BONCAT/BONLAC labeling, mass spectrometry quantifications, and imaging‑derived transport traces) to discover novel modulators and regulatory motifs in neurotrophin biology. He is interested in supervised and unsupervised approaches to integrate orthogonal numerical data types — from peptide‑level abundance to single‑particle retrograde transport velocities — to reveal scaffold interactions (ARMS/Kidins220), modulators (NRH2), and adaptor usage (TRAF6, RIP2) that control signaling fate. Chao values methods that preserve mechanistic interpretability: sparse models, causal inference, and representation learning that highlight biologically coherent modules. Practical goals include prioritizing candidates for perturbation, mapping spatially resolved signaling states, and translating proteomic signatures into predictors of cellular survival, differentiation, or transport defects.

research_interests.research_interest_title: AI and Quantum Computational Tools for Complex Neural Systems
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Chao is eager to explore how AI and emerging quantum computing methods can accelerate analysis and simulation of complex neuronal signaling systems. He is particularly interested in quantum‑inspired optimization and quantum machine learning applied to high‑dimensional numerical problems arising from combinatorial receptor states, stochastic trafficking models (dynein, sortilin), and large proteomic feature spaces. Practical avenues include hybrid classical–quantum workflows for accelerating parameter inference, dimensionality reduction of correlated phosphorylation patterns, and sampling from rugged likelihood surfaces where classical methods stall. Attending the workshop, Chao aims to learn which quantum algorithms and AI pipelines are mature enough to handle his numerical datasets and how they might provide speedups or new conceptual tools for dissecting multiscale neurotrophin signaling.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Atomically Precise On‑Surface Synthesis & Substrate Engineering
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Nestor designs and implements atomically precise on‑surface synthesis strategies to realize tailored graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) and nanographenes. He combines molecular precursor design with substrate engineering—using platforms such as Au(111), Au(322), PdGa, BiAg2/Ag(111) and h‑BN/Ni(111)—to control growth pathways, achieve selective width control via step templating, and enforce substrate‑independent chiral assembly. His work integrates selective halogen activation, regioselective debromination and multistep reaction choreography to transfer chirality and build covalent GNR–porphyrin–GNR hybrids. Chemical functionalization and intercalation strategies (edge NH2, F4TCNQ, AuCl) are exploited to tune doping and decouple ribbons from metal supports. Nestor’s experimental focus is on reproducible synthetic protocols and interface design that enable hierarchical control over structure at the atomic scale for downstream device and spintronic applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Electronic Structure, Spectroscopy and Emergent Quantum/Spin Phenomena
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Nestor investigates the electronic and quantum properties of GNRs and related nanographenes through a combination of high‑resolution STM/STS, ARPES, core‑level spectroscopy and DFT modeling. He systematically studies width‑dependent band gaps, Fermi‑level pinning, effective masses, edge and quantum‑well states, and topological phase transitions that arise from atomistic structure and substrate coupling. His research probes spin excitations, Kondo physics and magnetic anisotropy in single‑molecule devices and covalent hybrids, and develops methods to detect spin‑polarized edge states using ferromagnetic supports. By linking spectroscopy with theory, Nestor elucidates how chemical functionalization, intercalation and substrate choice reshape band alignment and many‑body phenomena, enabling strategies to engineer tunable electronic, topological and spintronic functionality at the nanoscale.

research_interests.research_interest_title: AI/ML for Imaging — CNNs Applied to STM, STS and ARPES Data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Nestor is keen to apply machine learning, especially convolutional neural networks, to extract richer information from STM/STS and ARPES image datasets. He aims to develop pipelines for denoising, super‑resolution and segmentation of atomic‑scale features, automated detection and classification of edge states, chiral motifs, and defects, and regression models to infer band gaps, effective masses or local doping from spatial and spectroscopic maps. Nestor is also interested in building curated, labeled datasets, exploiting transfer learning across substrates and instrument settings, and integrating model uncertainty and explainability to ensure physical interpretability. These ML tools are intended to accelerate experiment‑theory feedback, automate routine image analysis, and reveal subtle correlations in interfacial and spintronic phenomena that are otherwise laborious to detect by eye.

Name: Martin Mikkelsen
Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, University of Copenhagen

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics‑informed neural networks for PDEs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Martin develops and applies physics‑informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve forward and inverse partial differential equations arising in physical and biological systems. He focuses on embedding conservation laws and boundary conditions into neural architectures to shrink the feasible solution space, improve generalization from limited data, and accelerate traditionally expensive numerical solvers. His work includes designing PDE‑aware loss functions, adaptive sampling strategies that concentrate training where errors are largest, and hybrid schemes that couple PINNs with classical discretizations for improved robustness. Martin assesses these methods on benchmark problems and real‑world multiscale applications, emphasizing parameter inference, data assimilation, and uncertainty quantification when observations are sparse or noisy. He prioritizes reproducible implementations and interpretable priors to foster adoption in interdisciplinary teams.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum‑inspired algorithms and many‑body methods
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Martin explores quantum‑inspired algorithms and quantum many‑body techniques as tools for representing and computing with high‑dimensional, strongly correlated systems. He investigates tensor network factorizations, variational quantum algorithms and classical emulations that capture entanglement‑like structure to compress state spaces and reveal latent correlations in data. By translating ideas from quantum simulation—such as operator compression, efficient contraction strategies and entanglement measures—Martin develops methods that can accelerate classical machine learning tasks, improve scalability of simulations, and introduce principled regularizers for model training. His research emphasizes careful benchmarking against conventional approaches, identifying regimes where quantum‑inspired representations offer computational or statistical advantages, and designing hybrid workflows that are practical on current hardware and useful for complex system modeling.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Translational computational genomics and microbiome–metabolism integration
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Martin integrates machine learning with clinical epidemiology, molecular forensics and host–microbiome research to advance perioperative risk stratification and translational biomarker discovery. He applies supervised and probabilistic models to registry‑linked cohort data to evaluate prognostic biomarkers—covering renal injury, metabolic dysfunction and coagulopathy—and links these markers to outcomes, intensive care use, infections and mortality. Concurrently he develops bioinformatics workflows and ML‑driven deconvolution strategies for next‑generation sequencing assays, including mitochondrial genome sequencing and multiplexed barcoding, with emphasis on ISO‑compliant validation and robust uncertainty quantification. In preclinical studies Martin combines multi‑omics and intestinal transcriptomics with representation and causal learning to connect microbial shifts to host metabolic responses under therapeutic interventions, stressing interpretability, reproducibility and clinical translational value.

Name: Bo Milvang-Jensen

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for astronomical inference and uncertainty quantification
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Bo investigates the application of modern machine learning methods to astronomical problems with a strong emphasis on reliable probabilistic inference and bias assessment. Bo is interested in how classifiers and regressors trained on images, spectra, tabular measurements and time series can produce well-calibrated posterior probabilities and predictive uncertainties, and how those outputs degrade under domain shifts such as changing instrument PSFs, noise properties, or wavelength coverage. This interest spans methods for uncertainty estimation (e.g., Bayesian deep learning, ensembles, calibration techniques), approaches to quantify and mitigate selection and training biases, and principled validation on synthetic and heterogeneous real datasets. Bo also explores the practical tradeoffs between model complexity, interpretability and robustness to ensure results are scientifically trustworthy and transferable to non-academic applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Precision multiwavelength survey processing and photometric catalogs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Bo focuses on building and refining deep multiwavelength survey pipelines that produce homogeneous, precision photometric catalogs across disparate instruments and resolutions. Bo develops and applies techniques such as PSF matching, profile‑fitting photometry (e.g., The Farmer), careful background and artifact removal, and consistent flux calibration to enable accurate colors and total flux measurements from optical to infrared bands. A central goal is to deliver robust inputs for photometric redshift and stellar population inference (EAZY/FAST style SED fits) for samples of hundreds of thousands to millions of sources to z≳6. Bo is particularly attentive to propagation of measurement uncertainties, treatment of non-detections, blending mitigation, and systematic error budgets so that downstream scientific constraints on luminosity and mass functions are reliable.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Galaxy evolution, AGN and transient host studies across cosmic time
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Bo studies the assembly and transformation of galaxies and their central engines by combining large photometric samples, targeted spectroscopy, and emission-line surveys. Bo quantifies stellar mass functions, the evolution of star-forming and quiescent populations, and the stellar-to-halo mass relation through abundance matching and clustering analyses. Bo leads narrow-band and spectroscopic programs to improve line flux and redshift accuracy, and conducts extensive GRB afterglow and host spectroscopy to probe metallicity, dust, molecular content, and reionization-era environments. By comparing observations to semi-analytic and hydrodynamical models, Bo seeks to constrain feedback processes, AGN/quasar demographics at moderate to high redshift, and the connection between transient progenitors and their host galaxies across cosmic time.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Unsupervised ML for ARPES spectral discovery
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Anders is focused on developing and applying unsupervised machine-learning approaches to angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) datasets, with the goal of extracting intrinsic surface electronic structure without heavy reliance on hand-labelled data. He explores clustering, manifold learning, and density-based methods to segment high-dimensional spectral maps into distinct electronic phases, surface states, and quasiparticle features. Anders is particularly interested in dimensionality reduction techniques that preserve dispersion relationships and in anomaly-detection algorithms to flag rare or emergent surface phenomena. He also prioritizes robust preprocessing pipelines — denoising, background subtraction, and normalization — that enable reproducible downstream inference. By combining unsupervised representations with physics-informed constraints, Anders aims to accelerate discovery of subtle surface effects and to lower the barrier for large-scale, reproducible ARPES analyses in collaborative experimental environments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Time-series and sequential analysis of pump–probe ARPES
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Anders seeks to apply advanced time-series and sequential-learning methods to time-resolved ARPES and other pump–probe surface experiments, aiming to characterize ultrafast dynamics at surfaces with higher sensitivity and interpretability. He investigates state-space modelling, hidden Markov models, and temporal convolutional and recurrent neural-network architectures to extract lifetimes, relaxation pathways, and non-equilibrium phase transitions from noisy transient spectra. Anders is especially drawn to methods that accommodate non-stationarity and irregular sampling — common in experimental runs — and to approaches for joint spatial-temporal segmentation that reveal where and when transient surface states emerge. He also emphasizes uncertainty quantification and model interpretability so that inferred dynamical mechanisms can be cross-validated against physical expectations and experimental controls. Ultimately Anders aims to build pipelines that translate dense time-series measurements into concise mechanistic narratives for surface electronic dynamics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Translational data-science and reproducible multi-lab pipelines
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Anders is interested in transferring rigorous data-science and longitudinal analysis methodologies from clinical epidemiology and immunology to surface-physics experiments, fostering cross-disciplinary tools for reproducible inference. Drawing on experience with cohort analysis, temporal trend synthesis, and mechanistic immunology experiments, he advocates robust protocols for metadata, batch-effect control, and hierarchical modelling of repeated measurements in experimental campaigns. Anders explores how meta-analytic thinking and causal-inference frameworks can help synthesize results across instruments, sample preparations, and measurement conditions, reducing false positives and improving external validity of ARPES studies. He also aims to build collaborative pipelines that integrate domain-specific physics knowledge with statistical regularization and ML-driven feature extraction, enabling multi-lab aggregation and hypothesis testing. Through these efforts Anders hopes to bridge methodological cultures and accelerate collaborative discovery in surface science.

Name: Daniel Murnane

research_interests.research_interest_title: Collider reconstruction & analysis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel develops and applies statistical and computational methods to confront particle physics models with collider data, focusing on reconstruction and analysis of LHC-style collisions. He builds tools such as ColliderBit to compute collider observables and likelihoods efficiently, enabling convergent Bayesian global fits for composite Higgs and beyond–Standard‑Model scenarios. Daniel emphasizes rigorous treatment of experimental constraints from LHC and LEP, novel fine‑tuning metrics, and transparent quantification of naturalness. His work bridges phenomenology and data analysis by producing open-source, reproducible pipelines that turn detector-level signatures into model-level inferences. He also evaluates how reconstruction choices and detector effects propagate to parameter fits, ensuring that algorithmic advances are assessed in the context of physics reach and experimental realities.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Geometric deep learning for detectors
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel leads and contributes to geometric deep learning techniques tailored for large-scale detector reconstruction and charged-particle tracking. His research combines learned graph construction (GravNetNorm), hierarchical and semi‑equivariant graph neural networks (HGNN, EuclidNet, VecNet), and the Influencer Loss for end‑to‑end condensation to produce robust, efficient algorithms for calorimetry, LArTPCs and tracking. He introduced TrackingBERT tokenization and worked on CUDA fixed‑radius searches and ONNX Runtime C++ inference to make models production‑ready for HL‑LHC conditions. Daniel prioritizes scalability, benchmarking across GPU/TPU platforms, and integration with experiment software stacks like ACTS and ATLAS ITk. The work targets both methodological novelty and deployable performance: demonstrating physics-level metrics under realistic pileup while providing open-source implementations that experimenters can adopt for future detectors.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Language-inspired models for physics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Daniel explores language-inspired models and sequence representations to tackle problems across particle, astroparticle and quantum physics. He frames event reconstruction, particle identification and anomaly detection as tokenization and sequence modeling tasks — leveraging pretraining, fine‑tuning and transfer learning to capture physical symmetries and detector context. Innovations like TrackingBERT demonstrate how transformer-style architectures can encode tracking and hit-level information for downstream classification and reconstruction. He studies interpretability, dataset curation and robustness to domain shift, and evaluates inference cost and latency for realistic deployment. By connecting ideas from NLP (tokenization, attention, self‑supervision) to physics-specific constraints, Daniel aims to create flexible, data-efficient models that improve physics reach while remaining compatible with resource-constrained experiment computing environments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for structured biological data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Marcus applies and develops machine learning methods tailored to structured numerical and multimodal biological datasets. He combines classical supervised and unsupervised techniques with generative models such as variational autoencoders to learn compact, interpretable representations of proteomic, lipidomic and CSF profiling data. His work emphasizes robust preprocessing, feature harmonization, and disentangling biological signal from technical confounds, and he has built automated deep‑learning tools (e.g., AnNoBrainer) to accelerate annotation workflows. Marcus is interested in methods for representation learning, domain adaptation, uncertainty quantification, and scalable model validation that support biomarker discovery and target prioritization. He seeks collaborative exchanges on model interpretability, reproducible pipelines, and how best to integrate structured clinical measurements with high‑dimensional molecular readouts to generate mechanistic and translationally relevant insights.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neuropeptide circuit regulation of arousal and metabolism
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Marcus investigates the neural circuit mechanisms by which neuropeptide signaling coordinates arousal, posture, locomotion and metabolic control. His earlier studies mapped orexin (hypocretin) receptor localization and identified circuit‑specific roles—such as OX2R actions in the tuberomammillary/posterior hypothalamus for wake maintenance and mesencephalic locomotor circuits linking orexin to posture and cataplexy. Complementary projects examine central regulators of energy balance and autonomic function, including ghrelin/GHSR, GLP‑1 and melanocortin pathways, and probe behavioral and anatomical substrates like hippocampal CA1 and prefrontal circuits implicated in attention. Marcus integrates neuroanatomical mapping, circuit manipulations and behavioral assays to define how neuromodulatory systems coordinate arousal and metabolic state, with an eye toward translating mechanistic findings into therapeutic hypotheses for sleep‑wake and metabolic disorders.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Translational therapeutics and biomarker development for proteinopathies
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Marcus pursues translational strategies targeting proteinopathies, with a focus on tau and alpha‑synuclein biology, drug development and biomarker discovery. He has led discovery and preclinical/early clinical development of O‑GlcNAcase inhibitors (e.g., MK‑8719) to elevate tau O‑GlcNAcylation, reduce pathological tau and prevent behavioral deficits in models such as rTg4510. Parallel work connects GBA1 mutations, glucosylsphingosine accumulation and hippocampal alpha‑synuclein vulnerability, motivating glucosylceramide synthase inhibitors that lower glycosphingolipids and alpha‑syn pathology. Marcus also develops translational readouts—large‑scale proteogenomic CSF profiling to identify causal PD proteins and molecular endotypes, PET ligands for alpha‑syn, multiplexed lipidomics, and novel autophagy‑engaging degraders that promote secretion or clearance of pathological species—aiming to bridge mechanistic targets to clinically actionable biomarkers and therapeutics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for inverse nonlinear inference
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Roman explores advanced machine-learning strategies tailored to inverse, nonlinear inference problems that arise in particle physics. He is particularly interested in methods that can map complex, high-dimensional parameter spaces of beyond-Standard-Model theories onto observable signatures while respecting theoretical constraints and uncertainty quantification. Roman champions Kolmogorov–Arnold networks as promising architectures for efficient, interpretable inference and for reconstructing latent model parameters from collider and cosmological data. His work emphasizes integration of physics priors, hybrid analytic–data-driven pipelines, fast surrogate models for Monte Carlo calculations, and diagnostics for robustness and systematic errors. At the workshop he seeks to exchange practical implementations and evaluation metrics with ML experts to translate these algorithms into reliable tools for parameter estimation, model selection, and discovery in fundamental physics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Nonperturbative QCD and proton substructure
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Roman studies nonperturbative and small-x QCD with a focus on revealing the proton's internal landscape and its observable consequences. He develops and applies color-dipole and k_t-factorisation formalisms to exclusive and diffractive processes, quarkonium photo- and electroproduction (including Melosh-spin effects), Drell–Yan phenomenology, and heavy-flavor production. Roman also advances model-independent techniques — Lévy imaging, gluon Wigner/GTMD analyses, and related tools — that have helped uncover proton substructure and provided evidence for phenomena such as the Odderon. Complementing analytic work, he builds Monte Carlo implementations for dynamic color screening and factorization-breaking diffractive mechanisms, aiming to produce predictions that can be tested against current and future collider measurements.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Particle-physics cosmology and multi-messenger signatures
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Roman investigates connections between particle physics and cosmology, focusing on dark-matter candidates and multi-messenger signals of new dynamics. His interests span glueball and technibaryon dark matter scenarios, QCD-vacuum and graviton-mediated dark-energy proposals, and ultralight bosons relevant for strong-gravity phenomenology. He studies phase-transition dynamics in dark sectors and the resulting gravitational-wave spectra from multi-step or strongly first-order transitions, and develops strategies to model and classify these signals for terrestrial detectors. Roman also explores how modern computational approaches — including GANs for waveform libraries and ML-driven searches — can accelerate identification of subtle cosmological signatures and link them back to concrete particle-physics mechanisms.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Time-resolution enhancement for detector signals
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Brigitte develops and applies regression-based deep-learning pipelines (dense networks and convolutional neural networks) to raw detector waveforms to improve time resolution and signal fidelity. She designs architectures that capture temporal structure, performs denoising and deconvolution, and optimizes preprocessing to preserve timing information. Her work emphasizes realistic training using experimental and simulated datasets, careful evaluation of timing jitter and bias, and validation across detector conditions. Brigitte also explores data augmentation, transfer learning between channels, and deployment constraints to make models robust to noise and variations. The ultimate goal is to push the achievable time resolution of nuclear physics detectors, enabling more precise event reconstruction and downstream physics analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Event classification from correlated physics observables
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Brigitte applies classification and pattern-recognition models to combine correlated physics observables for robust event identification in nuclear physics experiments. Using architectures ranging from dense multilayer perceptrons to convolutional networks and ensemble methods, she maps high-dimensional detector features into discrete event classes or labels, paying attention to correlations and physical constraints among observables. Her workflow integrates feature engineering, class-imbalance handling, and cross-validation strategies to ensure generalization. Brigitte evaluates performance with physics-driven metrics (efficiency, purity, ROC curves) and investigates interpretability techniques to link model decisions to underlying detector physics. She also works on multi-task setups that simultaneously classify events and predict auxiliary observables, improving performance and offering richer outputs for subsequent analyses and real-time trigger systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Custom loss functions and physics-aware training
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Brigitte designs and experiments with customized loss functions and training objectives tailored to physics-driven regression tasks, with a focus on improving time resolution and preserving physically meaningful quantities. By incorporating terms that penalize timing bias, emphasize peak alignment, or weight rare but critical signal features, she adapts standard mean-squared or likelihood-based losses into domain-aware objectives. Her approach also includes regularization informed by detector response, uncertainty-aware losses to propagate model confidence into downstream analyses, and differentiable approximations of evaluation metrics so models optimize what matters for physics. Brigitte validates these losses on simulated and real datasets, studying convergence behavior, robustness to noise, and their effects on calibration. The result is better-aligned models that respect experimental constraints and produce outputs that are directly useful for nuclear-physics measurements.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformers, VAEs and Uncertainty-aware ML for Scientific Data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Troels explores modern representation learning with a focus on transformer architectures, variational autoencoders and principled uncertainty estimation for scientific applications. He works on melding information‑bottleneck ideas with hybrid training schemes that combine supervised, self‑supervised and generative objectives to produce compact, interpretable latent spaces. Particular interests include handling variable‑size point clouds (e.g. calorimeter clusters or particle clouds), robust likelihoods for out‑of‑distribution detection, and Bayesian/ensemble methods that quantify model and data uncertainty. Troels develops and benchmarks architectures that keep physics symmetries, support scalable inference and integrate with downstream analysis tasks such as particle identification, anomaly detection and parameter estimation. His approach emphasizes reproducible evaluation on realistic detector simulations and transfer to experimental data with calibrated uncertainties suitable for high‑stakes physics measurements.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Large-scale Optimization and Collaborative GPU Infrastructure
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Troels focuses on the practical and algorithmic challenges of scaling deep learning for large experimental datasets, with attention to optimization strategies and shared GPU infrastructure. He studies optimization at scale — large‑batch schedules, adaptive optimizers, mixed‑precision training, memory‑efficient backpropagation and gradient compression — to accelerate convergence without sacrificing statistical fidelity. Equally important is building and coordinating GPU/cluster resources, containerized pipelines, reproducible experiment tracking and efficient data I/O to support multi‑group collaborations. Troels advocates for tooling and workflows that enable distributed hyperparameter search, fault‑tolerant training, and accessible model serving for analysis teams, bridging the gap between research prototypes and productionized, audit‑ready ML systems for particle and astro‑particle experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Detector Performance, Calibration and Physics-driven ML
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Troels applies advanced statistical and machine‑learning techniques to detector performance, calibration and precision physics measurements. His work spans jet and b‑jet calibration, jet‑energy‑scale and tracking performance studies (including ITk and semiconductor tracker R&D), in‑situ calibration methods and heavy‑flavor/weak‑boson measurements. He integrates ML tools—graph neural networks, deep classifiers and likelihood‑based calibrations—into analyses and searches (supersymmetry, long‑lived particles, exotic Higgs decays), always stressing data‑driven validation and uncertainty propagation. Troels also draws on cross‑disciplinary toolkits he helped develop (e.g., GraphNeT, DeepFRET, metaDMG) to transfer robust, interpretable methods between particle physics, earth sciences and biophysics, ensuring that ML advances concretely improve experimental sensitivity and systematic control.

Contributions.Title: Past Experiences with Machine Learning

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for gene regulatory networks and time-series classification
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Davey applies and evaluates state-of-the-art machine learning methods to problems in gene regulatory network (GRN) inference and time-series mechanism classification. He is interested in moving beyond network reconstruction to use ML for identifying dynamical regimes, classifying temporal expression patterns into mechanistic classes, and extracting interpretable features that link models to experiment. Davey experiments with supervised, unsupervised, and self-supervised approaches, integrating dimensionality reduction, sequence models, and representation learning to separate noise from functional signal in noisy experimental data. He is particularly focused on robust pipelines that can handle high-dimensional, heterogeneous time series from evolving GRN models and on methods that provide mechanistic insight rather than only predictive power. The goal is to make ML tools that both guide experiments and suggest hypotheses about underlying regulatory mechanisms.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Dimensional reduction and dynamical-systems analysis of differentiation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Davey develops and employs dimensionality reduction and dynamical-systems techniques to characterize developmental trajectories and epigenetic landscapes. Working with high-dimensional numerical models of gene expression and epigenetic feedback, he uses methods such as PCA, manifold learning, and tailored projection techniques to reveal low-dimensional structure that governs differentiation dynamics. Davey studies how dimensional reduction clarifies transitions between transient oscillatory states, channeled annealing processes, and rapid quenching into fixed points, and how these reduced coordinates map onto experimentally measurable quantities like expression variance. He prioritizes methods that preserve dynamical invariants and interpretability—enabling comparisons between simulated GRN evolution and experimental single-cell time series—so that reduced representations inform both mechanistic understanding and model selection.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Evolutionary design and origins — robust GRN evolution, habitability and ecology
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Davey investigates how evolutionary processes shape robust cell differentiation mechanisms and explores broader connections to origins-of-life, habitability, and ecological contexts. By evolving gene regulatory networks in silico, he studies selection pressures and design principles that produce robustness to perturbations and reproducible cell-type outcomes under epigenetic feedback. He also links these principles to questions in theoretical biophysics and planetary science: how environmental constraints and early ecological interactions could bias the emergence of regulatory architectures, and what implications network robustness has for the origins, persistence, and detectability of life in varied planetary environments. Davey combines evolutionary algorithms, high-dimensional numerical modelling, and cross-disciplinary theory to propose testable hypotheses that span molecular regulation to ecosystem- and planet-level considerations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Urban climate adaptation and resilience
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Asbjørn investigates how cities can anticipate and adapt to climate-related stressors by blending socio-ecological analysis with practical planning. He studies urban heat, flooding and infrastructure vulnerability through mixed methods that combine fine-grained observational data, stakeholder engagement and scenario modelling. Asbjørn is particularly interested in equitable adaptation pathways that account for differential exposures and capacities across neighborhoods, and in identifying governance arrangements that enable rapid learning and iterative implementation. His work aims to translate complex climate risk information into actionable strategies for planners and municipal decision-makers, emphasising co-produced solutions, cost-effective interventions and metrics for monitoring resilience outcomes over time.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Ecosystem and environmental modelling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Asbjørn develops and applies process-based and data-driven models to understand ecosystem dynamics and biogeochemical cycles in coastal and terrestrial systems. He integrates remote sensing, in situ measurements and model-data fusion techniques to quantify fluxes, biodiversity responses and degradation-recovery trajectories under changing land use and climate regimes. A core concern for Asbjørn is rigorous uncertainty characterisation — using sensitivity analysis, ensemble modelling and Bayesian calibration — to ensure robust inference and reliable forecasts. His modelling informs conservation prioritisation, restoration design and management of natural resources, aiming to provide transparent, reproducible tools that practitioners can use to evaluate trade-offs and long-term outcomes.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Computational methods for data-driven policy
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Asbjørn combines machine learning, network analysis and decision-support systems to translate large, heterogeneous datasets into policy-relevant evidence. He focuses on building reproducible analytical pipelines that integrate administrative records, sensor streams and participatory data to reveal systemic risks and intervention points. By constructing interpretable models and visual analytics, Asbjørn helps stakeholders explore scenarios, assess policy trade-offs and prioritise interventions under uncertainty. He is also committed to open science practices — developing open-source tools, shared datasets and documentation to enable transparent, collaborative policy analysis across disciplines and jurisdictions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: AI-driven materials discovery and generative modeling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Yaping pursues AI-driven materials discovery using generative and foundation models to reveal hidden structure–property relationships in complex two-dimensional systems. Yaping is particularly focused on developing and applying denoising diffusion probabilistic models, GANs, and other generative architectures to augment scarce experimental datasets and to propose novel hypothetical materials and spectra that are physically plausible. Yaping combines machine learning outputs with first-principles calculations and targeted experiments, creating closed-loop discovery workflows that prioritize emergent quantum functionalities. Yaping is interested in robustness to noisy measurements, uncertainty quantification, and interpretable latent representations that connect atomic motifs to macroscopic observables. Yaping seeks collaborations to scale generative proposals into experimentally realizable 2D heterostructures and devices, and to integrate foundation-model techniques for cross-modal transfer between imaging, spectroscopy, and computed properties.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Spectroscopy-driven ML for 2D materials (Raman and spectral data)
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Yaping applies machine learning to structured and spectral data, with a strong emphasis on Raman spectroscopy for rapid identification and characterization of two-dimensional materials. Yaping develops preprocessing pipelines, signal denoising methods, and CNN classifiers tailored to spectral fingerprints while leveraging denoising diffusion probabilistic models and GAN-based augmentation to overcome limited or noisy experimental datasets. By combining automated feature extraction with calibrated uncertainty estimates, Yaping aims to deploy robust, real-time workflows for experimental labs and high-throughput mapping. Applications extend to correlating spectral signatures with strain, ferroelectric order, and compositional heterogeneity in van der Waals heterostructures, and to clinical or imaging contexts where spectral reliability is critical. Yaping is keen to share datasets, benchmarks, and augmentation strategies that improve transferability across instruments and measurement conditions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph neural networks and multiscale modeling of quantum materials
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Yaping investigates graph neural networks and multiscale modeling to capture local atomic environments and non-trivial interactions in quantum and low-dimensional materials. Yaping builds atomistic graph representations from DFT, microscopy, and structural characterization data and trains message-passing architectures to predict electronic, optical, and transport properties while preserving symmetries and physical constraints. A central aim is to bridge atomic- and device-scale descriptions so that insights from GNN latent spaces can inform macroscale materials engineering, such as strain-mediated tuning, ferroelastic coupling, and heterostructure design. Yaping also explores hybrid models that couple physics-based priors with data-driven components to improve interpretability and robustness under sparse experimental sampling. Collaborative interests include integrating GNN outputs into experimental planning, inverse design, and active-learning loops to accelerate discovery of 2D materials with emergent quantum functionalities.
