research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine-learning guided discovery of integrable models
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Xin develops supervised learning frameworks to accelerate the discovery and characterization of integrable models in condensed matter and high-energy physics. By constructing labeled datasets from known integrable and non-integrable systems, Xin trains classifiers and regressors to identify signatures of integrability, predict conserved quantities, and propose candidate Lax pairs or commuting charges. Emphasis is placed on interpretable architectures and feature engineering that map learned patterns back to analytic structures, enabling hypothesis generation rather than black-box predictions. Xin also explores transfer learning across model families and active-learning loops that prioritize simulations or analytic checks for the most promising candidates. The objective is to combine domain knowledge with modern supervised methods to expand the catalogue of tractable models and to provide practical tools for theorists seeking new exactly solvable systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Integrable-model theory for low-dimensional quantum matter
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Xin studies integrable quantum models as a conceptual and quantitative foundation for low-dimensional condensed matter and high-energy problems. Working with spin chains, interacting fermion and boson models, and continuum field-theory limits, Xin applies Bethe ansatz, quantum inverse scattering, and form-factor techniques to compute spectra, correlation functions, and transport properties. Special focus is given to non-equilibrium dynamics, quantum quenches, generalized hydrodynamics, and entanglement growth in integrable settings, with the aim of connecting exact results to experiments in cold atoms, nanostructures, and quasi-one-dimensional materials. Xin also investigates the interplay between integrability and perturbations, mapping out stability regimes and crossover phenomena that inform experimental observables and suggest where emergent integrable behavior may simplify strongly correlated problems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Supervised ML for experimental analysis, reconstruction, and imaging
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Xin applies supervised machine-learning techniques to experimental data analysis and instrumentation problems, translating advances in neural networks and statistical inference into robust workflows for reconstruction, calibration, and background rejection. Drawing on experience with LArTPC signal processing, convolutional networks for cosmic-background suppression, and tomographic imaging, Xin develops supervised models that map labeled detector responses to physical quantities while quantifying uncertainties and controlling systematic biases. Projects emphasize physics-informed architectures, pruning and model-compression strategies for deployable inference, and rigorous validation using simulated and calibration data. Xin's work aims to deliver reproducible, interpretable supervised-learning tools that improve sensitivity in precision measurements and imaging applications across nuclear, particle, and condensed-matter experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Generalizable Deep‑Learning Frameworks for Detector Reconstruction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Aske develops open, detector-agnostic machine learning frameworks that enable robust reconstruction across diverse neutrino telescope geometries. He leads the design and implementation of GraphNeT and GraphNeT 2.0—libraries that unify graph neural networks, transformers, and normalizing flows to process sparse, irregular sensor arrays and time-series pulses. Aske emphasizes modular, reproducible code and multi-task learning strategies so models trained on one detector or simulation can transfer to others with minimal re-engineering. His recent work includes multi-task transformer architectures that jointly perform energy, direction and interaction-type inference while quantifying uncertainty. By prioritizing generalization, instrument independence, and open-source collaboration, Aske aims to accelerate community adoption of advanced deep learning methods for large-scale astroparticle experiments and enable rapid prototyping of algorithms for next-generation observatories.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Novel Signal Modalities and Neutrino Reconstruction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Aske explores unconventional signal modalities and reconstruction strategies to enhance neutrino flavor identification and sensitivity at low-to-intermediate energies. He has proposed and studied a neutron-echo technique that exploits delayed 2.2 MeV gamma emissions from neutron capture to discriminate ντ from νe events at sub-TeV energies, and he integrates such secondary signatures into likelihoods and learned reconstructions. Combining physics-driven ideas with data-driven models, Aske investigates how time-delayed, low-energy depositions and correlated topological features can be fused by graph-based and transformer architectures to improve flavor tagging and background rejection. His approach bridges instrumentation physics and machine learning, seeking practical reconstruction pipelines that can be deployed on IceCube-like detectors to open new discovery channels in neutrino astronomy.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Early‑Life Skin Biomarkers and Translational Dermatology
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Aske applies minimally invasive sampling and multi-omic analysis to identify early-life biomarkers that predict atopic dermatitis and inform prevention. Using skin tape-strip sampling in birth cohorts, he has characterized altered sphingoid-base and ceramide profiles—such as reduced phytosphingosine and shifts in C17/C18/C20 chains—alongside elevated TARC/CCL17 and lower filaggrin-degradation products. He integrates lipid ratios, cytokine signals (IL-8, IL-18), and clinical metadata into predictive models that demonstrate strong accuracy when measured at two months of age, supporting early identification of infants at risk. Aske focuses on translational impact: building robust, interpretable multi-feature signatures suitable for prospective validation and ultimately informing stratified prevention trials that could reduce the burden of atopic disease.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Sterile Neutrinos & Heavy Neutral Leptons (HNLs)
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Oleg develops theoretical and phenomenological frameworks for sterile neutrinos and heavy neutral leptons, connecting particle models to laboratory and cosmological probes. He studies production mechanisms, radiative decays and the implications of sterile states for structure formation and the Lyman‑α forest, and translates cosmological limits into particle-physics parameter space. On the collider and intensity-frontier side Oleg builds reinterpretation frameworks and sensitivity estimates for experiments such as SHiP, NA62, the LHC, FASER and MATHUSLA, clarifying how HNLs could show up across energy and intensity scales. He emphasizes robust constraint synthesis: combining astrophysical, cosmological and accelerator bounds to prioritize search strategies, propose targeted measurements, and guide experimental design toward the most promising regions of HNL parameter space.

research_interests.research_interest_title: X‑ray and Astrophysical Probes of Decaying Dark Matter
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Oleg focuses on observational strategies to detect radiatively decaying dark matter, most notably searches for the putative ~3.5 keV X‑ray line. He has led spatial-profile analyses across galaxies and clusters, and carried out blank-sky, M31, Perseus, Draco and Milky Way studies to test signal consistency and to quantify limits. His work develops robust diagnostics to separate genuine dark-matter-induced emission from astrophysical lines and instrumental artifacts, and maps observational bounds onto sterile-neutrino production scenarios and mixed warm+cold cosmologies. By combining X‑ray spectroscopy with structure-formation and satellite-population constraints, Oleg establishes cross-probe limits and produces concrete recommendations for future missions and observing strategies aimed at resolving ambiguous signals and improving sensitivity to faint radiative decays.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics‑aware Machine Learning, Simulations & Instrument Design
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Oleg develops physics-aware machine learning and novel simulation algorithms tailored to astrophysical and particle searches, embedding physical priors, conservation laws and causal structure to improve interpretability and robustness. He advances methods for instrument diagnostics and signal-background separation that combine principled statistical modeling with ML-driven feature extraction, and he proposes instrument concepts (Xenia, EDGE, LOFT) and observational strategies to maximize discovery reach. In computational plasma physics he has applied and extended algorithms to study chiral magnetohydrodynamics, demonstrating chiral dynamos and inverse cascades relevant for primordial magnetic fields. Oleg emphasizes uncertainty quantification, transferability between simulations and data, and the design of analysis pipelines that inform experiment requirements and prioritize follow-up observations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Lead‑free halide perovskites & low‑dimensional optoelectrics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mailde investigates lead‑free halide perovskites and low‑dimensional bismuth/antimony compounds using density functional and hybrid‑DFT methods combined with experimental crystallography and device characterisation. She performs atomistic analyses of A‑cation effects on polymorphism and dielectric/optoelectronic response across ASnI3 and APbI3 families, and maps how halide and trivalent‑cation substitution tunes band gaps, flat bands, exciton binding energies and spin–orbit contributions in zero‑dimensional Bi/Sb‑based materials. Mailde emphasises energetic stability and predicted photovoltaic limits, deriving design rules that prioritise non‑toxic, stable absorbers for synthesis. By integrating computed electronic structure with CCDC entries and device metrics, she rationalises observed behaviour and directs experimental efforts to promising compositions for photovoltaics and light‑emitting applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Strain‑engineered catalysis and surface alloys
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mailde develops theoretical and computational frameworks to understand how atomic distributions and long‑range strain in alloy monolayers modify catalytic activity. Combining phase‑separation models with DFT descriptors (notably ΔG*OH) she shows that AuxPt1‑x and AgxPt1‑x/Pt(111) surfaces produce competitive strain fields that alter adsorption energetics and enhance oxygen reduction reaction performance. Her hybrid‑DFT studies of (CeO2)6 clusters further reveal adatom‑induced charge transfer, polaron formation and oxidation‑state changes that control redox properties. Mailde links local coordination, noncovalent interactions and strain to experimentally accessible descriptors, guiding surface alloying strategies and surface architectures that balance activity and stability for fuel‑cell and energy conversion catalysts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for multiscale materials discovery
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mailde applies and advances practical machine‑learning approaches to accelerate multiscale materials design by integrating ML with DFT, hybrid‑DFT and experimental datasets. She builds surrogate models for formation energies, band gaps and adsorption energetics, constructs descriptors informed by local coordination and strain, and uses uncertainty quantification to prioritise candidates for high‑fidelity simulation or synthesis. Mailde also mines crystallographic databases (CCDC) to correlate structural motifs with device performance and to interpret experimental structures in light of computed predictions. Her data‑driven workflows enable rapid screening of lead‑free absorbers, alloy surface compositions and interface modifications while maintaining physical interpretability and transferability across chemistries.

Contributions.Title: Machine Learning for Predicting Catalyst Properties in Binary Alloys

research_interests.research_interest_title: Aerosol–Cloud Interactions & Biological Ice‑Nucleating Particles
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Maher investigates the role of biological aerosols as ice‑nucleating particles (INPs) and their influence on mixed‑phase cloud processes across scales. Using immersion‑freezing experiments (LACIS), targeted airborne sampling of Pseudomonas spp. and fragment analysis, he demonstrates that whole cells and fragments retain ice‑nucleating activity and can trigger heterogeneous ice formation in clouds. His work couples laboratory constraints with modeling tests of classical nucleation theory, quantifies bacterial impacts in numerical weather prediction experiments, and implements a novel PBAP emission scheme in the GISS‑E2.1 Earth system model. Maher emphasizes uncertainty quantification and the development of physically based parameterizations to translate microphysical measurements into actionable cloud and radiative effect estimates, seeking to improve representation of biosphere–atmosphere coupling in both regional and global models.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Volcanic Plume New‑Particle Formation and Aerosol Parameterizations
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Maher studies in‑plume aerosol production from volcanic emissions and develops parameterizations for new‑particle formation (NPF) in the free troposphere. Through airborne campaigns at Etna and Stromboli he collects in situ particle size distributions and gas‑phase precursor concentrations, documenting rapid NPF driven by volcanic gases and condensable vapors. These coordinated observational and modeling efforts have produced a new NPF rate parameterization applicable to volcanic plumes, improving estimates of particle number production, transport, and lifetime. Maher integrates these findings into larger‑scale modeling frameworks to assess volcanic contributions to regional aerosol burdens and radiative forcing, while carefully characterizing uncertainties and sensitivities that affect downwind cloud interactions and climate impacts.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Urban Climate, Air Quality and Emulators
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Maher is exploring neural network and machine learning approaches to improve urban atmospheric analysis, air quality forecasting, and efficient emulation of complex climate processes. He is particularly interested in applying ML tools for bias correction, surrogate modeling of subgrid physics, and enhancing predictive skill for urban heat island dynamics, including an upcoming project focused on the Copenhagen metropolitan area. Maher aims to combine physics‑aware architectures, data assimilation, and uncertainty quantification to produce interpretable, robust emulators that can be integrated into regional and Earth system models. His objective is to harness ML to accelerate model runs, improve representation of key physical processes, and support urban sustainability and mobility assessments with higher fidelity and computational efficiency.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Modeling Young Stars and Stellar Environments
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Emilie has a strong interest in the computational modeling of young stellar objects and their immediate environments. For her BSc thesis at the Niels Bohr Institute with Troels Haugbølle she explored how physical processes shape observable properties of nascent stars, combining simulation outputs with statistical analysis to infer key parameters. Emilie is particularly interested in bridging high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations and observational diagnostics, improving model–data comparison pipelines, and quantifying uncertainties that arise from both numerical approximations and incomplete observational coverage. She aims to develop workflows that make it easier to test theoretical predictions against survey data, to identify which physical ingredients most strongly influence early stellar evolution, and to propose targeted observations that can discriminate between competing formation scenarios.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Emilie is keen to learn and apply frameworks that embed physical knowledge and theoretical constraints directly into machine learning models. Motivated by the workshop goal of using physical theories in ML, she wants to explore hybrid approaches that enforce conservation laws, symmetries, and known differential operators—either through bespoke architectures, physics-based loss terms, or constrained training procedures. Emilie is interested in improving generalization and data efficiency by leveraging domain knowledge, reducing unphysical extrapolations, and building models that provide interpretable, physics-consistent predictions. She is also curious about methods for integrating analytic approximations with learned components, uncertainty-aware physics priors, and strategies to validate that physics-informed models remain robust when faced with real observational noise and systematic biases.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Applied ML Methods: Random Forests and Neural Networks
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Emilie has hands-on experience applying machine learning techniques such as random forests and fully connected neural networks to astrophysical problems, which she used in her BSc thesis to model stellar properties. She is interested in systematically comparing classical ensemble methods with neural architectures for regression and classification tasks in astronomy, studying trade-offs in interpretability, calibration, and computational cost. Emilie wants to refine feature engineering strategies for simulated and observational datasets, investigate approaches to quantify predictive uncertainty (e.g., ensembles, Bayesian approximations, dropout), and scale models to larger datasets. Additionally, she is eager to learn best practices for hyperparameter optimization, validation with synthetic observations, and tools to make ML models transparent and trustworthy for the astrophysics community.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformers and Noncommutative Operator Algebras
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Martin investigates conceptual and formal links between transformer architectures and noncommutative operator algebras, aiming to recast self-attention and layer composition as algebraic operations with noncommuting elements. Martin explores how operator-algebraic notions (spectra, commutators, states) can be used to characterize expressivity, generalization, and inductive biases of transformer layers, and how extremization of carefully chosen functionals yields principled architecture constraints or training objectives. Martin pursues variational formulations where optimal attention patterns emerge from extremal principles on operator-valued cost functionals, connecting deep learning practice to rigorous spectral and algebraic tools. This line of work intends to provide mathematical structure for designing architectures that respect noncommutative symmetries and to suggest interpretable regularizers and initialization schemes derived from operator theory.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph Neural Networks and Graph-Theoretic Methods
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Martin develops and applies graph neural networks and graph-theoretic methods to model structured physical systems, seeking representations that respect topology, locality, and symmetry. Martin focuses on message-passing architectures that encode interaction graphs of many-body and quantum systems, using graph invariants and spectral embeddings to improve sample efficiency and extrapolation. Martin investigates how graph structure can be leveraged to learn effective Hamiltonians, reduced dynamics, and coarse-grained operators, and how combinatorial properties (cycles, cuts, centrality measures) inform architecture choices and equivariant layers. Martin also evaluates GNNs as surrogate models for expensive simulations and as components in hybrid physics–ML pipelines, emphasizing robustness to graph perturbations and interpretability of learned edge and node features in physical terms.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Open Quantum Systems, Nonequilibrium Dynamics and Quantum Computing
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Martin studies open quantum systems and nonequilibrium dynamics with an eye toward implications for quantum information processing and noise-resilient control. Martin analyzes Lindblad and non-Markovian evolution, steady-state structure, and transport phenomena, and uses these insights to benchmark decoherence channels relevant for near-term quantum hardware. Martin pursues connections between dynamical extremization problems (e.g., action principles, entropy production minimization) and operational tasks in quantum computing, using variational optimization to design control protocols and error-mitigation strategies. Martin aims to bridge theoretical descriptions of dissipation with data-driven identification of effective models, enabling improved modeling of environment-induced errors and principled strategies to stabilize desired quantum states in nonequilibrium settings.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for disk imaging and anomaly detection
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Rajeeb is focused on translating general ML experience (classification, clustering, anomaly detection) to problems in observational astrophysics. He is particularly interested in applying supervised and unsupervised techniques to au-scale continuum and spectral-line images to identify subtle disk substructure, detect episodic outbursts, and flag kinematic anomalies indicative of embedded companions or accretion shocks. His goals include adapting convolutional neural networks, autoencoders, and domain-adaptation methods to heterogeneous interferometric datasets, developing robust anomaly-detection pipelines for rare events in time-domain surveys, and combining probabilistic models with physical priors to provide interpretable detections. Rajeeb aims to benchmark ML approaches against traditional kinematic and imaging analyses, quantify selection effects, and produce tools that can be applied across ALMA/VLA programs to accelerate discovery while maintaining physical interpretability.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Early disk and planet formation from high-resolution interferometry
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Rajeeb leads observational programs that characterize the earliest stages of disk and planet formation using high-resolution interferometry (ALMA, VLA, SMA). He studies Class 0/I protostellar disks at au-scale resolution to measure Keplerian rotation curves, infer dynamical protostellar masses, and map dust continuum and molecular line distributions. His work emphasizes the surprising differences between embedded disks and more evolved Class II systems—compact, often optically thick dust disks with fewer prominent rings—and seeks to understand how disk warps, annular features, and accretion streamers shape early planet-forming environments. Rajeeb also investigates multiplicity and circumbinary architectures, very-low-mass protostars near the brown-dwarf regime, and observational signatures of episodic accretion, leveraging multiwavelength surveys to connect disk structure with early planet-formation pathways.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Radiative transfer, chemistry and kinematic modeling of protostellar disks
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Rajeeb combines radiative transfer and chemical modeling with kinematic analyses to interpret molecular line and continuum observations of embedded disks. He uses tools such as RADMC-3D and NAUTILUS to model dust thermal structure, vertical settling, resolved two-dimensional snow surfaces, and CO snowlines, and to predict molecular abundances and line excitation in the presence of viscous heating and radial drift. By forward-modeling observations, he extracts dynamical masses, measures disk temperature and density profiles, and constrains grain-size populations through chemistry-sensitive tracers. Rajeeb also explores how shocks (SO, SiO), accretion streamers, and episodic heating events alter observable chemistry and kinematics, with the larger aim of linking physical and chemical initial conditions to outcomes for planet composition and demographics.

Name: Florian Sickert
Seniority/Role: Master student, Earth and Climate Physics

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics-aware ML for Ocean Simulations
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Florian is interested in machine learning approaches that explicitly respect the physics of ocean dynamics for use in simulation and forecasting. He wants to explore methods that embed conservation laws, boundary conditions and known PDE structure into learning algorithms so that learned surrogates remain stable and physically consistent. Key topics Florian plans to investigate include physics-informed neural networks, hybrid models that couple neural nets with numerical solvers, operator-learning approaches for mapping between fields, and strategies to enforce mass/energy conservation and stability across scales. Because ocean processes are multiscale, nonlinear and often sparsely observed, Florian is especially keen to understand how physics-aware models generalize outside training regimes and how to constrain them to produce interpretable, robust predictions for his master’s thesis work at KU.

research_interests.research_interest_title: State-of-the-art Machine Learning Methods
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Florian aims to identify and master contemporary ML architectures and training strategies that are most relevant for environmental and ocean physics problems. Although his ML experience so far comes from coursework, he wants to learn how to apply convolutional and recurrent models, transformers, graph neural networks for irregular meshes, operator-learning frameworks (e.g., DeepONet, Fourier Neural Operators), normalizing flows for probabilistic modelling, and Koopman-inspired linearization methods. He is also interested in practical topics such as transfer learning, domain adaptation, regularization techniques that incorporate prior knowledge, and evaluation metrics tailored to physical systems. Florian’s goal is to build a toolbox of methods and best practices so he can select, adapt and rigorously evaluate state-of-the-art ML approaches in the context of his master’s project.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Computational Tools, Surrogates and Data Assimilation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Florian is focused on computational strategies that make ML useful in real-world environmental physics workflows, including surrogate modelling, reduced-order modelling, and data assimilation. He wants to learn how to construct efficient emulators for costly ocean models, couple ML surrogates with existing simulation pipelines, and integrate learned components within data assimilation frameworks so observations can correct and constrain model states. Uncertainty quantification, interpretable diagnostics and computational efficiency are priorities: Florian wants methods that provide calibrated error estimates and can run within limited compute budgets. For his thesis at the University of Copenhagen, he seeks practical guidance on implementing end-to-end workflows, benchmarking surrogates against numerical solvers, and designing experiments that demonstrate robustness and utility for environmental decision-making.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine-assisted analytic calculation and verification
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mattias explores using machine learning as a generator of educated analytic guesses that are then subjected to rigorous symbolic or numerical verification. He is particularly interested in workflows where ML models propose compact ansätze for amplitudes or low-energy constants and conventional analytic checks—symmetry constraints, series expansions, and exact identities—quickly accept or reject candidates. This hybrid approach leverages the observation that verifying an exact result is often far cheaper than discovering it, allowing ML to accelerate searches over large functional spaces while preserving the exactness required in field-theory calculations. Mattias works on integrating ML proposals with automated algebraic simplification, constraint enforcement (unitarity, crossing), and reproducible verification pipelines so that candidate solutions can be certified and incorporated into downstream EFT and lattice analyses.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Automated amplitude computation and low-energy effective field theory
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mattias develops automated and mathematically rigorous tools for low-energy particle phenomenology, focusing on chiral perturbation theory, nonlinear sigma models, and effective-field-theory constraints. He builds flavour-ordering algorithms and software that generate tree-level amplitudes with many external legs and higher-derivative operators, and extends structural properties such as double-soft theorems and stripped-amplitude uniqueness. On the phenomenological side he derives NLO and NNLO results—three-pion scattering, scheme-dependent three-particle K-matrices, and one-loop six-meson amplitudes for QCD-like symmetry classes—and formulates NNLO positivity bounds that translate analyticity, unitarity and crossing into efficient inequality systems. Across these efforts Mattias emphasizes automation, reproducibility, and interfaces between continuum theory, mathematical constraint solving, and the numerical inputs used in precision physics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Energy-landscape modelling of gene regulatory networks (CELLoGeNe)
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mattias builds energy-landscape frameworks to map Boolean gene regulatory networks into asymmetry-free energy functions that reveal attractors, transition paths, and reprogramming barriers. His CELLoGeNe approach constructs visualization and stochastic-analysis tools to explore multistability and noise-driven transitions, making it easier to identify attractor basins and roadblocks to cellular reprogramming. He emphasizes mathematically controlled mappings, numerical sampling, and software that permits reproducible exploration of high-dimensional landscapes. By combining logical models with energy-based diagnostics, Mattias aims to bridge qualitative network structure and quantitative stochastic dynamics, providing interpretable metrics for stability and control that can inform both theoretical studies and experimental design in systems biology.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Heavy Neutral Lepton phenomenology and experimental recasts
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jean-Loup develops detailed theoretical and phenomenological studies of Heavy Neutral Leptons (HNLs) with an emphasis on realistic model assumptions and experimental reinterpretation. He performs full recasts of collider limits (for example ATLAS HNL searches) within two‑HNL neutrino‑oscillation frameworks, demonstrating that simplified assumptions can misestimate sensitivities by orders of magnitude. His work integrates spin correlations and multivariate classifiers to design discriminants (e.g. Majorana versus Dirac hypotheses) and to assess oscillation resolution in displaced and prompt signatures. Jean-Loup consistently ties theory to experiment by producing cross sections, efficiency parameterizations and simulation cards so that recasts are reproducible, and he produces sensitivity projections for facilities ranging from SHiP and NA62 to the LHC and future muon colliders.

research_interests.research_interest_title: HNL–ALP interactions and novel collider signatures
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jean-Loup explores the phenomenology arising from couplings between Heavy Neutral Leptons and axion‑like particles (ALPs), identifying novel and experimentally clean search channels. He investigates how HNL‑ALP interactions modify decay topologies and propose distinctive final states such as multi‑jet plus dilepton channels with displaced or semi‑displaced components that can evade standard searches. His analyses quantify signal kinematics, backgrounds and projected sensitivities, providing strategies to isolate these signals with realistic detector effects. By connecting model building, detailed simulation and experimental reach, Jean-Loup shows where existing searches have blind spots and where targeted analyses or dedicated triggers could open discovery potential for coupled feebly interacting sectors.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Open tools, reproducible forecasting and machine learning for FIPs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jean-Loup places strong emphasis on community tools and reproducibility: he develops and releases public software (SensCalc/senscalc) for unified sensitivity estimates across experiments, and supplies ancillary simulation cards, cross sections and efficiency maps to enable faithful recasts. He regularly produces sensitivity forecasts for a broad set of facilities using common frameworks so results are directly comparable. Complementing phenomenology, Jean-Loup contributes to machine‑learning methodology for small data regimes — notably ensemble distillation (BabyLlama) to improve sample efficiency on limited corpora — and applies advanced classifiers (BDTs) in analyses. He also coordinates community efforts through workshop reports and white papers to standardize approaches to feebly interacting particles.

Name: Chamilla Terp
Affiliation: Master student at The Cosmic DAWN Center

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for galaxy classification and regression
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Chamilla applies and adapts machine learning methods to classify and quantify properties of galaxies observed during cosmic dawn. With practical experience in clustering algorithms and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Chamilla builds models to identify morphological features, emission-line signatures, and subtle spectral patterns in JWST imaging and NIRSpec spectra. Beyond classification, Chamilla explores regression techniques to predict physical parameters such as stellar mass, star-formation rate, ionization state, and Lyα damping strength, while emphasizing uncertainty quantification and cross-validation. Chamilla also investigates transfer learning and hybrid approaches that combine physics-driven models with data-driven inference, aiming to produce interpretable, robust tools suitable for heterogeneous, noise-dominated high-redshift datasets. The ultimate goal is to integrate these ML tools into reproducible pipelines and public code releases that accelerate discovery and enable rigorous statistical comparison with simulations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Epoch of Reionization overdensities, Lyα emission and DLA diagnostics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Chamilla focuses on the properties and environments of z ≈ 5.5–8 galaxies to understand how early overdensities shaped reionization topology. Using a new Lyα damping parameter developed in their work, Chamilla separates intrinsic emission strength, intergalactic medium neutral fraction, and local H I column effects to interpret both strong Lyα emitters and pervasive damped Lyα absorption (DLA) systems. Chamilla analyses statistical trends showing that LAEs preferentially trace low-metallicity, UV-faint systems while DLAs occur across diverse properties but preferentially at very early, metal-poor epochs. By combining large archival samples, targeted case studies, and spatial clustering measurements, Chamilla probes connections between massive H I reservoirs, proto-cluster environments, and the timing and patchiness of reionization, providing observational constraints that challenge and refine cosmological simulations of early galaxy assembly.

research_interests.research_interest_title: JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, data pipelines and public catalogs
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Chamilla develops end-to-end spectroscopic workflows for assembling and analyzing large archival JWST datasets (e.g., JWST-PRIMAL, DAWN/JWA-Spec). Chamilla designs reduction pipelines and novel diagnostics to extract, flux-calibrate, and quality-assess NIRSpec spectra, and is committed to releasing spectra, software, and catalogs to the community. These tools enable consistent measurements of line ratios, Lyα damping, and continuum properties, which Chamilla uses alongside SED fitting and FIR constraints to infer stellar masses, ages, gas fractions, dust-to-gas ratios, and escape fractions. By standardizing products and metadata, Chamilla aims to make high-redshift spectroscopy reproducible and accessible, to streamline follow-up strategies (including ALMA FIR line searches), and to provide benchmark datasets that facilitate robust comparisons with theoretical models and future surveys.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Heavy Neutral Leptons & Low‑Scale Leptogenesis
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Inar develops a unified, quantum-kinetic framework for heavy neutral leptons (HNLs) and low-scale leptogenesis that connects resonant leptogenesis and baryogenesis via neutrino oscillations. Inar's work systematically investigates νMSM dynamics and the generation, survival and washout of late-time lepton asymmetries through freeze‑in and freeze‑out processes, explicitly including magnetic-field effects and chiral-anomaly contributions. Inar derives robust theoretical constraints from tree-level unitarity and charged-lepton-flavor-violation searches, mapping how viable HNL parameter space can extend into the TeV–PeV window. Inar also explores the cosmological consequences of HNL-driven scenarios for dark matter production and for early-universe plasma dynamics, producing precise, testable predictions that guide which regions experiments and cosmological probes should prioritize.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Collider Phenomenology & Reinterpretation Tools
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Inar builds practical reinterpretation tools and analysis-ready resources that translate collider searches into realistic constraints for multi-HNL and hidden-sector models. Inar supplies ancillary Monte Carlo cards, efficiency parametrizations and reconstruction prescriptions tailored to ATLAS, LHCb, NA62, SHiP and general-purpose LHC analyses, and demonstrates how realistic multi-HNL spectra can relax published limits by orders of magnitude. Inar develops strategies to distinguish Dirac versus Majorana HNL signatures, to resolve tiny oscillation splittings at intensity-frontier experiments such as SHiP, and to project sensitivity to neutralinos and other hidden-sector states. Inar's contributions emphasize reproducibility, experiment-theory synergy and prioritized search recommendations for experimental collaborations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Gravity, Inflation & Dark‑Matter Production
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Inar explores gravitational portals and inflationary model-building with direct implications for dark-matter genesis, studying Einstein–Cartan gravity as a mediator to dark sectors and developing variants of Higgs-driven inflation (Palatini, Einstein–Cartan, Higgs–Dilaton). Inar investigates nonperturbative post-inflationary dynamics via lattice preheating, quantifies scalar-decay uncertainties relevant for reheating-era particle production, and assesses how these processes affect relic abundances and small-scale cosmology. Inar also examines how combined theoretical constraints (unitarity, flavor violation) and cosmological bounds restrict model space, producing cross-disciplinary predictions that connect high-energy model-building to observational and experimental tests.

research_interests.research_interest_title: ML for Data Analysis Optimization
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Yasmine is interested in using machine learning to optimize and streamline data-analysis workflows in experimental solid-state physics. She focuses on identifying bottlenecks where ML can reduce manual effort and increase throughput, such as automated pre-processing, feature extraction, and experiment-planning. Yasmine is particularly curious about methods for pipeline optimization (including hyperparameter tuning and automated model selection), active learning to prioritize costly measurements, and uncertainty quantification to make ML-driven decisions reliable. She values reproducibility and scalable solutions that integrate with existing analysis tools, and she is keen to learn how others balance automation with domain oversight to maintain physical interpretability and robust error estimates in the analysis chain.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Deep Learning for Image-based Solid-State Characterization
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Yasmine applies convolutional neural networks to image analysis tasks in solid-state physics and wants to deepen and broaden this work. Her interests include using deep learning for microscopy image segmentation, defect detection, phase identification, and quantitative feature extraction from experimental images. She is curious about practical aspects such as transfer learning from related imaging datasets, data augmentation strategies for small experimental datasets, and methods to extract physically meaningful features from learned representations. Yasmine also wants to explore ways to combine deep models with physical constraints so that image-based predictions remain consistent with known material properties and experimental conditions.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Exploration and Evaluation of Machine-Learning Methods
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: As someone relatively new to machine learning beyond CNNs, Yasmine is eager to explore and critically evaluate a broad range of ML methods relevant to solid-state physics. She wants to learn comparative strengths and limitations of supervised, unsupervised, and probabilistic approaches; classical algorithms vs. modern deep architectures; and physics-informed or hybrid models. Her priorities include practical benchmarking workflows, strategies for model interpretability, approaches for handling limited or noisy experimental data (e.g., transfer learning, domain adaptation, and Bayesian methods), and guidelines for selecting appropriate methods for different analysis goals. Yasmine hopes to adopt best practices from others to make principled choices when expanding her ML toolbox.

research_interests.research_interest_title: High-resolution X-ray instrumentation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Takashi develops and refines high‑resolution X‑ray spectrometers and beamline instrumentation that push the limits of energy resolving power and real‑time capability. He designs slit‑less flat‑field and Rowland spectrometers, varied‑line‑spacing gratings, triple‑path collectors and stabilized beamline environments to enable E/ΔE >10,000–30,000 and atmospheric‑pressure operation. His instrumentation work also includes liquid flow and spectro‑electrochemical cells, depth‑selective hard‑XPS setups and high‑throughput detector integration. Takashi combines optical and mechanical innovation with calibration, alignment protocols and instrument modeling to extract subtle electronic and vibrational signatures from weak signals. These advances translate into clearer site‑selective measurements across liquids, interfaces and functional materials, and provide robust platforms for coupling experiment with theory and advanced analysis methods.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Chemical physics of liquids and interfaces
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Takashi investigates chemical‑physical phenomena in liquids, solutions and interfaces using site‑selective X‑ray spectroscopies to reveal local bonding, hydrogen‑bond networks and vibrationally mediated dynamics. His work on water explores temperature and isotope dependence, bimodal tetrahedral versus distorted motifs, core‑hole dynamics and associative hydroxide states, connecting spectroscopic signatures to microscopic heterogeneity and breakdowns of simple molecular‑orbital pictures. Takashi applies valence and core spectroscopies to solvated ions, acids, proteins and layered interfaces to probe in‑gap or charge‑transfer states that govern reactivity and electronic function. He routinely integrates DFT, MD and semiclassical Kramers‑Heisenberg simulations with experiment to disentangle electronic, magnetic and vibrational contributions, enabling targeted insight into catalysts, electrocatalysts and 2D materials.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for detectors and spectra
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Takashi is interested in applying machine learning to detector images and spectral data to accelerate interpretation, denoise weak signals and discover hidden correlations across heterogeneous experiments. He seeks collaborations to adapt supervised, unsupervised and physics‑informed learning approaches to tasks such as spectral deconvolution, peak finding, background subtraction, image‑based artifact removal and multivariate fingerprinting of site‑selective signals. By combining ML with instrument models, ab initio simulations and experimental error propagation, Takashi aims to produce robust, interpretable models that respect spectroscopic physics and can operate on high‑resolution datasets from slit‑less and Rowland spectrometers. He welcomes partnerships to benchmark algorithms, curate labeled datasets from beamlines, and integrate real‑time inference into stabilized beamline workflows for automated feedback and adaptive experiments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Kinetic Astrophysical Plasmas & Radiation Diagnostics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jacob studies kinetic plasma processes in relativistic astrophysical flows and their observational signatures. He investigates magnetic-field generation by Weibel-type and mixed-mode instabilities, kinetic Kelvin–Helmholtz dynamics in shear flows, and in-situ particle acceleration tied to current filaments, contrasting electron–proton and pair-plasma regimes. His work connects small-scale, sub-Larmor magnetic turbulence to jitter radiation and follows spectral evolution through field growth, trapped-electron effects, and the crossover to synchrotron limits. Jacob applies these physical insights to interpret time-dependent spectra and polarization from GRB prompt and afterglow emission, AGN jets and laboratory experiments, emphasizing what specific kinetic signatures would be measurable by present and future instruments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: High-order Numerical Methods & Scalable PIC Frameworks
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jacob develops and validates high-order, scalable numerical frameworks for kinetic plasma simulation and coupled radiative diagnostics. His methodological contributions include the photon–plasma high-order PIC code, a trans-Debye hybrid PIC–Monte Carlo framework for GRB wakefields, and optimal particle merging/splitting via k-means clustering to control computational load while conserving invariants. He emphasizes verification against analytic limits, multi-model comparisons from MHD to full kinetics, and efficient parallel scalability and load balancing for large-scale runs. Jacob also explores resistive reconnection, chaotic island dynamics, and the numerical requirements needed to resolve non-Fermi acceleration mechanisms and polarization signatures robustly across models.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Structured Scientific Data & Graph Learning
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Jacob is interested in applying machine learning to structured numerical data (including images and grid outputs) and to representations built from graph data for problems across astrophysics, climate science and geophysics. He focuses on methods that respect underlying physics and conservation laws: physics-informed architectures, uncertainty-aware regression/classification, and graph-building strategies that convert spatial–temporal simulation outputs into meaningful graph topologies for downstream learning. Jacob explores feature engineering for spectral and polarization diagnostics, optimal data reduction (e.g., informed particle merging), and interpretable models that can accelerate parameter inference, surrogate modeling, and multi-model comparison while preserving diagnostic fidelity for observational prediction.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for many- and few-body physics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Luuk investigates how a broad palette of machine learning techniques can be applied both directly and indirectly to problems in many- and few-body physics. He does not commit to a single algorithmic family; instead he assesses method–problem fit, exploring supervised and unsupervised learning, physics-informed models, surrogate emulators for expensive simulations, and probabilistic approaches for uncertainty quantification. Practical goals include accelerating many-body simulations, extracting low-dimensional collective coordinates, automating phase classification, and improving experimental parameter estimation in few-body scattering and bound-state problems. Luuk emphasizes interpretable models and robust validation against known physics, seeking workflows that combine domain knowledge with flexible statistical learning to yield reliable, experimentally actionable insights.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Quantum optics and cold atomic gases
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Luuk studies quantum optics and ultracold atomic gases with a focus on emergent many-body phenomena and controllable light–matter interactions. His interest spans experimental and theoretical perspectives: designing and probing quantum simulators, characterizing non-equilibrium dynamics, and leveraging coherent control to realize tailored Hamiltonians. He is particularly interested in measurement techniques and the information they provide about correlations, entanglement and collective modes, and how that information can feed back into model refinement. Luuk also explores connections between controlled atomic platforms and broader condensed-matter problems, using cold atoms as clean testbeds for concepts that range from few-body bound states to strongly correlated many-body phases.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Participatory visual methods and scientific communication
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Luuk cultivates an interdisciplinary practice that combines participatory landscape design, photography, and computational visualization to bridge scientific work and public or stakeholder understanding. Drawing on experience with collaborative workshops, site-specific design, and visual narrative projects, he is interested in co-creative processes that surface multiple perspectives and translate complex data into intuitive, place-sensitive representations. In the context of physics, this extends to crafting visualizations and interactive tools that help experimentalists, modelers and non-experts reason together about system behavior, experimental design, and research priorities. Luuk values methods that are dialogic, reproducible, and that respect local knowledge while leveraging computational techniques for exploration and communication.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for materials design
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Lidiia applies machine learning to accelerate materials design, focusing on predictive modeling and inverse design workflows that connect structure, composition and functional properties. Lidiia builds surrogate models, ensembles and active learning loops to reduce experimental load and guide high-value experiments. Lidiia emphasizes interpretable ML and uncertainty quantification so that model suggestions can be trusted by experimentalists; Lidiia explores feature engineering from domain-aware descriptors and graph-based representations for crystalline materials. In collaborative projects Lidiia integrates physics-informed constraints and multi-fidelity data to improve generalization across synthesis routes. At the workshop Lidiia seeks methods to better couple ML-driven hypotheses with lab workflows, and to identify opportunities for cross-disciplinary collaboration that translate models into tangible materials improvements.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Photoluminescence analysis of perovskites
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Lidiia studies photoluminescence (PL) of perovskite materials using data-driven analysis to unravel recombination pathways, defect states and stability trends. By combining time-resolved and steady-state PL datasets with statistical and machine learning tools, Lidiia extracts latent features that correlate with degradation mechanisms and optoelectronic performance. Emphasis is placed on automated preprocessing, denoising and feature extraction pipelines that can handle heterogeneous spectroscopy formats across labs. Lidiia also develops methods to integrate PL measurements with complementary characterization (e.g., XRD, microscopy) to build multi-modal fingerprints for rapid materials screening. Through these efforts, Lidiia aims to make PL experiments more quantitative and predictive, enabling faster iteration between materials synthesis and device evaluation.

research_interests.research_interest_title: NLP & LLMs for scientific insight extraction
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Lidiia explores natural language processing and large language models (LLMs) to help researchers extract insights from complex scientific data and literature. Lidiia develops pipelines for automated literature mining, structured data extraction, experimental protocol standardization and semantic search across heterogeneous sources. Particular interests include domain-adaptive fine-tuning, prompt engineering to elicit reproducible scientific summaries, and approaches to quantify model confidence and hallucination risk in technical contexts. Lidiia is interested in combining LLM outputs with structured knowledge graphs and downstream analytical tools so that extracted insights can feed into modeling and experimental planning. At the workshop Lidiia hopes to learn practical strategies for integrating LLMs into materials research workflows while maintaining traceability and reproducibility.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Fast generative simulation for particle detectors
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Erik explores fast generative models to accelerate high-energy physics simulations while preserving the fidelity needed for background and detector-response studies. Building on GEANT4 reference simulations used in LDMX and ATLAS ITk work, he investigates conditional generative approaches — including normalizing flows, GAN variants, and diffusion models — to reproduce photon interactions, veto responses, and subtle detector features at orders-of-magnitude speedup. He places emphasis on explicit uncertainty quantification and physics-driven validation so surrogate models remain trustworthy for sensitivity estimates and systematic studies. Erik is interested in conditioning on beam-energy scenarios (e.g., LCLS-II 8 GeV), integrating surrogates with downstream analysis, and defining metrics that validate physics observables rather than only low-level image similarity. The goal is deployable fast simulators for large-scale studies, rapid detector design iterations, and online emulation.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Edge ML and FPGA-embedded inference for experiments
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Erik focuses on running ML inference on FPGAs and embedded platforms to meet tight latency, power, and reliability constraints in experimental environments. He studies hardware-aware optimizations such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and works with high-level synthesis flows that translate compact networks into logic- and memory-efficient implementations. His interests include compiling GNNs and tree-based approximations into FPGA fabric, building low-bitwidth generative components for fast simulation, and ensuring deterministic timing for trigger and DAQ systems. Erik evaluates trade-offs between accuracy, resource utilization, and throughput while considering radiation tolerance, thermal limits, and maintainability of deployed firmware. The practical aim is robust toolchains and ML models that can be integrated into front-end electronics and embedded controllers used in detectors and industrial maintenance systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Detector reliability, QA and predictive maintenance
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Erik works on detector reliability, systematic quality assurance, and predictive maintenance using ML and statistical approaches. Drawing on thermal-cycling certification for ATLAS ITk Strips and preventive maintenance studies for rolling bearings, he develops data-driven acceptance criteria, anomaly-detection pipelines, and lifetime-prediction models that combine detailed simulations with in-situ sensor data. He leverages graph neural networks to capture spatial correlations across module networks and boosted decision trees for interpretable failure-risk scoring and feature importance. His approach emphasizes rigorous validation protocols, stress-testing, and traceable diagnostics that feed manufacturing QC and operational scheduling. The goal is to increase operational continuity, reduce costly failures, and provide actionable, scalable QA pipelines for large-scale experimental systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformers for Spatiotemporal Climate Modeling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mattis develops transformer-based approaches tailored to spatiotemporal climate modeling, focusing on numerical gridded datasets and long-range dependencies. He adapts attention mechanisms to respect spatial structure and anisotropic scales in atmospheric and oceanic fields, experimenting with patching, hierarchical attention and multi-resolution inputs to capture phenomena from synoptic storms to seasonal cycles. Mattis evaluates transformers as fast, accurate surrogates for high-resolution simulations and for skillful forecasting and downscaling, while addressing challenges of training stability, computational cost and interpretability. He integrates physical priors and embedding layers that preserve conservation properties and grid geometry, and explores pretraining strategies on large reanalysis ensembles to improve transfer across regions and variables. The goal is scalable, physics-aware transformer models that improve climate prediction and accelerate numerical experimentation.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Climate Processes
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mattis works on physics-informed machine learning methods for fundamental climate processes such as convection, boundary-layer dynamics and ocean mixing. He designs hybrid architectures that couple differentiable components of numerical solvers with learned parameterizations, embedding conservation laws, symmetries and known PDE structure as hard or soft constraints. This approach improves stability, reduces physically implausible predictions and increases generalization across regimes not seen during training. Mattis investigates ways to quantify and propagate uncertainty arising from both numerical discretization and learned components, and develops diagnostics that reveal when the ML components violate physical constraints. By marrying domain knowledge with flexible function approximators, Mattis aims to produce interpretable, robust models suitable for use in climate model development and policy-relevant impact studies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Numerical Data Engineering & Assimilation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Mattis focuses on numerical data engineering and assimilation techniques that make large climate datasets usable for machine learning. He develops preprocessing pipelines for heterogeneous sources—satellite retrievals, reanalysis products and model outputs—harmonizing differing grids, temporal sampling and error characteristics into consistent training sets. Mattis applies advanced data-assimilation ideas to combine observations with learned priors, designing loss functions and emulators that respect observation operators and uncertainty covariances. He also researches scalable storage, batching and augmentation strategies for high-resolution 3D+time tensors, and methods for handling missing data and nonstationary measurement biases. The end goal is reproducible, uncertainty-aware datasets and interfaces that allow ML models, including transformers and physics-informed networks, to be trained efficiently and deployed reliably in climate applications.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine‑learning–driven symbolic and foundation-model tooling
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Matthias develops and applies modern machine‑learning paradigms — from transformers and foundation models to symbolic regression and genetic programming — to accelerate and interpret computations in perturbative QFT. He uses transformer-based models and large-code/self-supervised paradigms to propose analytic ansätze, automate algebraic manipulations, and generate candidate integrand simplifications. Symbolic-regression and genetic-programming pipelines are exploited to discover compact closed-form expressions, conjecture relations between special-function bases, and identify useful change-of-variable heuristics. In practical workflows Matthias integrates ML suggestions with domain constraints (symmetries, branch-cut structure, transcendental weight) to produce human-interpretable results, and he refines traditional IBP and reduction heuristics through learned priors. His approach emphasizes transparency and verifiability: models propose hypotheses that are then validated by exact analytic or numeric checks, closing the loop between statistical inference and rigorous mathematical proof.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Algebraic and geometric structures of multi‑loop integrals
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Matthias investigates the algebraic-geometry and motive-theoretic origins of multi-loop Feynman integrals, with a focus on elliptic and higher Calabi–Yau geometries that appear beyond multiple polylogarithms. He analyzes elliptic double-boxes, infinite elliptic ladders, and examples leading to K3 and Calabi–Yau threefold families, extracting the underlying modular and period structures that control analytic continuation and functional identities. Building on symbol technology, he formulates extensions such as elliptic “symbol prime” constructions and Schubert-inspired bootstraps to encode iterated integrals on elliptic and higher-genus domains. Matthias combines explicit integration techniques, momentum-twistor rationalizations, and insights from integrability to classify letters and monodromies, aiming to produce systematic bases of special functions and to map how geometric invariants determine perturbative amplitude data.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Bootstrapping amplitudes, form factors and integrability
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Matthias pursues bootstrap and integrability approaches to compute high-loop amplitudes and form factors, particularly in planar N=4 SYM, and to connect these results to physical observables. He bootstraps multi-loop form factors and scattering amplitudes to very high loop orders, uncovers antipodal dualities, and formulates an operator-product expansion for form factors with novel transition kernels. Using on-shell methods and the Quantum Spectral Curve he extracts dilatation operators and computes thermal/Hagedorn data. His work blends bootstrap constraints with explicit checks from direct integration and IBP-refined computations, and he explores how these theoretical advances inform precision collider and gravitational-wave applications, for instance by classifying post‑Minkowskian geometries. Collaboration and cross‑fertilization with numerical and ML techniques are central, enabling him to push analytic results to regimes previously inaccessible by brute force.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neural networks for high-redshift simulations
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhen investigates the application of neural networks to extract physical quantities and patterns from cosmological simulation outputs of high-redshift galaxies. He focuses on building regression and classification models that take structured numerical fields — 3D distributions of density, temperature, metallicity — and time-series galaxy properties like stellar mass and star formation rate, to predict observable signatures and latent physical parameters. His interests include developing emulators to accelerate expensive hydrodynamical simulations, applying convolutional and volumetric neural networks to capture spatial correlations, and leveraging transfer learning and data augmentation to bridge simulation and observational domains. He aims to use data-driven models both to discover subtle signatures of early galaxy formation that may be missed by traditional diagnostics and to provide rapid surrogate models for parameter inference and forward-modeling in comparison with observational surveys.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Graph neural networks for merger trees
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhen pursues graph-based representations to capture the hierarchical and relational nature of galaxy formation. He is particularly interested in applying graph neural networks (GNNs) to merger trees, halo-subhalo networks, and spatial neighbor graphs constructed from simulation particles or halo catalogs. By treating galaxies, halos and their progenitors as nodes with time-evolving attributes and mergers or spatial links as edges, he explores architectures that learn dynamical evolution, predict descendant properties, and identify assembly-driven signatures in the first billion years. This work emphasizes permutation-invariant representations, handling variable node counts, and integrating physical priors such as conservation laws. He also investigates methods for mapping GNN outputs to observable quantities to facilitate direct comparison with high-redshift surveys and to flag interesting progenitor pathways for targeted simulation follow-up.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Interpretable, physics-aware ML for observation comparison
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhen aims to bridge large-scale hydrodynamical simulations and observations with interpretable and physics-aware machine learning. He emphasizes uncertainty quantification, interpretability, and causal reasoning so that ML discoveries can be trusted by astrophysicists. His interests include developing physics-informed neural networks, Bayesian neural networks for calibrated error estimates, saliency and feature-attribution techniques tuned for 3D fields, and surrogate models that preserve physical constraints. He also prioritizes domain adaptation and synthetic-to-real transfer techniques to ensure robustness against simulation systematics when comparing to JWST and other high-redshift observations. The goal is to extract testable hypotheses about early galaxy formation, provide diagnostic visualizations to guide theory, and create ML-augmented pipelines that accelerate simulation-experiment cycles while maintaining physical interpretability.

research_interests.research_interest_title: ML-driven state estimation and anomaly detection for optoelectronic devices
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhiping focuses on applying probabilistic and machine‑learning state‑estimation methods to monitor and diagnose OLEDs and luminescent devices in real time. He leverages time‑series modelling, Bayesian filtering, and recurrent/temporal neural networks to fuse electrical, optical and environmental sensor streams, aiming to estimate hidden device states such as exciton populations, trap densities, and degradation modes. A key objective is robust anomaly detection and uncertainty quantification to flag early signs of performance roll‑off, material phase changes, or fabrication defects that compromise EQE, lifetime, or color purity. Zhiping emphasizes interpretable models and calibrated confidence measures so that predictions can guide targeted experiments and process interventions, accelerating failure analysis, in‑line quality control and the translation of lab‑scale chemistries into reliable, manufacturable devices.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Interpretable graph learning for molecular design of luminescent emitters
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhiping explores graph‑based machine learning to uncover chemically interpretable motifs that govern multi‑resonance TADF, chiral emission, and organometallic phosphorescence. By combining graph neural networks, subgraph attribution methods and motif discovery, he seeks to identify structural patterns—such as heteroatom placement, tetraborated cores, steric interlocks, or chiral clusters—that control oscillator strengths, singlet–triplet gaps, and electric–magnetic dipole alignments linked to dissymmetry factors. His approach integrates high‑throughput quantum calculations and experimental labels into active‑learning pipelines for inverse design, prioritizing candidate scaffolds with clear synthetic feasibility. The emphasis on interpretability ensures that the extracted graph features map directly to actionable synthetic strategies and device‑relevant properties, enabling principled exploration across color tuning, narrowband emission and circularly polarized light emitters.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Image‑based ML for photophysical characterization and device diagnostics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Zhiping develops image‑analysis and computer vision approaches to extract mechanistic insight from hyperspectral EL/PL maps, CPL imaging, microscopy of aggregates and device thermal maps. He applies convolutional and transformer‑based models for segmentation, feature extraction and anomaly detection to localize emissive hot spots, quenching sites, morphological heterogeneities and chiral domains in films and devices. Coupling image features with physics‑informed priors allows interpretable attribution of how mesoscale morphology and microstructure influence FWHM, color purity and g‑factors. These tools are designed for both lab diagnostics—rapidly correlating microscopic defects with macroscopic device metrics—and scaled workflows for process optimization, enabling automated feedback between imaging, synthesis, and device fabrication to accelerate robust, high‑performance optoelectronic development.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Label-free magnetic levitation and microfluidic single-cell separation
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Esra develops and applies magnetic levitation and hybrid microfluidic platforms for noninvasive, density-based single-cell analysis and continuous sorting. Her work focuses on force-balance engineering that gently separates cells and microparticles by exploiting differences in density and hydrodynamic drag, enabling applications such as isolation of low-density cancer cells, sensitive detection of adipogenic differentiation, and levitation-enabled tissue biofabrication. Esra emphasizes throughput and accessibility—achieving continuous sorting at practical flow rates while preserving viability for downstream assays—and translates these principles into compact, low-cost devices suited for point-of-care diagnostics and bench-to-bedside studies. She is interested in improving sorting efficiency, integrating downstream functional assays, and validating label-free metrics against biological ground truths to expand adoption in adipogenesis research, circulating tumor cell capture, and translational biophysics.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Lensless holographic imaging and automated image analysis for portable diagnostics
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Esra designs and integrates lensless digital inline holographic microscopy with magnetic levitation (HologLev) to create compact, affordable systems for density readouts and live-cell monitoring. She works on automated image-processing pipelines that reconstruct holograms, segment levitated objects, and extract quantitative features related to mass, shape, and dynamics at single-cell resolution. A key aim is to make image analysis robust to variations in hardware and sample conditions so that compact devices produce reproducible, user-friendly outputs for non-expert operators. Esra seeks computational strategies that reduce manual annotation, accelerate reconstruction and feature extraction on low-power hardware, and translate visual readouts into actionable biological metrics for diagnostics, longitudinal culture monitoring, and rapid phenotypic screening.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning for small, noisy time-series and live-cell imaging data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Esra is keen to explore machine learning approaches tailored to experimental biophysics problems characterized by limited labeled data, noisy measurements, and temporally resolved signals from live-cell imaging and sorting experiments. She is interested in pragmatic strategies—transfer learning, self-supervised pretraining, data augmentation, few-shot learning, denoising autoencoders, and Bayesian uncertainty estimation—that improve robustness and interpretability in low-data regimes. Esra also prioritizes temporal models and feature engineering for time-series derived from cell dynamics, and practical pipelines for model validation, cross-lab generalization, and integration with existing experimental workflows. Her goal is to learn which ML tools can deliver incremental, reproducible gains in the lab and to establish collaborations that pair experimental assay design with appropriate modeling choices.
