research_interests.research_interest_title: High-resolution basal-melt mapping
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Ann-Sofie focuses on developing and applying high-resolution remote-sensing approaches to map basal melt and resolve fine-scale channelized melting on polar ice caps and Antarctic ice shelves. She pioneered a Lagrangian framework that combines 2 m REMA strips with CryoSat‑2 altimetry to produce 50 m basal-melt maps, revealing pinning-point control, coastal channels and melt channels previously unresolved at coarser scales. Her work demonstrates that channelized melt can be 42–50% higher when resolved, with important implications for incision, breakthrough timing and ice-shelf vulnerability. By documenting rapid channel development on George VI Ice Shelf linked to ocean warming and ENSO, and coupling observations with melt modelling, she clarifies coupled melting and fracturing processes that inform monitoring, targeted field campaigns and refined sea-level projections.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Inversion methods for ice-thickness and velocity
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Ann-Sofie develops and critically evaluates inversion and estimation methods to derive ice thickness and surface velocity from remote sensing and physical constraints. She has produced and compared five approaches — SIA inversion, the semi-empirical SEITMo, PISM iterative inversion, velocity-based inversions and Monte Carlo sampling — validating outputs against Operation IceBridge and using results to support drill-site selection. SEITMo in particular demonstrated strong computational efficiency, enabling rapid sensitivity testing and probabilistic assessments. Her comparative analyses identify strengths, limitations and resolution-dependent biases of each approach, and she integrates uncertainty quantification and validation workflows to produce robust, scalable pipelines that inform observational design, model development and risk assessment for Arctic and Antarctic ice studies.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine learning and open Earth-observation workflows
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Ann-Sofie explores machine learning techniques and open Earth-observation workflows to accelerate detection, mapping and uncertainty quantification in cryospheric science. Working with imagery and structured data, she integrates Landsat-derived velocity fields, REMA products, CryoSat‑2 altimetry and Google Earth Engine to generate high-resolution diagnostics. She investigates supervised, semi-supervised and physics-informed ML methods to detect melt channels, fuse heterogeneous inputs, estimate rates and reduce inversion runtimes while maintaining physical plausibility. Emphasizing reproducible, open-platform pipelines and computational efficiency, she seeks to bridge ML advances with climate-physics knowledge so that scalable tools can support monitoring, rapid assessment of vulnerability and improved inputs for sea-level projection models.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Passive GNSS-based Time Synchronization and TDoA
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Timotej investigates passive time synchronization and single-record time-difference-of-arrival (TDoA) measurement techniques using broadband satellite and GNSS signals across L-, X- and Ku-bands. He develops and evaluates methods that estimate clock bias and time transfer via direct cross-correlation, relative pilot code phases, and common-view approaches, aiming for sub-nanosecond alignment without relying on disciplined oscillators or wired links. His work emphasizes practical deployment for distributed receiver networks and radar arrays where cable synchronization is infeasible, focusing on ADC front-ends, signal preprocessing, and robust estimation under multipath, Doppler and frequency-dependent delays. Timotej benchmarks computational cost, hardware requirements and the trade-offs between passive approaches and dedicated timing hardware, exploring limits of accuracy, reliability in noisy environments, and strategies for calibration and uncertainty quantification to enable scalable, cost-effective time alignment for real-world sensing systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Machine Learning for Numerical Time-Series Classification
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Timotej researches machine learning and signal-processing pipelines for classification of numerical time-series, with a focus on broadband time signals used in sensing and communications. He explores feature extraction, time- and frequency-domain representations, deep architectures (CNNs, temporal convolutional networks, recurrent units) and hybrid models that combine physics-based preprocessing with learned components to improve accuracy and robustness. His interest centers on building classifiers that operate in real time and cope with variable sampling rates, synchronization offsets and limited labeled data through transfer learning, augmentation and self-supervised approaches. Timotej also assesses model interpretability, failure modes and dataset biases, quantifying risks such as overfitting to simulation conditions, sensitivity to noise or adversarial perturbations, and computational cost, with the goal of delivering practical, generalizable classifiers with calibrated uncertainty for experimental and field deployments.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Optical Biophysics and Real-time Brewster Angle Microscopy
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Timotej studies optical biophysics with an emphasis on real-time imaging of thin films and interfacial processes using Brewster angle microscopy and complementary optical methods. He investigates the dynamics of monoclonal antibody film reconstitution after mechanical stress at the air–liquid interface, developing imaging protocols, polarization-based contrast enhancement and quantitative image-analysis workflows to extract surface phase behavior, film thickness variations and kinetic rates. His research integrates optical instrumentation design, time-resolved imaging and careful control of interfacial conditions to capture fast phenomena while minimizing perturbation of delicate biological films. Timotej examines experimental uncertainty sources such as thermal drift, surface contamination and alignment, and creates reproducible metrics and automated analysis tools that link microscopic optical signatures to macroscopic biophysical function in pharmaceutical formulations and soft-matter systems.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Neutrino oscillations and low-energy detector sensitivity
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Rasmus studies atmospheric neutrino oscillations with a focus on low-energy sensitivity enabled by IceCube DeepCore and the forthcoming IceCube Upgrade. He works on translating the hardware improvements — denser string spacing, multi-PMT modules, and enhanced calibration devices — into quantifiable gains for oscillation parameter measurements in the GeV range. His work spans improved simulation of the denser detector geometry, optimized event selection for low-energy tracks and cascades, and reconstruction methods tuned to the higher channel multiplicity. By combining detector-specific modeling with statistical analyses of oscillation signatures, Rasmus aims to deliver updated sensitivity forecasts and robust analysis pipelines that exploit the Upgrade’s capabilities while managing new systematic and computational challenges introduced by the expanded instrumentation.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Transformers for long-sequence detector data
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Rasmus explores transformer-based architectures tailored to the long, sparse, and irregular time-series data produced by neutrino telescopes. He investigates how attention models can ingest long readouts from thousands of PMT channels, capture subtle temporal correlations across wide time windows, and integrate spatial geometry and per-channel metadata. His work includes experimenting with efficient attention variants, hierarchical and chunked encoding strategies, geometry-aware positional encodings, and hybrid architectures that combine convolutional front-ends with transformer blocks. The goal is to boost reconstruction accuracy and classification performance for rare neutrino events while keeping inference and training costs tractable for large-scale IceCube datasets, including partially constructed detector epochs and future high-channel-count configurations.

research_interests.research_interest_title: Novel attention mechanisms and scalable reconstruction algorithms
research_interests.research_interest_long_description: Rasmus is interested in developing novel attention mechanisms and scalable algorithms that address the computational bottlenecks of high-channel-count detectors. He focuses on sparse and structured attention patterns that exploit detector topology, multi-PMT grouping, and event-level sparsity to reduce memory and latency without sacrificing physics performance. His research also covers differentiable surrogate simulators, uncertainty-aware reconstruction, and scalable training strategies (mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, data-parallel pipelines) to enable deployment in production analysis chains. By designing attention and reconstruction components matched to the IceCube Upgrade’s instrumentation, Rasmus aims to make end-to-end simulation, selection, and reconstruction feasible for next-generation datasets while preserving sensitivity to subtle astrophysical and oscillation signals.
